public_statements.boeing:
We said we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were all ready. We've done the work to get here: the development programmes we had in front of us are done, and the balance sheet is back where it belongs. So today we are launching a new Boeing single-aisle airplane.

We're planning for entry into service in 2040, and that plan has headroom built into it. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We won't build airplanes ahead of a mature design. We'll work the certification plan with the FAA from day one. We'll develop this airplane with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On engines, we've asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to bring us their best. CFM is our baseline, and we want more than one source of supply on this airplane.

Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs decide our rates. Debt stays first in our capital allocation. I'm not going to give you any more dates today. The financials will follow our production performance. We still have a lot of work to do.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. On that basis, Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. We prepared it through a decade of technology roadmaps, and we are launching it now because those technologies are mature, not to meet anyone else's calendar. We target entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Customers have been well served by a choice of engines on the A320 family, and the same will apply to its successor. We have selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and we invite all three to join the programme as risk-sharing partners. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up and continued work to secure our supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We will fund the programme with financial discipline, as disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. A stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry is built on one well-prepared programme at a time.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Nothing new has launched yet in the narrowbody. When it does, our customers decide the aircraft and the timing, not us, and we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM is launching a new ducted engine programme, so that every airframer has a CFM engine to choose on whatever comes next. CFM is also partnering with Embraer, putting a CFM engine in front of a third airframer. And at GE we're launching a GEnx upgrade for the 787 and the airlines that fly it.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded. But it's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. If an airframer launches a new narrowbody now, the open fan won't be ready for it, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with which engines. We won't give you dates our testing hasn't earned. You'll get them when it has. We'll fund this within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is. We want to be on all the critical platforms that matter in the decades ahead. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Bad news first. For too long the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF, and the fleet comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the fleet, and no new programme takes parts or engineers away from that work. We control what we can control.

Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, sole source or shared, on standard commercial terms. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch: 2036 for a 2030 commitment, and no earlier. Every life-limited part will be at full life at entry into service, and durability will be validated in severe-environment testing before then. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

We are making no Joint Venture commitment this round. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates; those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it, in the round it selects it. Not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit once its commitment is on the record. Widebody is our core, and we will not put it at risk. We won't do anything not profitable. We don't commit that easily; when we commit, we deliver.

boeing.move: Engine competition with CFM as the baseline
boeing.detail: We invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the new airplane under code 7. CFM is the baseline launch engine and certifies first. A P&W or Rolls-Royce engine follows in sequence once it shows maturity and durability [BX-1298]. CFM must be able to support both our rates and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Goal: two or three engine sources on our narrowbody and three narrowbody engine makers in the market.

boeing.move: Certification plan with the FAA from day one, and no production-certification concurrency
boeing.detail: We agree a transparent certification plan with the FAA before detailed design freezes. We build no production airplanes ahead of a mature, certifiable design [BX-1263, BX-1309]. We blame no one: we own the schedule [BX-1323].

boeing.move: No fixed-price development
boeing.detail: Development contracts with suppliers and partners are cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed-price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

boeing.move: Balance sheet first in capital allocation
boeing.detail: Debt repair stays first [BX-1305, BX-0556]. I recommend to the Board no shareholder returns and no new equity until we are solidly investment grade; the Board reserves both decisions. The $10B of undrawn revolvers stays undrawn.

boeing.move: 737 MAX and 787 customer commitment
boeing.detail: Production stability on the 737 MAX and 787 lines comes first, gated by KPIs. The new airplane is built for commonality with the 737 fleet so that our customers' transition is planned, not forced [BX-1273, BX-1274].

airbus.move: Public invitation to engine makers to share risk on NGSA
airbus.detail: Airbus has selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7) and invites all three to bring a new narrowbody engine to NGSA as risk-sharing partners, with entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. This supports the enabler (dual or triple sources, three narrowbody engine makers). It is unpriced, and it is a recommendation only, as the Board noted.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for the A320 family ramp
airbus.detail: Continue to bring critical work packages in-house and to de-risk titanium and rare earths for our own production system [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063]. This is aimed only at our own disciplined and controlled ramp-up. It is not aimed at any rival's supply chain.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy through industry coalitions
airbus.detail: Keep working with industry partners, Boeing included, for a tariff-free aerospace trade regime [AX-0088, AX-0046].

cfm.move: Offer a CFM engine to every airframer on every new narrowbody
cfm.detail: This is H1: we refuse no airframer and lock none out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. The offer is a LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine, as each customer chooses. No price or terms are stated in public: CFM narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

pratt_whitney.move: Public conditional GTF2 offer on standard terms
pratt_whitney.detail: Pratt & Whitney will commit GTF2 in any round an airframer selects it, sole or shared source. It is ready six years from launch (2036 for a 2030 commitment, no earlier), with all life-limited parts at full life at entry into service and durability validated in severe-environment testing first. Standard commercial terms: no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The offer books no selection and names no airframer date.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: Continued insertion of the Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet, charged on standard commercial terms and not given away [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. It has no effect on the game board. The fleet comes first [PX-0080].

rolls_royce.move: Open door to Pratt & Whitney on the Joint Venture
rolls_royce.detail: Our preferred route is a partner. We commit to the Joint Venture once P&W's commitment is on the public record. This round there is no commitment and no terms.

boeing.move: Supplier readiness: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
boeing.detail: We fund lagging suppliers and keep them running above our rate, and we hold buffers [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043]. Priorities: (1) engines, since LEAP-1B is the 737's sole source and engines have bound the line before [B-1449]; (2) any supplier flagged on the supplier-shortages KPI [B-2283]. The ladder: embed staff, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire. With Spirit in-house since December 2025 [BG-0064], we control the 737 fuselage.

boeing.move: Stage-gated governance of the launch
boeing.detail: Before the full Board votes, the Aerospace Safety Committee reviews the launch with the Chief Engineer's readiness view. After launch, each development stage gate is KPI-based, with no subjectivity [BX-1259]. If the plan has to move, we reset it once, conservatively, never in serial slips [BX-1318, BX-1321]. No launched programme is ever cancelled (H5).

boeing.move: Workforce: retain, train before we build, hire in stages
boeing.detail: One enterprise retention incentive [BX-1314]. We train before we build [BX-1258]. Engineering hiring is staged toward a peak around 2038-39, since the risk case prices talent poaching and supply-chain bottlenecks at 5 pp for 5 years from EIS.

airbus.move: Certify NGSA engines in sequence, with CFM as the anchor
airbus.detail: This is Wagner's mitigation for the unpriced load of integrating three engines. CFM integrates and certifies first, and the other makers follow in sequence, as on the A320neo. Shared engineering teams are protected for the A320 rate and A350F absorption.

airbus.move: Engine-code review at the 2035 round
airbus.detail: Keep code 7 unless the 2035 bulletin shows that P&W or Rolls-Royce has not launched, or has an engine that is off track for a 2037 entry into service. In that case, remove that maker only. The change is never made in reaction to Boeing.

airbus.move: Payout guardrail during NGSA development
airbus.detail: This is Toepfer's condition. Shareholder returns stay inside the stated 30-50% payout range, with no equity raise. If ramp cash stays near the FY2025 level, returns are kept at the lower end of the range in 2030-2036 rather than drawing on net cash. The $35.52B programme charge at entry into service is reported beside the cash view. No internal long-term-plan targets are disclosed.

cfm.move: CFM partner consultation on the Ducted and Embraer launches
cfm.detail: Both CFM orders go through CFM governance with Safran. Consent is assumed, with stated reasons. The Ducted keeps both airframers' next aircraft on a CFM engine, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally. Embraer puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer, which fits 'serve every airframer'. The record shows no Safran position, so none is asserted. GEnx is GE alone and needs no gate.

cfm.move: Supply-base readiness for a three-project stack (FLIGHT DECK reviews)
cfm.detail: Ali's condition is taken up. GEnx upgrade work is paced behind the Ducted's development peak; GEnx counts no earlier than 2042 without a Re-engine. Monthly operating reviews cover the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. LEAP OE delivery and spares come first, and spares never crowd out OE [CX-0529]. The trigger to drop Embraer and GEnx is a supply 'no' from Ali on field data.

cfm.move: Cross-functional design and test gates on the Ducted
cfm.detail: Every Ducted design and test gate is a cross-functional call, never one person's [CX-0012]. Durability is not traded for fuel burn or schedule [CX-0208]. The 2036 ready year stays inside the company until a turn-on, turn-off test backs it [CX-0009].

cfm.move: Keep RISE funded as technology and set the gates for the 2035 product call
cfm.detail: There is no cancel and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. Ali's milestones must be in hand by the 2035 round: (1) the ground and flight test done; (2) compact-core durability turned on and off, with the HPT dust testing closed; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. The product call is made in 2035, on the bulletin and these tests.

cfm.move: Fund the package inside the capital allocation framework
cfm.detail: The package needs about $1.0B a year of new R&D and strain ($0.67B Ducted plus $0.33B strain) against about $2.5B of room. Returns stay at or above 70% of FCF [CX-0645], and the A-range balance sheet is held. Any unbudgeted spend comes out of buybacks, not the dividend or the rating. That is analyst context only, per Ghai.

pratt_whitney.move: Ring-fence the fleet's parts and engineering from GTF2
pratt_whitney.detail: This is Eddy's condition, adopted. If GTF2 is triggered, its test hardware and later production ramp take no castings, forgings or powder-metal disks from the GTF fleet's AOG recovery or from Hot Section kit insertion. The fleet durability team stays ring-fenced, GTF2 is staffed from the GTF Advantage engineering pool [PX-0351], and the pacing parts are reviewed weekly. If anything gives, the date moves, not the testing.

pratt_whitney.move: 2035 cancel test written into the plan (Mitchill's corrected form)
pratt_whitney.detail: This applies only if GTF2 is triggered this round. In 2035, cancel it (write-off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, saving $0.33B) only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code, and only if the 2035 brief's hold row does not beat its cancel row at Mitchill's weights. The test is NOT the literal 'no selection': that would kill a ready GTF2 in exactly the column where it earns its +10 pp. A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036 and cannot be cancelled after 2035.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture review trigger for 2035
pratt_whitney.detail: Re-test `jv_with_rr: commit` on the 2035 grid if Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. The tests are Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233]. A live GTF2 would fold in and count toward our $2B share.

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan before EIS (Watson)
rolls_royce.detail: Applies only if the conditional order triggers. Partner MRO agreements on our Singapore Joint Venture model signed by 2034. The first partner shop inducting engines and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology) in place by 2036. That is ahead of an entry into service no earlier than 2037. Narrowbody work goes only to high-performing suppliers. The gate dates are internal and inference, and are not disclosed.

rolls_royce.move: Funding plan if triggered (McCabe)
rolls_royce.detail: $8B over 7 years, about $1.14B or £0.84bn a year for 2030-37, funded from free cash flow. Buybacks give way first. The 30-40% dividend payout is untouched. No equity, no borrowing for distributions, leverage nowhere near 1.5x, and net cash positive throughout.

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline
rolls_royce.detail: No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, and value is remunerated on a win-win basis [RX-0081, RX-0097].

boeing.public_statement:
We said we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were all ready. We've done the work to get here: the development programmes we had in front of us are done, and the balance sheet is back where it belongs. So today we are launching a new Boeing single-aisle airplane.

We're planning for entry into service in 2040, and that plan has headroom built into it. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We won't build airplanes ahead of a mature design. We'll work the certification plan with the FAA from day one. We'll develop this airplane with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On engines, we've asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to bring us their best. CFM is our baseline, and we want more than one source of supply on this airplane.

Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs decide our rates. Debt stays first in our capital allocation. I'm not going to give you any more dates today. The financials will follow our production performance. We still have a lot of work to do.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: fps launch_10yr with fps_engine_code 7; rate_737 hold; re787 hold. This is the plan I framed (plan B), and both test memos recommend it.

1. MY RULINGS ON H1 AND H3 FOR 2030, IN WRITING, WITH EVIDENCE.
- H1 (no fps in Round 1) is LIFTED for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and an unrepaired balance sheet [B-2326, BX-1305], and all of them have closed:
  - the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550] and turns cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547];
  - MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026 [BX-1873]. The brief reports no certification trouble, so I treat both as done (inference);
  - debt repair is complete on the GM's tracker: net debt reaches $0 at end-2029 (base) and end-2030 (stress), with no new programme;
  - in July 2026 I said we needed about two more years to be financially ready, with a launch expected around 2029-2030 [BG-0068];
  - the three work streams have converged [B-2303, BX-1296]. Market: the narrowbody demand is there, and Do Nothing loses $3.64-6.26B if Airbus moves. Boeing: finances repaired, and Pope confirms engineering can carry one clean-sheet development. Technology: GTF2 and UltraFan NB, if launched on selection, are ready in 2036 and 2037, and CFM is always ready.
  - The lift is conditional, and every condition has passed: Malave's buffer and fundability tests and Pope's readiness results.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) no longer binds as a hard rule. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and that has closed. I still HOLD the Re-engine on four grounds:
  - the Board's -$1B Downside limit: it adds -3.58 in S3 and S4;
  - my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239];
  - company doctrine (profile §11.4: keep the 787 a cash source, no Re-engine before 2036);
  - the premium: holding it costs $0 in my expected column.
  H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind (earliest EIS 2037). H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no certification trouble.

2. THE TEAM RULE.
- Malave's buffer test (slip leg = S5, the brief's Risk case; floor = Do Nothing's -3.64 less $2B = -5.64):
  - plan B passes at -0.78, $4.86B above the floor;
  - every via-Embraer row fails ($11.83-13.94B below the floor). That veto binds and I accept it.
- Pope's KPI veto does not bind: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. It is moot anyway, since I hold the rate.
- Everything else is my call.

3. THE GRID. Board items are the fps launch and the engine code that rides with it. rate_737 and re787 sit at their default (hold).

| Plan | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 (expected) | S5 (risk case) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Submitted: fps 10-yr + 787 hold | +3.50 | +0.66 | +0.88 | -1.96 | -0.78 |
| Same with fps at its default (Do Nothing) | 0.00 | -3.64 | -2.62 | -6.26 | -3.64 |
| Value of the launch | +3.50 | +4.30 | +3.50 | +4.30 | +2.86 |

- The launch beats Do Nothing by more than ε in every column, so debt-first passes. The grid already nets the discounted debt penalty; I do not subtract it again. Undiscounted, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B.
- Worst column: -1.96 (S4). In no column does the item lose more than $1B against its default.

4. RAMP: 10-YEAR OVER 7-YEAR.
- Against the 7-year the 10-year is +1.30 / -0.46 / +1.30 / -0.46 / +0.05. It is ahead in three columns, more than ε ahead in two, and behind only by 0.46 in S2 and S4, inside ε. Its mean across the five columns is +0.46 against the 7-year's +0.11.
- In my expected S4 the 7-year is the best grid plan by $0.46B. That is a tie, and the team rule breaks it on doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. Both point to the 10-year:
  - a $4.68B smaller bill and $2.9B less undiscounted debt penalty;
  - a 2036 cash peak of about $8.4B against about $12.5B in 2034;
  - every debt line kept, the stress case included (peak $0.0B). The 7-year borrows $0.7B under stress and is still above zero at the 2035 hold year;
  - three years of headroom against our clean-sheet slip record (787-8: May 2008 to September 2011 [B-0031, B-0526]), and no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263], which is my red line.
- The 7-year's S2/S4 edge and its incumbency in 2040 both exist only if it meets NGSA's 2037 EIS to the year. A three-year slip turns it into the 10-year airplane with a bigger bill. Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].
- Doctrine also points to the 10-year ramp: profile §11.4, "Ramp-up speed: the 10-year ramp".

5. OBJECTIVE LEDGER (Control's mission; it never changes the payoff).
- Debt: plan B reads 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) in every column. The 7-year misses the stress line in every column.
- Incumbency, by my sketch of the public share rules:
  - the 10-year holds 40% or more throughout in S1 and S3, but dips to about 37% in 2040 in S2 and S4 (about 32% in S5). It recovers to about 42% by 2045 and about 47% by 2050 on the 3-year lead rule;
  - the 7-year holds in S1-S4 and dips to about 38% in 2040 in S5.
- In every column the 10-year misses no more objectives than the 7-year: S2/S4 trade one miss for one, and in S1, S3 and S5 the 7-year misses more.
- 50/50 is out of reach for every plan.
- I weigh debt, which is on my own ranked list [BX-1305], above an incumbency gain that depends on a schedule our record says we would not hold.

6. 787 RE-ENGINE: hold.
- It adds +2.20 in S1, S2 and S5 and -3.58 in S3 and S4. That is a bet on an A350 choice we cannot see, and it fails the Board's -$1B Downside limit.
- In S4 holding it costs nothing.
- The cost I accept, unpriced: on the 10-year a 2035 Re-engine would overlap 5 years and break H4, so the next H4-legal round is 2045. Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317], and the 787 stays a cash source. Doctrine, not my record, drives this.

7. RATE INCREASE: hold.
- It adds -0.74 in every column beside the launch, so it fails its business case. Its +2.30 alone needs fps on hold and S1 or S3, and even then it assumes neither new narrowbody is ever launched.
- This is the only round the board offers it, so the deferral is a loss I accept, not a wait.
- It is not a reply to anyone (H6).

8. ENGINE CODE 7: costs nothing on the board.
- On today's record the fitted source at a 2040 EIS is CFM (1).
- If P&W (GTF2, ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce (UltraFan NB, ready 2037) launch on selection this round, both are ready 4 and 3 years before EIS: three sources by 2050 and three narrowbody engine makers.
- Code 7 is in no disallowed pair. Doctrine and my Low-confidence lean were code 3; code 7 keeps CFM as the fallback and serves the supply-stability enabler.

9. PREMIUM (H8): $0.46B, logged.
- What it is: the 10-year against the best S4 plan (7-year), counted in S2 and S4.
- Why: doctrine (higher-confidence plan with headroom, doing less, no concurrency) plus objective (the stress-case debt line).
- Re-engine hold $0, rate hold $0, code $0. Total $0.46B, $1.54B inside the cap.
- What would break it: an expected column of S1, S2 or S5, where the Re-engine hold would read $2.20B. In that case the hold rests on the Board's veto and H-rules, not on doctrine.

10. DEBT PATH, plan B (Malave's reconstruction, matching the brief's cells within $0.05B):
- base net debt $16.5B (2027), $6.7B (2028), $0 every year from 2029;
- stress $18.3B, $11.7B, $3.3B, then $0 from 2030, with at least $2.5B of headroom (2036);
- programme cash: about $3.0B in 2030, rising to about $8.4B in 2036;
- no new equity and no shareholder return in the plan.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Both seats are thin, and I weighed them that way. Malave's record is one call (Low), so I treated his buffer test as binding and the rest of his memo as advice.

Binding: every Solo row passes the slip leg, and plan B sits $4.86B above the -5.64 floor. Every via-Embraer row fails, and I accept that veto.

Advice I adopted:

recommendations.text: Rule on H1 and H3 in writing. Both were written for a round sealed in 2026, and this round is 2030. The record we expect cited: the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027, MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026, and the 777X was due to turn cash-positive in 2029. The CEO said in July 2026 that Boeing needed about two more years to be financially ready. The brief's tracker has net debt at $0 by 2029, and at $0 in the 2030 stress case. If the conditions are met, say so and lift H1. Without that ruling, a launch fails our Boeing-ready test.

Bring one well-founded Solo fps launch, not a bet. Either ramp passes all our tests. They differ by more than ε in S1 and S3 (10-year ahead by $1.30B), so our rule prefers the ramp with the higher worst column: the 7-year (-1.50 against -1.96 in S4). It also enters service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched now. By our reading of the public rules, Boeing then stays at or above 40% of the narrowbody market. The 10-year would leave Boeing near 37% around 2040 if Airbus launches now. If the ExCo prefers the 10-year to keep the stress-case debt line (the 7-year peaks at $0.7B of net debt), we will approve it. Log the $0.46B it gives up in S2 and S4 as objective premium.

No 787 Re-engine this round. It loses $2.48B to $4.51B whenever Airbus re-engines the A350 (S3, S4), beyond our $1B limit. With the 7-year fps it also overlaps development by 5 years. Test it again in the 2035 round, when Airbus's A350 choice is public. A 7-year fps (development 2030-2037) leaves room for a Re-engine launched in 2035 with only a 2-year overlap. A 10-year fps (development 2033-2040) does not.

Treat the Rate Increase as a production call on its own merits. With any fps launch it loses $0.74B in every column; it pays only if neither new narrowbody is ever launched. Bring it only with fps: hold, stable KPIs, an FAA-cleared rate path and a reason that is not Airbus.

Choose fps_engine_code 7 (Rolls-Royce, P&W and CFM). CFM is always fitted, so supply is never left without an engine. The code can trigger P&W's and Rolls-Royce's conditional launches this round. GTF2 would be ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both by either EIS. That gives the brief's three sources on the fps in 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers, against one with Do Nothing. Code 7 is in none of the disallowed pairs, and the code does not change Boeing's payoff. We will ask our Aerospace Safety Committee to review each maker's readiness for EIS.

Show the debt path for the chosen plan, base and stress case, from the brief's objective-metrics table. Keep shareholder returns off and seek no new equity until the rating is solidly investment grade. The Board reserves those decisions.

In the public statement, give a conservative EIS with headroom if fps launches, and no date otherwise. Log every premium. Bring the launch to the Aerospace Safety Committee with the Chief Engineer's readiness view before the full Board votes.

frame.question: Have the three work streams converged by 2030: the market, Boeing's readiness in finances and capacity, and the technology? If they have, I lift H1 and launch one Solo fps. That leaves three questions: which ramp (7-year or 10-year); whether the 787 Re-engine and the 737 Rate Increase stay out of this round; and which engine code gives us a stable supply of engines from more than one maker. The grid, Malave's slip leg (S5) and Pope's readiness results decide this. Airbus's calendar does not.
