pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Bad news first. GTF2 has not yet earned its durability record, and our dates have slipped before. GTF2 is in development for NGSA and fps. It will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before it enters service it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. Those are gates, not claims. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that neither the GTF2 ramp nor any Joint Venture work takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control.

Airbus has invited us onto its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner. We accept on standard commercial terms: we carry our own engine's development, and there is no launch-style discount, no concession and no free upgrade. On fps we follow in sequence once we show maturity and durability. That is the right test, and we will meet it with test data, not with price.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only if and when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change.

We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. Those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit` (row 'GTF2: hold + commit to JV': +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88). It is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and both pass every veto. overrides is empty.

1. Constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- On the board GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps's 2040. Eddy's binding readiness test passes on both.
- Bad news first: the real margin is thinner than the board's. The Advantage slipped about a year, and the company prior for a derivative is +1.5 to 2 years, which would land GTF2 around 2037.5-2038, after NGSA's EIS. My own dates have slipped by one quarter to two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- So I book nothing on the date. The two gates (severe-environment validation, full-life LLPs at EIS) are gates, not claims, and the date moves, not the testing. Mitchill prices a slip past 2037 at up to 21.32 (the S2 outcome). That is a red-line cost, not traded.
- The Joint Venture must not touch GTF2's configuration, team or date (Eddy's conditions b and c).
- Fleet first [PX-0080]: the 2036-37 ramp is the real draw, so it is ring-fenced under the weekly pacing-parts review, and new capacity is qualified before it ships.

2. GTF2: hold.
- The demand is visible: code 7 on both live airframes, on the record [PX-0109].
- Cancel trails hold in every column: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. That is -29.26 at my weights and -29.05 at Mitchill's. It would write off $1.67B to save $0.33B and throw away two selections.
- I do not harvest a programme its customers chose. This is inference from [PX-0064][P-1342]: we reset what has stopped working, and this has not.
- Mitchill confirms hold carries a selected engine, so ground 2 does not reach it.
- From 2036 GTF2's $2B is sunk and the cancel option lapses.

3. Joint Venture: commit.
- My round-1 trigger is met: code 7 on both live airframes includes Rolls-Royce.
- The item against hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51, never negative. That is +0.55 at my weights, +0.44 at Mitchill's and +1.38 at equal weights.
- It needs $0 of new cash: GTF2's $2B equals our share, so the fold write-off is $0 (Mitchill). It beats a buyback, which is about $0 NPV at the 10% WACC.
- I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low). This is company doctrine (profile.md §6, dashboard_game.md §5; [P-1233][P-1676]) plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test as my evidence. I call our GTF partnerships 'critical' [PX-0038].
- Terms: risk and investment shared, never the gear, core or GTF2 technology, which stay P&W modules under P&W design authority.
- Eddy's flag that Rolls-Royce claims favourable geared IP is rebutted in the terms: P&W keeps the gear team and data. No core-technology red-line flag is left standing.
- Architecture loyalty would have kept me on GTF2 alone. The grid says the commit costs GTF2 nothing, so loyalty does not get to cost PV.

4. Veto check.
- Mitchill, ground by ground:
  - ground 1 (dividend or debt): no new R&D; GTF2 cost $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope; dividend covered; debt on its pre-ASR path; no envelope stretch.
  - ground 2 (unselected engine): pass.
  - ground 3 (aggressive terms): standard terms in the Airbus and Boeing answers, no buy-in payment.
  - ground 4 (booking upside): $0 booked on the commit, and nothing is presented as formed.
- His two conditional binding vetoes are respected in the statement and other moves:
  - ground 4: Rolls-Royce's commitment and the formation are not presented as done; the +5.51 is not announced; durability is written as gates.
  - ground 3: no concession, discount, fee or fixed-price development.
- Eddy: both grounds pass on the orders as proposed. His standing conditions (configuration freeze; staffing outside the fleet and validation teams) are written into other moves, so neither is invoked.

5. Red lines.
- No new engine without a committed airframer: GTF2 fired on code 7 selections.
- Shared-source relief on code 7 (NGSA and fps) is declared again, as in round 1. On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference: [PX-0058][P-1292]).

Control what you can control. Both new narrowbodies now carry code 7. NGSA and fps have each selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and our 2030 `launch_if_selected` fired. GTF2 is live and will be ready in 2036, ahead of both entries into service on the record. This is the last round in which GTF2 can be cancelled: it is ready in 2036, and after that its bill is sunk. On the rules it is also the last round in which either airframer can change its code before entry into service, since the next round is 2045 (inference). So I put three questions to the ExCo.

(1) Do we keep GTF2 whole? On the grid, cancel loses in every column, and it would throw away two selections our customers put on the record.

(2) Both live airframes now carry a Rolls-Royce code, so do we put a standing, public Joint Venture commitment on the record, and on what terms? Risk and investment are shared. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay ours.

(3) What protects the code 7 selections? They are worth more than any order on this grid: losing NGSA (S1 to S2) swings 21.32, and losing fps (S1 to S3) swings 11.81. The lever is durability validated before entry into service, not price, and the fleet still comes first.

My usual questions apply. Is the demand visible? It is on the record. Do the business model, timing and volume work? Is durability mature at entry into service? Is this a responsible bet with a responsible payback? Is the dividend safe?

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public):
"Bad news first. GTF2 will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and our dates have slipped before. So we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before GTF2 enters service on NGSA or fps it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. We control what we can control. We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks."

ops.proposal:
PROPOSAL (Eddy, operating seat; Calio decides). gtf2_solo: hold. jv_with_rr: commit, on four technical conditions.

- gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 has been live since the 2030 trigger and is ready in 2036. NGSA (EIS 2037) and fps (EIS 2040) both carry code 7, so it serves two live airframes that include P&W. Hold row, S1-S4: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37. My record says nothing on cancelling. Hold is the default, and company doctrine on a slip is "add testing, do not cancel" (profile §5 row 10). Cancel is flagged to Mitchill and Calio below.
- jv_with_rr: commit. My trigger is met: a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (code 7 on both). The technical tests pass on the board. If it forms in 2035 (S4), the engine is GTF2 by the fold, ready 2036. Item against hold: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51 (brief §3, Mitchill's number). It adds no engineering until it forms. My record has no evidence on a Joint Venture, so this is seat and company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1875]. Conditions:
  (a) The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules, with P&W keeping design authority [P-1233]. Risk and investment are shared as with our collaboration partners [P-1714][P-1744].
  (b) GTF2's configuration is frozen through entry into service. No UltraFan NB content goes into GTF2 before EIS. Merged content comes later as a derivative with its own durability programme.
  (c) Integration is staffed outside the fleet durability team and GTF2 validation.
  (d) The 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test is written in.
  If (b) or (c) fails, I invoke ground 1 or ground 2. A failure of (a) is a company red line, not my ground, and I would flag it at the veto check.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS
1. Orders: as above.
2. GTF2 readiness: ready 2036 (launch 2030 + 6). Margin is 1 year to NGSA 2037 and 4 years to fps 2040.
- Severe-environment validation: I can't give a status. The board carries no test results, and I won't call them done [PX-0112].
- The gates are the Advantage's: endurance testing at representative severe conditions [PX-0128], more than double the original programme's [P-0779], and every LLP at full life at EIS [P-0785].
- On the board there is no slip. The real margin is thinner. The Advantage aimed at mid-2024 and certified in 2025, about a year late. The company prior for a derivative is +1.5 to 2 years (profile §3).
- So 1 year of slip uses up the NGSA margin, and slipping at the prior puts GTF2 at about 2037.5-2038, after NGSA's EIS. fps absorbs it.
- What gives first is the date, and with it our slot at NGSA's entry, not the testing. If that happens we follow on NGSA as Boeing already sequences us.
3. Fleet:
- No 2035 AOG count and no pacing-parts count. I cannot give them. My data stop at 10% AOG in June 2023 [PX-0120], about 350 AOG on average through 2026 with a 600-650 peak [PX-0300][P-1039], and about 30 pacing parts [PX-0123].
- Hot Section kit progress in 2035 is not in evidence. From 2026 the kit carries 90-95% of the Advantage's gains, and it is charged [P-1363][P-1813].
- The 2036-37 GTF2 ramp is the real draw. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062]. So: ring-fence it from the AOG recovery and kit insertion, review pacing parts weekly [PX-0131], and qualify new castings, forgings and powder-metal capacity before it ships parts (contain first, inference) [PX-0121].
4. Joint Venture readiness:
- If it forms in 2035 (S4), it is ready in 2036 through the GTF2 fold. UltraFan NB (2037) also folds, and the earlier date counts. Against 2037 and 2040: pass.
- If it forms in 2045, both airframes are already in service. GTF2 would be about 8 years into service on NGSA and 5 on fps, possibly mid-campaign (prior: 2-3 retrofit campaigns in years 1-5; about 2 years each [P-0895]).
- "One engine" is then a fiction: two certified, fielded engine types and two support chains [P-1875].
- We would share risk on UltraFan NB durability that we never validated. Partners pay their share of defects [P-1563].
- For the 2045 re-test: technical due diligence on RR fleet data, and no draw on GTF2 fleet support.
5. Technical conditions: yes, by module ownership. This is the collaboration model in which P&W is principal and keeps 51-57% [P-1744][P-1747]. Design teams mirror the architecture, so each module's owner keeps that module's team [P-1240]. In 2035 the fold makes one engine (GTF2), with UltraFan NB stopped as a separate product [P-1875]. Staffing outside the fleet and validation teams is my condition. RR claims favourable geared IP [P-2004]: the gear is where IP would cross, so P&W keeps the gear team and data.
6. Engineering load: one programme. GTF2 validation, the ramp and any fold make one engine. Integration is an overlay. The peak is 2035-37. Advice only; the board has no strain charge.
7. Evidence for the airframers:
- For Airbus before 2037: severe-environment endurance results, full-life LLP certification, test-engine teardown findings (inference), and the GTF fleet's kit record.
- For Boeing 2036-40: all of that, plus NGSA field data if NGSA enters on time. The benchmark is about 1M fleet hours to surface issues [P-0847], so that gives about one fix campaign before fps (inference).
- Data on a cadence, not time-on-wing claims. Durability, not price, protects code 7.
8. Vetoes:
- gtf2_solo hold: passes both grounds.
- cancel: neither of my grounds; I propose hold.
- jv_with_rr commit: passes both grounds on conditions (b) and (c).
- Option D: neither of my grounds. Its Joint Venture engine is ready 2037 through the UltraFan fold, zero margin to NGSA (advice).
- Disclosure draft: passes. 2036 and no earlier, with gates rather than claims.

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. GTF2 has not yet earned its durability record, and our dates have slipped before. GTF2 is in development for NGSA and fps. It will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before it enters service it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. Those are gates, not claims. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that neither the GTF2 ramp nor any Joint Venture work takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control.

Airbus has invited us onto its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner. We accept on standard commercial terms: we carry our own engine's development, and there is no launch-style discount, no concession and no free upgrade. On fps we follow in sequence once we show maturity and durability. That is the right test, and we will meet it with test data, not with price.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only if and when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change.

We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. Those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit` (row 'GTF2: hold + commit to JV': +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88). It is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and both pass every veto. overrides is empty.

1. Constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- On the board GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps's 2040. Eddy's binding readiness test passes on both.
- Bad news first: the real margin is thinner than the board's. The Advantage slipped about a year, and the company prior for a derivative is +1.5 to 2 years, which would land GTF2 around 2037.5-2038, after NGSA's EIS. My own dates have slipped by one quarter to two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- So I book nothing on the date. The two gates (severe-environment validation, full-life LLPs at EIS) are gates, not claims, and the date moves, not the testing. Mitchill prices a slip past 2037 at up to 21.32 (the S2 outcome). That is a red-line cost, not traded.
- The Joint Venture must not touch GTF2's configuration, team or date (Eddy's conditions b and c).
- Fleet first [PX-0080]: the 2036-37 ramp is the real draw, so it is ring-fenced under the weekly pacing-parts review, and new capacity is qualified before it ships.

2. GTF2: hold.
- The demand is visible: code 7 on both live airframes, on the record [PX-0109].
- Cancel trails hold in every column: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. That is -29.26 at my weights and -29.05 at Mitchill's. It would write off $1.67B to save $0.33B and throw away two selections.
- I do not harvest a programme its customers chose. This is inference from [PX-0064][P-1342]: we reset what has stopped working, and this has not.
- Mitchill confirms hold carries a selected engine, so ground 2 does not reach it.
- From 2036 GTF2's $2B is sunk and the cancel option lapses.

3. Joint Venture: commit.
- My round-1 trigger is met: code 7 on both live airframes includes Rolls-Royce.
- The item against hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51, never negative. That is +0.55 at my weights, +0.44 at Mitchill's and +1.38 at equal weights.
- It needs $0 of new cash: GTF2's $2B equals our share, so the fold write-off is $0 (Mitchill). It beats a buyback, which is about $0 NPV at the 10% WACC.
- I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low). This is company doctrine (profile.md §6, dashboard_game.md §5; [P-1233][P-1676]) plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test as my evidence. I call our GTF partnerships 'critical' [PX-0038].
- Terms: risk and investment shared, never the gear, core or GTF2 technology, which stay P&W modules under P&W design authority.
- Eddy's flag that Rolls-Royce claims favourable geared IP is rebutted in the terms: P&W keeps the gear team and data. No core-technology red-line flag is left standing.
- Architecture loyalty would have kept me on GTF2 alone. The grid says the commit costs GTF2 nothing, so loyalty does not get to cost PV.

4. Veto check.
- Mitchill, ground by ground:
  - ground 1 (dividend or debt): no new R&D; GTF2 cost $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope; dividend covered; debt on its pre-ASR path; no envelope stretch.
  - ground 2 (unselected engine): pass.
  - ground 3 (aggressive terms): standard terms in the Airbus and Boeing answers, no buy-in payment.
  - ground 4 (booking upside): $0 booked on the commit, and nothing is presented as formed.
- His two conditional binding vetoes are respected in the statement and other moves:
  - ground 4: Rolls-Royce's commitment and the formation are not presented as done; the +5.51 is not announced; durability is written as gates.
  - ground 3: no concession, discount, fee or fixed-price development.
- Eddy: both grounds pass on the orders as proposed. His standing conditions (configuration freeze; staffing outside the fleet and validation teams) are written into other moves, so neither is invoked.

5. Red lines.
- No new engine without a committed airframer: GTF2 fired on code 7 selections.
- Shared-source relief on code 7 (NGSA and fps) is declared again, as in round 1. On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference: [PX-0058][P-1292]).
- No core technology to the Joint Venture [P-1233].
- The dividend never funds an engine.
- Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100].
- No widebody [PX-0027].
- No airframer dates or rates [PX-0062].

6. Premium: $0 this round.
- No Board item trails hold, and neither a doctrine nor an objective premium is needed.
- Round-1 doctrine premium: $0.26B, reported separately. The cumulative ledger is $0.26B inside the $1B cap.

7. Objective.
- Restore credibility is met (on the board) in every column: on NGSA and fps in S1/S4, fps in S2, NGSA in S3. It holds only while GTF2 is ready by EIS. We do not claim it in public.
- Capitalise is met in S1 and S4 (+3.37 / +8.88) and fails in S2 and S3 in every row. No order moves those columns; only durability data the airframers believe does.

8. Expected column: S1, rivals hold.
- Airbus keeps 'a choice of engines', Boeing wants two or three sources, and Rolls-Royce waits for our commitment to be on the record.
- I lowered S4 from 0.15 to 0.10 on Mitchill's point that orders are sealed and simultaneous, and raised S2 to 0.11 on GTF reputation risk.
- Expected PV +0.39 against hold's -0.16.

What would change my mind:
- Joint Venture terms needing P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B: back through the gate.
- A slip or parts shortfall that Eddy reports: hold/hold, and the date moves.
- In 2045, the written re-test.

decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1, 'GTF2: hold' and 'GTF2: hold + commit to JV' tie at +3.37 (103.1%), and the brief lists 'GTF2: hold'. The submitted row (hold + commit) equals it in S1 and is never below it in any column (+8.88 against +3.37 in S4). So it is the best expected row: +0.39 at my weights against -0.16 for hold.
decision.premium_reason: No premium this round. The only Board item, `jv_with_rr: commit`, never trails hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), and `gtf2_solo: hold` is the default. No doctrine-favoured order differs from the best expected row, and no objective premium is needed: both hold rows meet Restore credibility, and Capitalise fails in S2 and S3 in every row. Reported separately: the round-1 doctrine premium of $0.26B (`launch_if_selected` over an unconditional launch). The cumulative ledger is $0.26B inside the team's $1B cap. recommendations.text: Durability and parts reporting before NGSA's EIS, not with the next package. The decision says the first AOG and pacing-parts count 'comes to the Board with the next package', but the next round is 2045, after both EIS dates (2037 and 2040). Eddy himself advised against waiting. Through GTF2's entry into service, the Board's Governance and Public Policy Committee (product safety and quality) should receive on a standing cadence: the GTF fleet AOG and pacing-parts count, Hot Section kit progress, severe-environment validation status and full-life LLP certification. Eddy reads the real margin as thinner than the board's, about 2037.5-2038 at the derivative prior, and losing NGSA costs 21.32. If testing threatens 2037, disclose fast and let the date move, not the testing. The Board accepts that red-line cost.

Align the 2045 hold-or-withdraw rule with the Board's Premature exit test. A 2045 withdraw is a Board item and passes only if its weighted item value on the 2045 grid, at Mitchill's weights, is at least 0. Clauses (1) and (2) of the written rule fit that test. Clause (3), withdraw on any lapsed condition, could produce a withdraw that trails hold. Bring any such withdraw with its 2045 grid numbers and the lapsed condition named, and the Board will test it. Because orders are simultaneous, a standing commitment held in 2045 forms if Rolls-Royce commits that round, so the decision must be in the sealed 2045 orders. Carry Mitchill's $2B contingency, for the case where a ready GTF2 no longer counts toward our share, into that test, not into today's value.

Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B is a new capital appropriation. That covers a contribution under Airbus's risk-sharing invitation beyond our own engine's development, a Joint Venture top-up or buy-in, a fresh share in 2045, and a post-EIS merged derivative carrying UltraFan NB content. Each comes through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and, for a derivative, its own durability programme. The commit is worth +0.44 at Mitchill's weights only because it is free.

Public statement: it passes Disclosure. It says ready in 2036 and no earlier, gives validation and full-life LLPs as gates, names no airframer date, and says the Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits. One tightening: write 'the Joint Venture does not change GTF2's configuration, date or team' rather than 'GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change'. Otherwise the line can be read as a promise of 2036, which Eddy's margin does not support and which sits against 'the date moves, not the testing'. Keep the credibility objective out of public claims, as Mitchill advises.

GTF2: the cancel option lapses with this round, and from 2036 GTF2's $2B is sunk, as the Board guided. Its whole-programme value against cancel is +32.79 / +11.47 / +20.98 / +32.79 (+29.05 at Mitchill's weights). In 2045, report GTF2's in-service value against this plan, together with the selections actually fitted on NGSA and fps. The Board once reviewed the GTF's NPV every year.

Dividend, debt and ledger: confirmed as reported. There is no new R&D this round, GTF2 cost about $0.33B a year (5.6% of the ~$6B envelope), the dividend is covered, debt is on its pre-ASR path and the Board's one-round stretch is unused. The premium ledger stands at $0.26B of $1B. Because the analyst models stop at 2030E, the 2045 memo should show GTF2's actual 2030-35 spend and any Joint Venture cash against the envelope and the debt path.

rolls_royce.public_statement: So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody stays on plan: ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. If testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan. Both airframers have selected all three engine makers, Pratt & Whitney included. So if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now. Last time we said we would commit once Pratt & Whitney's commitment was on the record. Frankly, with decisions made at the same time, waiting for that means deciding too late. So our Joint Venture commitment is on the record today, on one condition: it forms only if Pratt & Whitney commits too. If not, nothing is spent, and we will not hold it open. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that. We launch for any airframer that selects us where we can be ready by its entry into service. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We won't do anything not profitable. When we commit, we deliver.

WHY THE JOINT VENTURE NOW: rebutting last round's word and the ExCo's 'P&W first' default
Last round I said publicly that "we commit once its commitment is on the record". The ExCo's team default is partner first once P&W has committed. I am departing from the letter of both, for four reasons.
(1) Orders are sealed and simultaneous. P&W's commitment can reach the record only a round after it is made, so waiting means committing in 2045 at the earliest. By then NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are in service, and a fold would write off about $4B of a ready engine. The word would defeat its own purpose.
(2) The substance of the word survives. Its point was no Joint Venture without a partner and an airframe. Under the rules the Joint Venture forms only in a round when P&W is also committed. Both live airframes carry code 7, which includes P&W, and that meets the Board's partner limb [R-1010]. If P&W does not commit, nothing forms and nothing is spent.
(3) The fold condition I set last round is met: the fold row beats keeping the Solo in S4 and ties it elsewhere.
(4) It is a choice with a trigger, not options management [RX-0051]: withdraw in 2045 by default. It is the same logic as last round's `launch_if_selected`.
The Board said it would not ask me to break a public word for +$0.23B. I am not breaking it for the money. I am squaring it in public, in today's statement, and giving the reason. "There's no change of strategy" [RX-0098]: partnership is our stated preference [RX-0118]. On cash, the +2.28 in S4 is in substance the $2.29B of Solo spend avoided, with our narrowbody share unchanged at 36.5% in 2050.

MATURITY: no claim of a new engine by 2037
A Joint Venture formed in 2035 folds GTF2 (ready 2036) and our Solo (ready 2037). It carries a folded engine on its own frozen test plan, ready no later than 2037 on the board's rule; Watson confirms it. I do not count on an UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine in service by 2037. That configuration would be a later engine with its own full programme. No Joint Venture date is disclosed.

VETO CHECKS
- McCabe co-signs the commit: worst column 0; capex £0.84bn a year on hold, £0 in S4 after the fold; funded from free cash flow, buybacks giving way first.
- Her binding withholds (the upgrade, UltraFan WB, a cancel paired with the commit) all apply to orders I do not give.
- No balance-sheet ground arises.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. I have met the three grounds he reserved for step 4:
  (a) No Joint Venture ready date, explicit or implied. I struck 'a partnership can still serve them' and used his wording, 'if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now'. No UltraFan NB date before 2037. Nothing on airframer dates.
  (b) No claim of a new configuration by 2037.
  (c) The joint partner-shop support plan before the first EIS is carried as a private other move.
- Red-line flags: none stands. The cancel, the upgrade and UltraFan WB are all struck. Strain stays at $0. `overrides` is empty.

PREMIUM
$0. The submitted plan is the best expected grid plan, and no item is held below the best plan.

CONTROL'S METRICS (own NB money / strain / RR WB share 2050 / RR NB share 2050)
- S1: $8.0B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5%
- S2: $8.0B / $0 / 55.2% / 19.7%

- S5: $8.0B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5% (Airbus WB airframe share 30.2%)

Expected own NB money: $7.77B. Stated plainly: no order this round brings it within $4B. Hold leaves $8.0B, a cancel $5.7B, and a fold in S4 $5.7B. The cause is the 2030 trigger on a double selection. We never cancel or fold for the metric alone.

2045 PLAN
If our commitment stands and P&W commits only in 2045, the Joint Venture would form after both airframes are in service. A ready Solo would then fold, with about $4B written off and shares equalised. So the 2045 default is `withdraw`, unless that round's grid shows the commit at or above withdraw in every column, the worst column at or above 0, and fleet support undisturbed. Both McCabe and Watson back this.

DOCTRINE NOTE
My own record is Medium on narrowbody launch behaviour and Low on Joint Venture terms. The partner test, the 2045 trigger and the ramp ranges are doctrine and McCabe's numbers, not my record.

Our widebody share is 58% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, when the GEnx upgrade counts, so it stays above our 50% line. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes back to the board before it arises.

WIDEBODY

"So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody stays on plan: ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. We won't do anything not profitable. When we commit, we deliver."

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view in seven cases.

(1) Watson reports that 2037 cannot be met without compressing testing. The date then moves, and we drop off NGSA: S2 becomes the base case and hold is +8.75. A 2035 Joint Venture that folds GTF2 (ready 2036) would then be the only route to NGSA, which makes me weigh the commit more, not less.

(2) Watson finds that a fold compresses testing or gives a Civil veto ground. The commit goes to hold at a declared $0.23B premium, and I would sign that.

(3) Evidence that the Joint Venture needs RR cash beyond its $4B share. I would re-price it, and it must still be at or above 0 in every column.

(4) The 2045 grid. I keep the standing commitment only if it is at or above withdrawing in every column.

(5) A 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, or an A350 Re-engine, goes on the record. I would re-test the upgrade and UltraFan WB with the $5B strain stacked. Each must stay within its own bill or carry a premium within the caps.

(6) Delivered numbers show narrowbody early-unit or durability costs above the top of my $2-5B range, or a flying-hour shock threatens cash breakeven. I would re-phase and bring the buyback changes to the Board first.

(7) RR widebody share heads below 50%.
cfo.memo:
Safety first, then the balance sheet. Nothing here touches either.

I confirm Tufan's weights (0.65/0.10/0.05/0.10/0.05/0.05) and his numbers: Joint Venture +0.23, worst 0; cancel -33.63; cancel plus Joint Venture -30.16; upgrade -6.01; UltraFan WB -8.80. Hold is +27.34.

The Solo stays. Keeping it beats cancelling in every column, by 15.03 to 36.35, for $2.29B still to spend: about £0.84bn a year in 2035-36, roughly 9-12% of analyst free cash flow. Buybacks give way first. The dividend is not in play. No equity, no borrowing.

I co-sign the Joint Venture commit. It is never below hold: +2.28 in S4, which is the $2.29B of Solo spend we avoid, with our share unchanged at 36.5%. If Pratt & Whitney does not commit, nothing is spent. Last round's word is Tufan's to answer; on the numbers, holding costs $0.23B. A standing commitment needs a 2045 trigger: withdraw unless that grid shows it at or above withdrawing in every column.

I withhold on the upgrade and UltraFan WB. Each loses more than its own bill once the $5B strain is stacked on it.

Two things the grid does not show. Control's $4B line stays breached: $8.0B, or $5.7B in S4, and no order cures it. And the narrowbody ramp after 2037 will cost us: $2-5B on my range, more if durability bites. My record on launch economics is thin; that is inference.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

ops.memo:
UltraFan NB, launched 2030, is ready 2037: zero margin against NGSA's 2037 entry into service, three years against fps 2040. Zero margin is a named pass, not a veto. The record shows no slip; gearbox sizing is the risk we test hardest. If the endurance test needs longer, the Committee hears it first and the date moves, not the test plan. A late engine drops us from NGSA; S2, -21.32, is the nearest measure.

Support: the Singapore-model partner MRO agreements (2034 gate) and the first partner shop with an EIS support team (2036 gate) are on plan. The board doesn't track them, so I re-commit them here. High-performing suppliers only. We go from 197 engines a year to 1,657 by 2040.

Joint Venture: no Civil ground. Formed in 2035, it folds GTF2 (2036) and our Solo (2037), so it is ready no later than 2037. Two conditions. It carries a folded engine on its own test plan; an UltraFan core with P&W's gearbox is a later engine with its own full programme. And we disclose no Joint Venture date. Structure is Tufan's call; I lean to partnership.

Widebody: 58% to 2041, 55.2% from 2042, every column. No widebody programme beside the narrowbody: $5B of strain, for good. Time on wing carries the Trent fleet inside budget.

Statement: clean, except "a partnership can still serve them", which implies a ready date. Say "the time to decide it is now".

We're pacing that program properly.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan NB Solo (held)
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready at launch + 7 must be at or before the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin is a pass with a note, not a fail and not a veto ground. A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture, if P&W also commits in 2035
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier if a folded solo programme is further along. It must be ready by each live airframe's EIS. Formation must not compress any test plan.
tests.numbers:
On its own, formation 2035 + 6 = 2041. The rules make it earlier when a folded solo is further along. The folded programmes are GTF2 (2030 + 6 = ready 2036) and our Solo (2030 + 7 = ready 2037).

READY YEAR: no later than 2037, and 2036 if GTF2's date governs (inference; the bulletin shows the date only on formation). Against NGSA 2037: zero margin at worst, pass with a note. Against fps 2040: 3 years or more, pass. I CONFIRM the Board's reading, 'ready by 2037 at the latest'.

COMPRESSION: none on the board. The ready year is a folded programme's own launch + development years, so no test plan is shortened. In practice the risk is configuration. A merger two years before a zero-margin EIS must carry a folded engine on its own frozen test plan. An UltraFan core with P&W's gearbox is a new configuration: a new NPI with its own testing schedule, not a 2037 engine.

GEARBOX: P&W's gearbox could answer our gearbox-sizing constraint (dashboard_game.md §3). That is inference; I have no evidence of my own. It applies to the growth engine, through full testing.

FORMED IN 2045: formation comes after both EIS (2037, 2040) and would fold a ready, in-service Solo.

tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than: launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037); launch + 6 for UltraFan WB; formation + 6 for the Joint Venture, or the earlier date the bulletin shows for a folded solo (none shown yet). Nothing on any airframer's dates.

Judged on the CEO's draft; to be re-checked at step 4.

- 'where we can be ready by its entry into service': clean.

- UltraFan WB: not ordered.
- Joint Venture: no date drafted. Formation + 6 = 2041 unless a folded programme is further along. The bulletin shows no folded date yet, so no Joint Venture date, explicit or implied, may be given.

ONE WORDING FIX: 'so this is the round a partnership can still serve them' implies a Joint Venture ready by 2037-2040, earlier than formation + 6 and before the bulletin shows it. Replace it with 'so if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now.'

The statement names no airframer dates. The rationale must not present an UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine as ready by 2037.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (briefing constraint). A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS, and it must be carried in any package with a narrowbody launch, trigger or commit (inference).
tests.numbers:

(1) Singapore-model partner MRO agreements by 2034.
(2) The first partner shop inducting engines, and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology), by 2036. That is one year before the 2037 EIS and four years before fps 2040.

STATUS: on plan. The board neither prices nor tracks these gates, and the brief records no slip. So I report them on plan and re-commit them in this package; I claim no signature the record cannot show.

JOINT VENTURE: the commit is a narrowbody commit and needs the same plan before it goes in. If the Joint Venture forms, support moves to a joint network on the Singapore model: our partner shops plus the partner's in-service narrowbody shops (P&W flies the A320neo today, per rules.md; inference). Plan B (hold + commit to JV): strain $0. The Joint Venture is narrowbody and no widebody programme sits beside it. Overlap 0 years.

Plan F (UltraFan WB launched 2035, ready 2041) beside the Solo: 2 years of overlap (2035-37) and $5B. Against hold: -9.00 in S1-S4, -6.96 in S5-S6. Red line: no Re-engine on the record, and the Solo is not 'both selected'.

CONFIRMED:
- Hold and the Joint Venture commit both carry $0.
- Once the Solo is ready in 2037, no cancel removes it. Any widebody programme from now on, beside the Solo or a formed Joint Venture, carries a permanent one-off $5B, whatever its dates.

NOTE: the integration work of a 2035 fold is not in the grid.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief's year table. The board sets no capacity limit, so the result is 'not applicable' unless the brief reports a constraint. Flag a narrowbody ramp as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity, as advice.
tests.numbers:
ENGINES A YEAR (hold or Joint Venture; S1 and S4-S6):
- NB: 965 (2037), 978 (2038), 990 (2039), then 1,460 a year from 2040 (36.5% of 4,000).
- WB: 197 to 2041, 188 from 2042.

- About 10,233 UltraFan NB engines delivered by end-2044 in S1.

Shop visits: I use my figure (1,100-1,200 a year at midterm, RX-0279), not the 1,400-1,500 definition.

No capacity limit on the board and none reported in the brief, so not applicable.

ADVICE: the ramp lands behind the widebody ramp and needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity. A Joint Venture changes the plan. In S4, shares are equalised with P&W, and support is shared on the Singapore model through the partner's narrowbody shops. That reduces the MRO build we carry alone (inference).

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
RR WB share on hold, and on hold + Joint Venture: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050 (the GEnx upgrade counts from 2042), in every column S1-S6. The lowest is 55.2%, 5.2 points above the line.

- Test not triggered.

S5 EXPOSURE: Airbus's WB airframe share falls from 41.2% to 30.2% by 2050 (787 Re-engine alone). We power the A350 alone, and we are sole source on 3 platforms (RX-0292), so that is the franchise to watch, even though the board's engine share does not move.

PROPOSED OTHER MOVE (unpriced; public or private, the CEO's call): a Trent time-on-wing programme inside the existing fleet budget.
- Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000.
- Life extension for life-limited parts.
- UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent fleet.
- Trent XWB shop-visit cost down.
It is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, so it carries no strain.

tests.threshold: A cancelled, idle or folded UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. A qualitative note; grid values are never adjusted for it (inference).
tests.numbers: The Solo is held. UltraFan's geared-architecture technology (25% more efficient than the first Trent) keeps feeding time on wing on today's Trent fleet. If the Solo folds in S4, its technology stays with RR and still flows to the fleet: a 2-way flow. Qualitative; grid unchanged.

NONE INVOKED.

(1) Singapore-model partner MRO agreements, gate 2034. (2) First partner shop inducting engines and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology) by 2036, ahead of a first EIS no earlier than 2037. (3) Narrowbody work only with high-performing suppliers. If the Joint Venture forms, a joint support agreement goes into the formation documents in 2035-36, before the first EIS: our partner shops plus the partner's in-service narrowbody shops. other_moves.detail: About $2.29B (about £1.7bn, roughly £0.84bn a year in 2035-36) remains on the Solo, about 9-12% of analyst free cash flow. other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. other_moves.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
other_moves.detail: We answer Airbus's invitation on NGSA and Boeing's code-7 engine competition on fps on standard commercial terms: value remunerated, win-win, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We will show the maturity and durability Boeing's sequence asks for, and we do not speak for any airframer's dates.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody stays on plan: ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. If testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan. Both airframers have selected all three engine makers, Pratt & Whitney included. So if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now. Last time we said we would commit once Pratt & Whitney's commitment was on the record. Frankly, with decisions made at the same time, waiting for that means deciding too late. So our Joint Venture commitment is on the record today, on one condition: it forms only if Pratt & Whitney commits too. If not, nothing is spent, and we will not hold it open. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that. We launch for any airframer that selects us where we can be ready by its entry into service. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We won't do anything not profitable. When we commit, we deliver.

If the Joint Venture forms, the joint support agreement must be in the formation documents before 2037. The folded engine flies on its own frozen test plan, with no reconfiguration before EIS. An UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine comes to the board as a new programme with its own full test plan. Before fps in 2040, show Boeing's sequence the full test plan complete, life-limited parts at full life and NGSA in-service durability data.

The Joint Venture forward plan. The commitment stands until withdrawn. In the 2045 round, bring the withdraw row against the keep row, column by column. The default is `withdraw`, unless keeping it is at or above withdraw in every column, with the worst column at or above 0, no premium, and support of the in-service UltraFan NB fleet undisturbed. Confirm from the 2045 brief how a same-round withdraw is adjudicated against a P&W commit. A fold of a ready engine would write off about $4B, gain nothing on Control's metric, and could disturb fleet support. If the Joint Venture forms this round, report the $1.71B fold write-off as non-cash, on spend already made. Any request for RR money beyond our $4B share comes back to the board before it arises.

Funding order: reconcile McCabe's correction before the board pack goes out. Buybacks give way first, as in 2015. The 30-40% dividend ranks after the balance sheet in our capital frame. The remaining Solo spend (about $2.29B, about £0.84bn a year in 2035-36, 9-12% of analyst free cash flow) belongs to a selected programme in delivery, not new programme spend. It is not to be re-phased in any way that moves the date or compresses testing. Any step beyond buybacks, on the dividend or on programme phasing, comes to the board before it arises. McCabe should report quarterly, including the narrowbody ramp after 2037. That ramp is not in the grid: $2-5B is her base case, planned at the top, and about $10B her reasonable worst case.

The widebody core and Control's strain line. Strain stays at $0. From 2037 the Solo can no longer be cancelled, so every future widebody item will carry the $5B strain on top of its own bill, and we will judge it that way. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record (S5, S6), or RR widebody share heads toward 50%, bring the upgrade and UltraFan WB rows next round with the strain shown and the premium caps applied ($3B in all, at most $1B for UltraFan WB). Trent time on wing inside the existing budget is the right defence now. Watch the A350 sole-source exposure: Airbus widebody airframe share falls to 30.2% in S5, even though the board's engine share holds at 55.2%.

Control's terms and the public word. Keep stating plainly that our own narrowbody money is $8.0B ($5.7B only if P&W commits) against $4B. The cause is the 2030 double selection, and we never cancel or fold for the metric alone. The statement is clean on disclosure: no early date, no Joint Venture date, nothing on airframer dates. Next round, say plainly where the Joint Venture stands once P&W's 2035 orders are published, and do not describe a Joint Venture engine as able to serve either airframe before the bulletin shows a ready date. Answer Airbus's risk-sharing invitation and Boeing's code-7 competition on standard commercial terms, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection.

board_review.note: The board approves. Product safety is and always must be our most important priority, and nothing here compresses it. The Solo stays on its own test plan, ready 2037. A Joint Venture formed this round folds an engine ready no later than 2037, with no date disclosed and support in place first. The commitment is never below hold: +2.28 in S4 and 0 elsewhere, worst case 0 against a $4B bill. It spends nothing unless Pratt & Whitney commits too. McCabe co-signs and Watson raises no veto. The chief executive has squared last round's word in public, and he has our support. We note openly that our own narrowbody money stands at $8.0B against Control's $4B. No order cures that, and we will not cancel or fold for the metric. Zero margin at NGSA is the risk we do not underestimate. In 2045 we expect a withdraw unless that grid shows it pays.

public_statements.boeing:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for five years now, so let me tell you plainly where it stands. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Every step up in production is gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.

Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. We review how both engines are doing in service, every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first.

On the 787, we're not starting a new development this year. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs allow. We'd rather do less and do it better. When there's a business case for the next step on the widebody, we'll bring it, and not before.

The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it stayed there through the heaviest spending years. Debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it.

We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.
public_statements.airbus:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar.

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first.

The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer, and we will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We will take a further step on the A350 only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready.

We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are flying, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on the next order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record gets earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job now is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines arrive on time for our customers' deliveries first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Bad news first. An engine earns its durability record one flight hour at a time, and our new engine's record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. So we will report time on wing as fleet data, and we will claim nothing beyond the hours flown. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. The fleet data will show whether we have, not this statement.

Here is what is on the record. The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners committed. What we said then, that nothing had formed, no longer stands. Its engine is built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036, and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine. Any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, on standard commercial terms. We review the pacing parts every week. Our rule is that new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates or rates, or for Rolls-Royce. Those are theirs to announce.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. We said that when we commit, we deliver. We did. Now the fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the partner-shop network. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year, and we will not launch for the sake of it. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: KPI-gated fps production ramp, with every step reported to the Aerospace Safety Committee
boeing.detail:
fps production steps up in increments of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart. Each step is gated on the FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. The data decides, not the calendar [BX-1259, BX-1291, B-2283].

On the brief, deliveries go from 760 (2040) to 860 (2045) and 940 (2049): three steps of 5 in nine years, a sixth of doctrine's fastest tempo.

Pope tables the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Committee meeting. Any quality, FAA or supply problem goes to the Board as a live problem the day we see it. No production runs ahead of a mature design [BX-1263].

boeing.move: In-service durability reviews of both fps engine sources
boeing.detail:
CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, report reliability, durability and life-limited-part status to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting [BX-1298].

The fps is fitted CFM + P&W + RR, but the Joint Venture engine counts as one source. That leaves us at exactly two sources. If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone. Any durability finding is a live problem, and I would then want a third source.

CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket stays a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325]. It has eased: CFM's narrowbody share is 27% in 2040-44 against 76% before 2037, while the fps needs about 1,720 engines in 2045 and 1,880 in 2049.

boeing.move: 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated
boeing.detail: We grow the 787 from the capacity built in Charleston where customer orders are visible, gated on the same KPIs [BX-1317, B-2336]. It loads the factory, not engineering (strain $0), and it is our widebody answer in place of a second development: doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]. The board does not price it.

boeing.move: No fixed-price development; no new dates
boeing.detail: All development and support with suppliers stays on cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. We give no programme date before the data supports it [BX-1268, B-2315], and we blame no one, the FAA included [BX-1323].

airbus.move: Engine-maker risk-sharing invitation kept on standard terms
airbus.detail: On NGSA, CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine stay our partners on standard commercial terms. Airbus 'intends to offer a choice of engines'. We assume no concession, no refundable advance and no state support. The NGSA code was locked at entry into service and is unchanged: 2 sources and 3 narrowbody makers in 2045 and 2050. Unpriced.

airbus.move: Compete on A350 and A350F price and product
airbus.detail:
The A350 Re-engine is held. The A350 family, passenger and freighter, is sold on value, as the A330neo was [A-0090, A-0091].
- It runs on the existing A350 commercial and programme teams, and Wagner confirms it draws no NGSA or A320neo teams.
- On the engine side, the lever is Rolls-Royce's Trent XWB time-on-wing work, which it funds inside its own budget.
- It carries no programme cash.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply, for our own ramp only
airbus.detail: We continue to bring critical work packages in-house and to de-risk titanium and rare earths [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063]. This serves only our own disciplined and controlled ramp of NGSA and the A320neo, and is never aimed at a rival's supply chain. The Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee stays informed.

airbus.move: Delivery performance on NGSA and the A320neo
airbus.detail: Wagner's line: a disciplined and controlled ramp and delivery performance for our customers, on the existing production teams [AX-0010]. The fall from 1,260 deliveries (2039) to 1,140 (2045) comes from the board's share mechanics, not from supply. Unpriced.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy through industry coalitions
airbus.detail: We keep working with industry partners, Boeing included, for a tariff-free aerospace trade regime [AX-0088, AX-0046].

cfm.move: Keep RISE funded as technology, and report its gates as the state of the technology

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet, charged
pratt_whitney.detail: Insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard commercial terms. The kit is charged, not given away, and there are no discounted spares and no concessions [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. The fleet comes first [PX-0080]. AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. This respects Mitchill's conditional ground-3 veto. No effect on the game board.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture governance: one engine, P&W modules, P&W design authority
pratt_whitney.detail: The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and shares risk and investment, not technology [P-1233]. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules under P&W design authority [P-1744], and design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240]. P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data, which keeps Rolls-Royce's geared-IP claim closed [P-2004]. It is one engine and one support chain [P-1875]. Any configuration change to the in-service engine, such as UltraFan NB content insertion or a merged derivative, is not on this board. It would be a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and its own durability programme, under Eddy's ground 1. We do not speak for Rolls-Royce.

rolls_royce.move: Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service
rolls_royce.detail: The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.

rolls_royce.move: Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson)
rolls_royce.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. No dates disclosed.

rolls_royce.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
rolls_royce.detail: Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

boeing.move: Supplier health, engines first: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
Capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, sized on the stress case
boeing.detail:
Malave's sizing, which I endorse. This is inference: neither of us has a record on returns.

The proposal:
- Reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.4x by 2045 stress free cash flow of $16.35B.
- Add a flexible buyback of $0-5B a year, paced on actual free cash flow.
- Cap the two together at $8B a year: 49% of 2045 stress free cash flow and 38% of base ($20.94B). That is well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow [B-1164].
- Retain about $8.4-9.2B a year under stress for 2045-49. That builds liquidity of about $44B by end-2049, enough to carry a 2050 widebody bill of $5B many times over.

The safeguards:
- Net debt stays at $0 at every checkpoint, base and stress.
- The $10B of revolvers stays undrawn, with no new equity.
- Supplier funding comes first.
- The buyback goes to zero first if free cash flow runs more than about half below the stress case, or if Pope reports a live problem.
- The dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 82% below stress.

Rating view (Malave, inference): solidly investment grade on these metrics [BX-1305], to be confirmed against the agencies before the Board decides.

The Board revisits the cap at the 2050 review. Nothing is announced before the Board decides.

boeing.move: Widebody review in 2050, held only if the A350 has not been re-engined

airbus.move: Engine-supply and fleet status report to the Board's twice-yearly safety review
A350 Re-engine gate for 2050, with three conditions
Capital-return guardrail and the net-cash bridge
airbus.detail:
Toepfer's paper, adopted.
- Returns stay inside 30-50%, with no equity raise and no dividend cut.
- No new buyback is proposed now. Any buyback comes to the budget as a reserved Board matter, within the AGM authority and with the bridge attached, once reported FCF and net cash confirm it.
- On the FY2025 floor, hold adds about +$2.45B of net cash a year after a 48% dividend.
- No internal long-term-plan targets are disclosed [AX-0005].

airbus.move: A220-500 stays a study
airbus.detail: No launch this round (one launch at a time, rule 6), and no launch cash. Unpriced.

cfm.move: Fleet durability report to the full Board: the Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application and the GEnx upgrade
Joint CFM capacity plan re-based with Safran to the volume we actually have
cfm.detail:
This is a private planning basis built through CFM governance. It is not a commitment to anyone [CX-0184, CX-0944].
- The basis is the board's volume of 1,079 CFM NB engines a year from 2040. That is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year built to 2036. WB is 152 a year from 2042.
- 1,079 is the board's volume, not an airframer's agreed schedule. No capacity or rate number goes to an airframer or the public until that airframer's volumes are worked.
- The risk now is stranded capacity, not a missed ramp. So we build no new facility: lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue and goes to MRO turnaround on the fleet we have, not to OE lines.
- Priority: parts needed to clear a finding on a safety-critical part come first [CX-0658, CX-0010]; then OE engines ahead of spares [CX-0529].
- The load moves to the aftermarket: the LEAP fleet, the Ducted's first shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits, all behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. I take a quarter to a half off any shop-visit ramp promise as well as any OE promise [CX-0590, CX-0592].

cfm.move: Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP, Embraer and GEnx fleets, on standard terms
CFM parity record for a hold
cfm.detail: There is no new CFM narrowbody order this round. Fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice: both airframers fly CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219, CX-0184]. Safran cannot be consulted in this game, so this record asserts no Safran position. GEnx is GE alone, so no gate applies.

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet ring-fence, weekly pacing-parts review and a records look-back on the 2040 capacity step
pratt_whitney.detail: The weekly pacing-parts review [PX-0131] ring-fences the 1,460-a-year rate. The rule: neither the Joint Venture rate nor any Joint Venture engineering may take castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from GTF fleet AOG recovery or from kit insertion. New capacity is qualified before it ships. Following Eddy, contain first: run a records look-back on every part made on the capacity added for the 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062], and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039]. If the review shows the fleet short, Eddy's ground 2 binds and the rate waits.

pratt_whitney.move: Standing durability and parts report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: Weekly to ExCo and quarterly to the Committee, and at once on any escape. The quarterly cadence is Eddy's inference. It covers: Joint Venture engine fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122], against the ~1M-hour benchmark [P-0847]; removals and time on wing against plan; fix campaigns; AOG for both fleets; the pacing-parts count; kit insertion as a % of the fleet [PX-0116]; capacity qualification status; and any escape with its containment and a dated recovery. Treated as a product-safety matter [PG-0050][P-1360]. The 2035 'with the next package' wording is replaced by this standing cadence.

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet-data cadence to Airbus and Boeing
pratt_whitney.detail: Time-on-wing, removal and campaign data on the Joint Venture engine is shared with both airframers as it is flown, with no claim beyond the hours flown. Standard commercial terms: no concession, no free upgrade, no discounted spare engines or spares (Mitchill ground 3 respected). We name no airframer date or rate [PX-0062].

pratt_whitney.move: Capital-order note to the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: Written as an order of priority, not as a 2045 status (Mitchill's advice): the dividend first [PX-0081], then debt back to pre-ASR levels [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669]. The dividend never funds an engine. Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B (a Joint Venture cash call, top-up or buy-in, UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative) is a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and Finance to the Board. It needs a return case against hold and a buyback, must fit the ~$6B envelope, and needs its own durability programme. The 2045 lifecycle value ($13.2B against $8.7B nominal) is not free cash flow and is not presented as such. The extra engines likely cost cash first, at a negative engine margin, before the aftermarket repays it (inference). Mitchill's $2B 2035 contingency is released: the Joint Venture formed while GTF2 was live.

pratt_whitney.move: Whole-programme value against plan, reported to the Board
pratt_whitney.detail: Reported in the sealed rationale and board_response, as the Board once reviewed the GTF's NPV every year [P-1191]. It covers the 2030 plan, the 2035 grid and the 2045 outcome (+8.88, the 2035 S4 column), the S4 weighting miss, the 2035 statement tightening we did not take up, and the pre-EIS Committee reporting we cannot evidence.

rolls_royce.move: Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson)
Joint Venture governance and alignment note to the Board before the 2050 round
rolls_royce.detail:
Owners: Watson and McCabe. It covers:
(1) Design authority. Plainly: on the record P&W keeps the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology as its modules under its design authority. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan technology stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] applies to any later engine under our own design authority, which would come to the Board as a new programme with its own full test plan.
(3) Data. We ask for access to hot-section and life-limited-part data through the joint support agreement, since we carry an equal share of the risk.
(4) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Until that is settled we plan on half of a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; the worst case is about £2.2bn.
(5) Work share and revenue. Both should be reflected at 36.5% each, matching the equal narrowbody shares. If our content per engine is below half, the board's engine value overstates our cash, and McCabe re-prices it.
(6) The joint support network.
(7) Cash stays within our $4B share. Nothing more goes in without the Board.
The IAE lesson is not to drift out of alignment [R-0318]. Doctrine and McCabe's and Watson's inference: my own record is Low on Joint Venture terms.

rolls_royce.move: Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe)
