cfo.memo:
Safety first, then the balance sheet. Nothing this round touches either.

I confirm Tufan's weights, 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08, and his numbers. Hold is +32.37 (+32.38 at the Board's). The upgrade is -6.47 in every column against a $2B bill. UltraFan WB is -8.83, worst -9.00, against a $4B bill. With the $5B strain inside the rows, both lose more than their own bill in every column. I withhold my co-signature on each. Premium at hold: $0.

Capex: £0 of new development at hold. Either widebody item would add about £0.49bn a year.

One correction. Last round I said the Joint Venture roughly halves the ramp. It halves what we share, support and any retrofit, not the losses on our own 1,460 engines a year. Our base is about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn), held at the top; the worst case falls from about $10B to $7.5B (£5.5bn). The board carries no ramp line, so I report the range, not an actual.

The fold avoided $2.29B (about £1.7bn); the $1.71B write-off was non-cash. Our cash stays within the $4B share. No balance-sheet trigger stands. Buybacks give way first.

Now it is quality of cash: the net LTSA balance on the Joint Venture fleet, time on wing, and who pays for a fix in a Pratt & Whitney module. Plan on half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn, until the governance note settles it.

My record is thin on Joint Venture terms; this is inference. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture engine (held, in service)
tests.threshold: A narrowbody engine must be ready by each selecting airframe's EIS. Joint Venture engine ready at formation + 6, or earlier where a folded Solo is further along (the date the bulletin shows). A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Formed 2035. Formation + 6 would be 2041; the bulletin shows ready 2036, inherited from the folded GTF2 (2030 + 6). Our folded Solo was 2030 + 7 = 2037.
- NGSA (launched 2030, EIS 2037): ready 2036, 1 year of margin. PASS. Fitted: RR NB share 24.1% from 2037.
- fps (launched 2030, 10-year ramp-up, EIS 2040): 4 years of margin. PASS. Share 36.5% from 2040.
The engine is ready and in service, so no narrowbody readiness test applies to this round's orders, as the Board says. Both narrowbody fields are hold-only.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan WB, if launched (option C, not recommended)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB ready at launch + 6. It counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. It must be ready by that Re-engine's EIS (Re-engine EIS = launch + 5). A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
Launched 2045, ready 2051.
- S1: no Re-engine on the record, so it never counts.
- S2 and S3: a Re-engine launched in 2045 enters service in 2050. UltraFan WB is ready in 2051, one year late. RR WB share in 2050 stays 55.2%.
- 2050 round: a launch then is ready in 2056, six years after a 2045 Re-engine's EIS.
This is ADVICE on an order I do not recommend. It is not a veto. At hold there is nothing to fail.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the earlier ready date the bulletin shows, here 2036). No new programme date, nothing on Re-engines or airframer dates, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the record.
tests.numbers:
Judged on the CEO's draft; I re-check the final text at step 4.
- 'The Joint Venture ... formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies': on the public record (formed 2035, ready 2036, fitted on NGSA and fps). Clean.
- No date for any new programme. The upgrade would count from 2048, and UltraFan WB would be ready no earlier than 2051. Neither is ordered or named.
- Nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates.
- No Joint Venture terms: it does not describe the configuration, design authority or work share.
- 'Trent time on wing keeps improving' and 'we fix the fleet first and anything new waits': no date. Clean.
Caution for step 4: no retrofit, durability-kit or growth-engine date in public, and no claim that an UltraFan-core engine sits in the Joint Venture.

tests.name: Support before EIS (and support at volume)
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (briefing constraint). Any narrowbody launch, trigger or commit needs a support plan through partner shops before EIS (inference).
tests.numbers:
There is no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit this round, and both EIS are past (NGSA 2037, fps 2040). So no support-before-EIS test applies.

STATUS FOR THE COMMITTEE (internal; inference; the board does not track it):
- The joint support agreement went into the 2035-36 formation documents.
- The network is our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service narrowbody shops.
- Narrowbody work goes only to high-performing suppliers.
- I claim no signature or shop count the record cannot show.

VOLUME (brief's year table):
- 1,460 RR-share NB engines a year from 2040, beside 188 WB.
- About 10,233 delivered by end-2044, 17,533 by end-2049 and 18,993 by end-2050.
- P&W's public term is 'one engine, GTF2' at an equal 36.5% share. If so, the joint network supports about 2,920 engines a year, about 20,466 by end-2044 (inference).

IS ANYTHING SHORT? The board shows no constraint, and the brief reports none.
Watch items (advice):
(1) life-limited-part and hot-section spares. P&W holds design authority and reviews its pacing parts weekly, so it controls them;
(2) partner-shop induction slots ahead of the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts;
(3) spare engines for severe-environment operators.

tests.name: In-service durability (report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee)
tests.threshold: Mature in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, support able to intervene early. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new moves (attr.). The board does not model durability.
tests.numbers:
WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS:
- In service on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040.
- P&W's pre-EIS gates for GTF2: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life.
- The engine was ready in 2036 with no slip.
- No in-service event appears on the public record.
I claim no test or in-service data the record cannot show.

HOT SECTION EXPOSURE:
- P&W is still inserting its Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet.
- The Joint Venture engine is GTF2, with P&W's core under P&W design authority.
- Whether GTF2 carries that exposure is not on the record, and we cannot see it without P&W's data. That is the governance gap: an equal share of risk and investment, without design authority over the hot section.

ASK FOR THE NOTE:
- access to hot-section and life-limited-part data through the joint support agreement;
- life-limited parts declared at full life.

RETROFIT PLAN IF IT BITES (the Trent 1000 model):
(1) the Committee hears first, before anything is said in public;
(2) protect the fleet: inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool;
(3) the design authority (P&W, for gear and core) issues the kit, inserted at shop visit through the joint partner shops. The Board's precedent is fleet retrofit within two years;
(4) the date of anything new moves;
(5) the cost split is McCabe's number and the note's.
Shop visits: I use my 1,100-1,200 a year (midterm, widebody), not 1,400-1,500.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project (Joint Venture) beside a widebody project (UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade) carries a one-off $5B strain whenever both are on record, whatever their dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference; seat and company rule).
tests.numbers:
PLAN A (all hold): strain $0. Control's strain line is met. PASS.

PLAN B (upgrade):
- It runs 2045-48 beside a ramped Joint Venture fleet.
- The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and cannot be cancelled, so the $5B is permanent.
- Against hold: -6.47 in every column; -1.47 without the strain.

PLAN C (UltraFan WB):
- It runs 2045-51.
- Strain $5B. Against hold: -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02; -4.00 / -3.27 / -3.02 without the strain.

RED LINES:
- No UltraFan is in development, so the upgrade rule is not engaged.
- The Solo folded in 2035, so the UltraFan WB-beside-Solo rule is not engaged.
- Neither B nor C breaches a hard rule I enforce. Each breaks Control's strain line and is a Board would-veto.
The support case changes neither verdict. The upgrade uses the existing Trent network. UltraFan WB would need a support build for a Re-engine that is not on the record.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is 'not applicable' unless the brief reports a constraint. Flag the narrowbody ramp's need for partner MRO and high-performing suppliers, as advice.
tests.numbers:
ENGINES A YEAR:
- 1,460 NB plus 188 WB = 1,648 a year from 2042, against 197 in 2026 (8.4x).
- NB: 965 / 978 / 990 in 2037-39, then 1,460 from 2040.
- WB: 197 to 2041, then 188.
- The same in every column at hold.

The brief reports no constraint. ADVICE: concentrate supply on high-performing suppliers (GBP 685m of GBP 2.5bn in 2023), and add partner-shop capacity ahead of the narrowbody shop-visit wave.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
HOLD:
- 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050, in S1, S2 and S3.
- The GEnx upgrade counts from 2042.
- Worst year 55.2%, 5.2 points above the line. The franchise test is not triggered.

OPTIONS:
- Upgrade: 60.0% in 2050.
- UltraFan WB: 55.2%, because it is late.

S2 EXPOSURE: Airbus WB airframe share is 41.2% / 40.2% / 41.2% in 2050. We power the A350 alone. In S2 a re-engined 787 without UltraFan would also press our Trent 1000 slot after 2050. That is not on the board and is qualitative.

DEFENCE: the Trent time-on-wing work inside the existing budget, as an other move:
- longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000;
- life extension for life-limited parts;
- Trent XWB shop-visit cost down.
No programme, no strain.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: A cancelled, idle or folded UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. A qualitative note; grid values are never adjusted for it (inference).
tests.numbers:
The Solo folded in 2035 onto GTF2's frozen test plan, so UltraFan technology did not go into the Joint Venture configuration.
- It stays RR's and feeds Trent time on wing: a 2-way flow.
- That is also how our technology is protected under P&W's 'risk and investment, not technology' terms (inference).
- On the record we hold no module design authority in the Joint Venture engine. What we bring there is risk, investment and the support network.
- RX-0072 ('we are actually bringing a technology') applies to any later engine under our own design authority, and the governance note should say so plainly.
- The IAE lesson is alignment between partners (R-0318).
Qualitative; the grid is unchanged.

vetoes.plan: The CEO's lean: every field at hold (`ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`)
vetoes.ground:
NONE INVOKED.
- Maturity: no maturity is compressed. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps 2040.
- Early date: the draft discloses none.
- Support: no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit is ordered, so the support ground cannot arise.
TEST FAILS against the plan: none. BINDING VETOES: none.

vetoes.plan: RESERVED FOR STEP 4: the final public statement, the public other moves and the rationale
vetoes.ground:
Civil veto. It is binding under the team rule if triggered, and it rests on attributed turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283). Grounds:
(a) Any public date for a new programme earlier than launch plus development years (UltraFan WB 2051 if launched in 2045; the upgrade counting before 2048). Also any Joint Venture date other than the record's 2036, and any retrofit, durability-kit or growth-engine date.
(b) A statement, other move or rationale that counts on an engine before its ready year. For example: an UltraFan-core Joint Venture engine in service, or UltraFan WB counting on a 2050 Re-engine.
(c) Any narrowbody launch, trigger or commit without a partner-shop support plan before EIS. No such order is open this round.

vetoes.plan: `t1000_upgrade: launch` or `ultrafan_wb: launch` (options B and C)
vetoes.ground:
Neither is a Civil ground, and neither breaches a hard rule I enforce: no UltraFan is in development, and the Solo folded in 2035.
ADVICE, NOT BINDING:
- Each carries a permanent $5B of strain and breaks Control's strain line.
- Upgrade: -6.47 in every column, more than its $2B bill; -1.47 without the strain.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02, more than its $4B bill. It also fails Ready by EIS (2051 against a 2045 Re-engine's 2050 EIS).
The Board would veto both. Hold.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
I WOULD INVOKE THE BINDING CIVIL VETO AT STEP 4 IF:
- the final statement or a public other move gives a date for a new programme, a retrofit or a growth engine;
- it gives any Joint Venture date other than the record's;
- it gives any Re-engine or airframer date;
- it claims an UltraFan-core engine sits in the Joint Venture.

I WOULD PUT THE FLEET BEFORE ANY NEW ITEM, AND TELL THE COMMITTEE FIRST, IF:
- P&W's hot-section or life-limited-part data shows that GTF2 carries the GTF Hot Section exposure; or
- an in-service durability event appears on NGSA or fps.
The retrofit would then run through the joint partner shops before anything new.

I WOULD RE-TEST THE WIDEBODY ITEMS IN 2050 ONLY IF:
- a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record (S2, S3); or
- RR widebody share heads toward 50%.
Even then:
- an upgrade launched in 2050 counts from 2053 and still carries the $5B;
- UltraFan WB launched in 2050 is ready in 2056.
I would back either only if the grid shows it at or above hold, or within a declared premium under the caps.

I WOULD BACK THE UPGRADE ON THE SEAT'S USUAL LEAN only if its row beat hold. Today it is -6.47, and -1.47 even without the strain. Named airline durability results on the Joint Venture engine would strengthen the fleet case.
ops.memo:
The fleet comes first. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036: on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040, our share 1,460 engines a year, 10,233 by end-2044. No narrowbody readiness test applies, and no Civil ground arises at hold.

Durability: the record shows no in-service event, and I claim nothing beyond it. The gap is design authority. P&W keeps the gear and the core, and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. We carry half the risk without the hot-section data. The governance note must give us that data, life-limited parts at full declared life, and a fleet-first retrofit rule: Committee first, kit through the joint partner shops, as with the Trent 1000.

Support: the joint agreement and Singapore-model partner shops carry the volume. No shortfall on the board. Spares and shop slots before the first shop-visit wave are my watch items.

Technology: UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. On the record we hold no design authority here; we bring risk, investment and support. The note should say so.

Widebody: 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column. I'd normally push the upgrade with no UltraFan in development, but it's -6.47, and -1.47 without the strain. UltraFan WB would be ready 2051, a year after a 2045 Re-engine's EIS. Hold both; time on wing inside budget does the job.

Statement clean; every field at hold.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.

other_moves.move: Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson)
Joint Venture governance and alignment note to the Board before the 2050 round
other_moves.detail:
Owners: Watson and McCabe. It covers:
(1) Design authority. Plainly: on the record P&W keeps the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology as its modules under its design authority. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan technology stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] applies to any later engine under our own design authority, which would come to the Board as a new programme with its own full test plan.
(3) Data. We ask for access to hot-section and life-limited-part data through the joint support agreement, since we carry an equal share of the risk.
(4) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Until that is settled we plan on half of a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; the worst case is about £2.2bn.
(5) Work share and revenue. Both should be reflected at 36.5% each, matching the equal narrowbody shares. If our content per engine is below half, the board's engine value overstates our cash, and McCabe re-prices it.
(6) The joint support network.
(7) Cash stays within our $4B share. Nothing more goes in without the Board.
The IAE lesson is not to drift out of alignment [R-0318]. Doctrine and McCabe's and Watson's inference: my own record is Low on Joint Venture terms.

other_moves.move: Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe)
Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson)
other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. No dates disclosed.

other_moves.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
other_moves.detail: Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

other_moves.move: The 2050 test, set in advance
other_moves.detail:
This is the last round. Both widebody rows come to the ExCo only if a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record this round, or if RR widebody share heads toward 50%. Both carry the permanent $5B of strain.
- Upgrade launched in 2050: it counts from 2053. To pass the worst-case test it must be no more than $2.00B below hold in every plausible column, which needs about +$5B of engine value against about +0.53 today. Within the $3B cap it needs about +$4B.
- UltraFan WB launched in 2050: it is ready in 2056. It qualifies only against an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, on the record. It must be within $1.00B of hold, which needs about +$8B of engine value against +0.73 to +0.98 today.
I expect hold. The narrowbody fields stay at hold.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. We said that when we commit, we deliver. We did. Now the fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the partner-shop network. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year, and we will not launch for the sake of it. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
Every field is at hold:
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`
- `jv_with_pw: hold`
- `ultrafan_wb: hold`
- `t1000_upgrade: hold`
This is my framing proposal, unchanged. Both memos recommend the same orders, and there are no Board items. Do Nothing on widebody (Trent only) is right because no airframe can use a new widebody engine in time [RX-0058].

GRID (brief rows, S1-S3)
- "UltraFan NB: hold": +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61. Components: engine value +38.07, R&D -4.00, write-offs -1.71. It is the best plan in every column.
- Weights S1-S3: 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08. McCabe confirmed them.
  - S1 (rivals hold): neither airframer has signalled a Re-engine. Boeing puts 787 customers and Charleston capacity first; Airbus runs "one well-prepared programme at a time".
  - S2 (787 Re-engine): 0.12. Boeing is the likelier mover, with fps in service since 2040.
  - S3 (both Re-engines): 0.08.
- Expected PV: +32.37 at my weights, +32.38 at the Board's illustration (0.80 / 0.10 / 0.10), +32.40 at McCabe's stress weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20). Worst column +32.35. Premium $0.

ROWS STRUCK, as gain over hold
- "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade": -6.47 in every column, so -6.47 under any weights. Worst -6.47 against its own $2B bill. Without the $5B strain it is still -1.47: about +0.53 of engine value against $2B.
  - It fails the four-part gate on business model [RX-0030].
  - The franchise test is not triggered: widebody share is 55.2%, above the line.
  - The shortfall is $6.47B, above the $3B premium cap.
- "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB": -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02, so -8.83 at my weights and the Board's. Worst -9.00 against a $4B bill.
  - No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing has not named UltraFan.
  - Launched now, it is ready in 2051, a year after a 2045 Re-engine's 2050 EIS, so widebody share in 2050 stays 55.2%.
  - The shortfall is far above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap.
- Upgrade and UltraFan WB together: exclusive, not allowed.

VETO CHECKS
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on both widebody launches. Her binding withholds touch only orders I do not give. She invokes no balance-sheet ground: board debt is unchanged, no equity, leverage well below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto at hold. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, a year before NGSA's 2037 EIS and four before fps 2040. No support-before-EIS test arises.
- He reserved step 4 for the final text. I kept to his cautions:
  - no date for any new programme, retrofit, kit or growth engine;
  - no Joint Venture date beyond the record;
  - nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates;
  - no claim that an UltraFan-core engine sits in the Joint Venture;
  - no Joint Venture terms beyond the record.
- The statement says only that the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies, which is on the public record.
- `overrides` is empty.

RED-LINE CHECK
No colleague flagged a breach. All four fields are at hold, so:
- no UltraFan launches without a programme to fly it;
- no early date;
- no overlap and no strain (Control's strain line stays at $0);
- no cancel;
- no item can lose more than its own bill.
Nothing to strike.

CLOSED ITEMS
- Last round's private 2045 withdraw trigger was written for a P&W that had not committed. P&W committed in 2035 and the Joint Venture formed, so the trigger is moot and closed. Withdraw is not an order this round.
- The Solo folded in 2035; its $1.71B write-off is sunk.

WHAT THE ROUND IS REALLY ABOUT: quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]
- The cash now sits in the installed fleet: about 10,233 engines in our share by end-2044, 1,460 more a year.
- The Trent 1000 is the movie I have seen before [RX-0087, RX-0114].
- Watson names the gap plainly. P&W holds design authority over the gear and the core and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. We carry an equal share of risk without the hot-section data.
- McCabe names the money side. Who pays for a fix in a P&W module is not settled on the record; plan on half of a Trent 1000-type bill (about £1.1bn), with a worst case of about £2.2bn.
- Both go into the governance note to the Board before 2050, a private move. The test I apply to the partner is binary: it credits what we bring and shares data in proportion to the risk we carry, or the relationship is transactional [RX-0050, RX-0072]. That test on a partner is inference, not my record.
- I accept McCabe's correction: the Joint Venture halves what we share (support, any retrofit), not the early-unit losses on our own 1,460 engines a year.

CONTROL'S METRICS for the submitted plan, the same in every column
- Own narrowbody money: $5.71B against $4B. NOT MET, and final. It is the $4B Joint Venture share plus the $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. The cause was the 2030 double selection. No narrowbody order is open, and we never cancel or fold for the metric.
- Strain: $0. MET.
- RR widebody share in 2050: 55.2%. MET.
- RR narrowbody share in 2050: 36.5%. MET.
- Airbus widebody airframe share in 2050: 41.2% / 40.2% / 41.2%. The S2 A350 exposure is watched qualitatively.

WHERE THIS IS DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
- My record is Low on Joint Venture terms and on rivals. The partner alignment, retrofit-liability and data-access asks are company doctrine (the IAE lesson, R-0318) and McCabe's and Watson's inference.
- The funding order and the ramp numbers are McCabe's.
- The readiness and support views are Watson's.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Taken in full.
- She confirmed my weights (0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08) and every row: hold +32.37, upgrade -6.47, UltraFan WB -8.83 with worst -9.00. She showed the verdict holds under her stress weights too.
- Her binding withholds on both widebody launches stand. I give neither order.
- I adopt her correction that the Joint Venture does not halve the whole ramp. Our base is about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn), held at the top, and the worst case about $7.5B (£5.5bn). The quarterly report gives the range until actuals exist.
- Her quality-of-earnings risk goes into the governance note: work and revenue share against 36.5%, and cost following design authority on a retrofit. The board does not show it.
- Capex at hold is £0 of new development; either widebody item would add about £0.49bn a year. No balance-sheet ground. Buybacks give way first.
- Cash is an input [RX-0042]. Her numbers are my evidence on cash and downside.
memo_weighing.ops:
Taken in full.
- No Civil veto at hold. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA (2037) and fps (2040).
- I take his step-4 cautions into the final text. There is no date for any new programme, retrofit, kit or growth engine; no claim of an UltraFan-core engine in the Joint Venture; and nothing on Re-engines or airframer dates.

'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] belongs to any later engine under our own design authority. The governance note says so. In public I say nothing on terms.

public_statements.boeing:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We're holding the line where the data tells us to hold it. Every step in production has been gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. That doesn't change. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.

Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. Both engines are reviewed for how they're doing in service every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first. Our development and support work with suppliers stays on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On the 787, we're not starting a new development. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs and our customers' orders allow. We'd rather do less and do it better.

The balance sheet is where it belongs, and debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it.

I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.
public_statements.airbus:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar. We review the fleet and our engine partners' durability and capacity with our Board as a matter of routine, and we keep working with our partners to keep every source healthy.

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first.

The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer. We will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We have looked again at a further step on the A350. Today the engine and the business case are not both there, so we are not taking that step. As we have said, we will take it only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready.

We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We don't have a birthright on any order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record is earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines for our customers' deliveries come first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Bad news first. All of our new single-aisle business now rides on one engine, and that engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We have said we learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, not a finding, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement.

Our customers have said plainly where the bar is. An engine joins an aircraft, and stays on it, on proven durability, and any durability finding is a live problem. That is fair, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Our rule is that time on wing, removals and fix campaigns go to both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft, and how many sources it carries, is our customers' decision and theirs to announce.

What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. Insertion of the Hot Section durability kit continues across the GTF fleet, charged, on standard commercial terms. Our rules: we review the pacing parts every week, new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us, with containment and a dated recovery. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. Now it has to earn its keep in the fleet. The fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: KPI-gated fps production, with every step reported to the Aerospace Safety Committee
boeing.detail:
fps production holds at about 78 a month (940 a year from 2049 on the brief). Narrowbody share is flat at 47%, so visible demand calls for no further step. Any step stays in increments of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, and is gated on the six FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. The data decides, not the calendar [BX-1259, BX-1291, B-2283].

Pope tables the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Committee meeting. The brief gives none of them as numbers, so we invent none. Any quality, FAA or supply problem goes to the Board as a live problem the day we see it. No production runs ahead of a mature design [BX-1263].

boeing.move: In-service durability reviews of both fps engine sources
boeing.detail:
CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, report reliability, durability and life-limited-part status to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting, where the Committee brings its propulsion expertise to bear [BX-1298].

We sit at exactly two sources, and the Joint Venture engine is the single point of fragility. If it stumbles, CFM would need up to 1,880 fps engines a year, about 62% of what it built before 2037. That is feasible, but it leaves the fps on one source. CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket stays a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325].

boeing.move: Widebody question closed for this game: 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated
boeing.detail:
We are not starting a 787 Re-engine. We grow the 787 from the capacity built in Charleston where customer orders are visible, gated on the same KPIs [BX-1317, B-2336]. That loads the factory, not engineering (strain $0), and it is our widebody answer in place of a second development: doing less and doing it better [BX-1239].

The board does not price it. 2050 is the last decision year, so this is a close, not a deferral to a later review.

boeing.move: No fixed-price development; no new dates; no blame
boeing.detail: All development and support with suppliers stays on cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. We give no programme date before the data supports it [BX-1268, B-2315]. We blame no one, the FAA included [BX-1323], and we attribute no supplier problem to anyone else before exposure.

airbus.move: Engine-maker risk-sharing invitation kept on standard terms
airbus.detail: On NGSA, CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine remain our partners on standard commercial terms. Airbus 'intends to offer a choice of engines'. We assume no concession, no refundable advance and no state support. The NGSA code was locked at entry into service and has not changed: 2 sources, with 3 narrowbody makers in the market in 2050. Unpriced.

airbus.move: Compete on A350 and A350F price and product
airbus.detail: The A350 Re-engine is held. The A350 family, passenger and freighter, is sold on value, as the A330neo was [A-0090, A-0091]. The campaigns run on the existing A350 commercial and programme teams, and Wagner confirms they draw on no NGSA or A320neo teams. On the engine side, the lever is Rolls-Royce's Trent XWB time-on-wing work, which it funds inside its own budget. No programme cash.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply, for our own ramp only
airbus.detail: We continue to bring critical work packages in-house and to de-risk titanium and rare earths [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063]. This serves only our own disciplined and controlled ramp of NGSA and the A320neo, and is never aimed at a rival's supply chain. The Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee stays informed.

airbus.move: Delivery performance on NGSA and the A320neo
airbus.detail: Wagner's line: a disciplined and controlled ramp and delivery performance for our customers, on the existing production teams [AX-0010]. Deliveries of 1,060 a year from 2049 are 53% of a 2,000-aircraft market, which reflects the board's share mechanics, not supply. Unpriced.

airbus.move: Prepare the next generation on technology gates
airbus.detail: No programme cash and no date. The only next-generation engine technology on the record is CFM's RISE, which has no flight test, no compact-core durability result and no fuel-burn figure shown in engine test. So no engine gate for a next-generation airframe has been passed [AX-0020]. Draws on no NGSA or A320neo teams.

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy through industry coalitions
airbus.detail: We keep working with industry partners, Boeing included, for a tariff-free aerospace trade regime [AX-0088, AX-0046].

cfm.move: Keep RISE funded as technology, and report its gates as the state of the technology

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet, charged
pratt_whitney.detail: Insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard commercial terms. The kit is charged, not given away, and there are no discounted spares and no concessions [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. The fleet comes first [PX-0080], and AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. This respects Mitchill's conditional ground-3 veto. We publish no insertion percentage, because Eddy has no 2050 figure. No effect on the game board.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture governance: one engine, P&W modules, P&W design authority
pratt_whitney.detail: The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and shares risk and investment, not technology [P-1233]. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules under P&W design authority [P-1744], and design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240]. It is one engine and one support chain [P-1875]. Any configuration change to the in-service engine is not on this board, whether UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative. It would be a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and its own durability programme under Eddy's ground 1. We do not speak for Rolls-Royce. Change from 2045, on Eddy's advice: the geared-IP clause [P-2004] is taken out of public text and kept in the private governance move below.

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet-data rule toward Airbus and Boeing (the fact of the rule only)
pratt_whitney.detail: This is our answer to the 'one source' line, given with product and data and not with price [PX-0055][P-0768]. We publish the rule, not the data and not what the data shows. Time-on-wing, removal and fix-campaign data on the Joint Venture engine go to both airframers as the fleet flies, with no claim beyond the hours flown. It is written as a rule because the board cannot evidence that the 2045 cadence ran (Eddy; Mitchill's advice). It carries no figures and no characterisation such as 'on plan' or 'mature'. Standard commercial terms, with no concession, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee (Mitchill ground 3). It passes Eddy's ground 1 and Mitchill's ground 4. Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062].

rolls_royce.move: Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service
rolls_royce.detail: The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. We report what the fleet data shows and claim nothing beyond it. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.

rolls_royce.move: Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson)
rolls_royce.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. We keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically for the A350 family on standard terms, and watch our sole-source exposure there. No dates disclosed.

rolls_royce.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
rolls_royce.detail: Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

boeing.move: Supplier health, engines first: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
Third-source contingency for the fps, outside the board, held ready but not triggered
Capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, updated to 2050 and sized on the stress case
boeing.detail:
This is Malave's sizing, in the form the Board says it is minded to take, and I endorse it. It is inference: neither of us has a record on returns.

The proposal:
- reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.7x by 2050 stress free cash flow ($17.23B) and 7.3x by base ($21.83B);
- add a buyback of $0-5B a year, authorised by the Board each year on Finance Committee review and paced on actual free cash flow;
- cap the two together at $8B a year, 46% of stress free cash flow and 37% of base, well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow [B-1164].

Stress-case net debt (2026 $B, year end, full $8B paid every year): -9.24 / -18.27 / -27.11 / -35.77 / -44.23 for 2050-54. That retains about $9.2B a year and builds about $44B of net cash by end-2054. The $10B of revolvers stays undrawn and no new equity is needed.

Breakpoints:
- the buyback goes to zero first on any live quality, FAA or supply problem (a Joint Venture engine durability finding included), or if free cash flow runs below the $8B cap (54% below stress);
- the dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 83% below stress, and below that only while net debt stays at or below $0.

Condition: the package takes effect only on the rating agencies' written confirmation. Our files carry no rating and no rating thresholds. Last round's 'solidly investment grade' was our inference, and Malave withdraws it. If the agencies confirm investment grade but not a solid one, we recommend the dividend only.

Nothing is announced before the Board decides.

airbus.move: Engine-supply and fleet status report to the Board's twice-yearly safety review, with an unpriced contingency view
A350 Re-engine hold recorded as a business-case decision, closing it for the game
Capital-return guardrail and the net-cash bridge
airbus.detail: Toepfer's 2050-2055 bridge is on the FY2025 floor, after a 48% dividend. Net cash rises about $2.45B a year on hold, or about $1.44B with share-plan cover, and stays positive in every year. Returns stay inside 30-50%, with no equity raise and no dividend cut. No new buyback is proposed. Any buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter, within the 18-month AGM authority and with the bridge attached [AG-0035, AG-0059]. No refundable advances, risk-sharing or state support are assumed.

airbus.move: A220-500 stays a study
airbus.detail: No launch cash and no second programme. This keeps the one-programme-at-a-time discipline (rule 6).

cfm.move: Fleet durability report to the full Board: the Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application and the GEnx upgrade
Customer durability data given through CFM governance, jointly with Safran
cfm.detail:
Both airframers get the same data on the same engine: items (1) to (5) of the fleet report, plus the status of every open finding (root cause, turned on or not, turned off or not, the fix and its acceptance). It goes privately, through CFM governance, jointly with our partner.

We hold back claims, never findings. There is no projected time-on-wing gain, kit date or fix benefit until it has been turned on and turned off in test. A finding is never held back from a customer's safety review.

No commercial term goes with the data (Ghai's terms test): no time-on-wing guarantee, warranty extension, free kit or price offered to keep or win a source position. That includes the remark on a third source. We give no public answer to any airframer remark on engine sources [CX-0580].

cfm.move: Joint CFM capacity plan held with Safran at the board's volume, no new facility
cfm.detail:
Private planning basis: 1,079 NB engines a year (about 572 on NGSA and 507 on fps) and 152 GEnx. This is a planning basis, not a promise. It was built jointly with Safran through CFM governance.

- No new facility. The stranded-capacity line (Ghai, inference) is any new facility or OE-line capital sized above 1,079 without an agreed airframer volume. 1,079 is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year we built for to 2036. Even the customer's own worst case, fps back on CFM alone, is about 2,452 with NGSA and fits that footprint. Whether today's supply base carries it is unproven: Ali has no supplier field data, so there is no 'yes' on test.
- Lean flex only, and only once an airframer's volume is agreed [CX-0540, CX-0944]. Any ramp promise takes a quarter to a half off [CX-0590, CX-0592].
- Order of call: parts for safety-critical findings first, then OE before spares [CX-0529]. The ramp never trades against safety [CX-0603].
- Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue, aimed at MRO turnaround for the shop load. That load is LEAP, the Ducted's first and second shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits, behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613].
- No capacity or rate number goes to an airframer or the public before that airframer's volume is agreed, and never without Safran [CX-0184].

cfm.move: Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP, Embraer and GEnx fleets, on standard terms
cfm.detail:
On standard terms. Narrowbody prices are set jointly with Safran and kept private [CX-0184]. CFM-performed shop visits are split equally with our partner [CX-0219]. GEnx is GE alone.

No price is used to buy share or a source slot [CX-0493, CX-0609]. Durability fixes go through reserves and existing service agreements as contracted. Service contracts are modelled conservatively. This passes Ghai's price/cost test on those conditions.

cfm.move: CFM parity record for a hold
cfm.detail: There is no new CFM narrowbody order this round: Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer and Lobby are all at hold, so no Safran gate is triggered. Fleet support, customer data and the capacity plan for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stay within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally [CX-0219, CX-0184]. No Safran position is asserted. An Open Fan launch would have needed a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path, and we have none. GEnx is GE alone.

pratt_whitney.move: Data pack to both airframers' in-service reviews
Fleet ring-fence, weekly pacing-parts review and a DATED records look-back on the 2040 capacity step
pratt_whitney.detail:
The weekly pacing-parts review [PX-0131] ring-fences the 1,460-a-year rate. Neither the Joint Venture rate nor any Joint Venture engineering may take castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from GTF fleet AOG recovery or from kit insertion. New capacity is qualified before it ships.

The records look-back covers every part made on the capacity added for the 2040 step (990 to 1,460 a year, +47.5% in one year). It now carries a date: its result goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee's next quarterly meeting, and at once on any finding. If it cannot close by then, we say so plainly and give a new date. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062], and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039].

Contain first. If the review or the look-back shows the fleet short, Eddy's ground 2 binds and the rate waits.

pratt_whitney.move: Standing durability and parts report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
Weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, and at once on any escape [PG-0050][P-1360]. The first 2050 report must state in writing what earlier reports showed. Where nothing can be evidenced, it says 'not available' instead of filling the gap.

Contents:
- Joint Venture engine fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122], against the ~1M-hour benchmark [P-0847]. The benchmark surfaces problems; it does not prove durability.
- Removals and time on wing against plan, LLP status, and fix campaigns.
- AOG on both fleets and the GTF fleet.
- The pacing-parts count at the 1,460 rate (the last count was about 30, in 2023 [PX-0123]).
- Kit insertion as a % of the GTF fleet [PX-0116].
- Capacity qualification status and the look-back result.

pratt_whitney.move: Top enterprise risks to the Audit Committee and the full Board
pratt_whitney.detail:
Three entries go into the annual top enterprise risks [PG-0034]:
(1) The Joint Venture engine's in-service durability, with hot-and-harsh operation named.
(2) The capacity added for the 2040 step to 1,460 engines a year.
(3) The concentration of all P&W new NB share (36.5%) on one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply. This is common-mode risk across both airframes.

On Eddy's advice, the lack of fleet data on the record is logged as a control gap.

Value at stake, on Mitchill's numbers:
- +2.39 $B in 2026 PV from deliveries in 2051-56 is still to be earned on the board.
- The board does not count deliveries after 2056 (about $1.1B in 2026 PV), share loss from a durability finding (codes are locked at EIS), an in-service charge (the last one was a $5.4B sales charge), negative engine margin or partner shares.
We book nothing either way.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture technical governance, private clauses
pratt_whitney.detail: P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data, which keeps Rolls-Royce's geared-IP claim closed [P-2004]. This is kept out of public text on Eddy's advice, because in public it reads as a point scored off our partner. Any pressure for UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative is reported to ExCo at once and treated as a new appropriation with its own durability programme. Eddy sees none on the 2050 record.

pratt_whitney.move: Capital-order note to the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
Written as an order of priority, not as a 2050 status: the dividend first [PX-0081], then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669]. The dividend never funds an engine.

The analyst baseline runs to 2030E only:
- dividend $5.0-5.6B, covered 2.3-2.4x by FCF;
- net debt 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, back below Mitchill's pre-ASR approximation by about 2028E (inference);
- buybacks $4.0-5.0B.
From 2031 to 2050 the line rests on the board alone, and the note says so.

Lifecycle value is not cash. The 2050 figure is $14.7B against $9.7B nominal, +$5.0B. Of that, about $3.1B is engine price (sales value, not margin) and about $1.9B is aftermarket collected later. Free cash flow from it this year: $0. The extra 500 engines a year likely cost cash first, at a negative engine margin (inference). The 5.4x is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return.

Mitchill's advice is recorded: the Board's ease toward 3 should wait until debt is shown to be held at pre-ASR levels, not just reached. Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B needs a new appropriation through his gate and Finance, with a return case against hold and a buyback.

pratt_whitney.move: Whole-programme close-out against plan, reported to the Board

rolls_royce.move: Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson)
Joint Venture governance note to the Board, delivered now (Watson and McCabe)
rolls_royce.detail:
The note the Board asked for before 2050. Company doctrine (the IAE lesson) and inference: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms.
OPERATING SIDE (Watson):
(1) Design authority, stated plainly. On the record P&W holds the gear, the core and GTF2 as its modules under its design authority. It is one engine and one support chain. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network. We hold no module design authority.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] belongs to a later engine under our own design authority, not this one.
(3) Data. Hot-section, life-limited-part and severe-environment fleet data through the joint support agreement, in proportion to our equal 36.5% share of the risk. Without it Watson cannot report durability to the Committee beyond the public record.
(4) Support network. Our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service shops. Induction slots, spares and a spare-engine pool planned jointly ahead of the 2037-40 wave. Any kit goes in at shop visit through these shops.
MONEY SIDE (McCabe):
(5) Work share and revenue share at 36.5% each, matching the equal engine shares. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points of content below half takes about $7.7B off the narrowbody value: at 40% content engine value is about +30.3 and hold about +24.6; at 30%, about +22.6 and +16.9. Service revenue counts as much as build work share.
(6) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Planning figure: half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; worst case about £2.2bn. That anchor comes from a smaller widebody fleet, so it is a planning figure, not a ceiling. Any finding comes to the Board with a fresh number before anything is public.
(7) Cash. Our money stays within the $4B share. No Rolls-Royce money beyond it without the Board.
(8) Configuration. Any UltraFan NB content or merged derivative is a new programme: it comes to the Board on its own return case and its own durability record, as P&W's public terms also require.
(9) Alignment. Who books the service contracts on our 36.5% is to be settled in the note, so the narrowbody float is proven, not assumed. We left IAE for want of alignment; we will not drift there again.

rolls_royce.move: Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe)
rolls_royce.detail:
Our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with P&W, held at the top of the base range until actuals exist: about $4.3B (£3.1bn) against a base of about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn). Reasonable worst case about $7.5B (£5.5bn) with a retrofit shared 50/50, or about $9B (£6.7bn) if we carry a retrofit alone. The window rolls forward to the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts.
Also each quarter: the net LTSA balance (no narrowbody float booked until the governance note settles who holds the service contracts), time on wing (no upside booked before it is delivered), and any onerous-contract provision, booked plainly if a Joint Venture contract turns loss-making.
Order: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No balance-sheet trigger stands.

other_moves.move: KPI-gated fps production, with every step reported to the Aerospace Safety Committee
other_moves.detail:
fps production holds at about 78 a month (940 a year from 2049 on the brief). Narrowbody share is flat at 47%, so visible demand calls for no further step. Any step stays in increments of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, and is gated on the six FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. The data decides, not the calendar [BX-1259, BX-1291, B-2283].

Pope tables the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Committee meeting. The brief gives none of them as numbers, so we invent none. Any quality, FAA or supply problem goes to the Board as a live problem the day we see it. No production runs ahead of a mature design [BX-1263].

other_moves.move: In-service durability reviews of both fps engine sources
other_moves.detail:
CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, report reliability, durability and life-limited-part status to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting, where the Committee brings its propulsion expertise to bear [BX-1298].

We sit at exactly two sources, and the Joint Venture engine is the single point of fragility. If it stumbles, CFM would need up to 1,880 fps engines a year, about 62% of what it built before 2037. That is feasible, but it leaves the fps on one source. CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket stays a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325].

other_moves.move: Supplier health, engines first: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
Third-source contingency for the fps, outside the board, held ready but not triggered
Widebody question closed for this game: 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated
other_moves.detail:
We are not starting a 787 Re-engine. We grow the 787 from the capacity built in Charleston where customer orders are visible, gated on the same KPIs [BX-1317, B-2336]. That loads the factory, not engineering (strain $0), and it is our widebody answer in place of a second development: doing less and doing it better [BX-1239].

other_moves.detail:
This is Malave's sizing, in the form the Board says it is minded to take, and I endorse it. It is inference: neither of us has a record on returns.

The proposal:
- reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.7x by 2050 stress free cash flow ($17.23B) and 7.3x by base ($21.83B);
- add a buyback of $0-5B a year, authorised by the Board each year on Finance Committee review and paced on actual free cash flow;
- cap the two together at $8B a year, 46% of stress free cash flow and 37% of base, well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow [B-1164].

Stress-case net debt (2026 $B, year end, full $8B paid every year): -9.24 / -18.27 / -27.11 / -35.77 / -44.23 for 2050-54. That retains about $9.2B a year and builds about $44B of net cash by end-2054. The $10B of revolvers stays undrawn and no new equity is needed.

Breakpoints:
- the buyback goes to zero first on any live quality, FAA or supply problem (a Joint Venture engine durability finding included), or if free cash flow runs below the $8B cap (54% below stress);
- the dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 83% below stress, and below that only while net debt stays at or below $0.

Condition: the package takes effect only on the rating agencies' written confirmation. Our files carry no rating and no rating thresholds. Last round's 'solidly investment grade' was our inference, and Malave withdraws it. If the agencies confirm investment grade but not a solid one, we recommend the dividend only.

Nothing is announced before the Board decides.

other_moves.move: No fixed-price development; no new dates; no blame
other_moves.detail: All development and support with suppliers stays on cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. We give no programme date before the data supports it [BX-1268, B-2315]. We blame no one, the FAA included [BX-1323], and we attribute no supplier problem to anyone else before exposure.

boeing.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We're holding the line where the data tells us to hold it. Every step in production has been gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. That doesn't change. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.

Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. Both engines are reviewed for how they're doing in service every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first. Our development and support work with suppliers stays on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On the 787, we're not starting a new development. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs and our customers' orders allow. We'd rather do less and do it better.

The balance sheet is where it belongs, and debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it.

I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.
boeing.rationale:
**Decision.** Every order stays at its default:
- fps: hold;
- fps_engine_code: null;
- rate_737: hold;
- re787: hold.

That is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 in S1 and +0.57 in S2. No order goes to the Board as a change.

**How the team rule ran (teams.md §9)**
1. *Malave's buffer test.* The brief (round4.md §3) labels no risk-case column. Malave and I read the rule the same way: there is no slip leg this round, the test does not apply, and no binding veto stands.
   - For the Board he ran S2 as if it were the risk case. The floor is +0.57 - 2.00 = -1.43.
   - Do Nothing passes by $2.00B. The Re-engine row (-0.43) passes by $1.00B.
   - This is advice only.
2. *KPI doctrine veto (Pope's seat).* It is moot. rate_737 is hold only, and Pope states explicitly that the brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem.
3. *My decision.* The only live choice is the 787 Re-engine. Both colleagues recommend all hold, code null, and their non-binding objections to the Re-engine match mine.

**The 787 Re-engine against hold: +0.05 in S1, -1.00 in S2**
- **Doing less, better [BX-1239].** +0.05 is far inside ε ($1B), so the plan with less to execute wins.
- **Doctrine's Re-engine rule.** A Re-engine needs a gain above ε (dashboard_game.md §6; doctrine, not my record). It fails.
- **Higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].** Hold's worst column is +0.57; the Re-engine's is -0.43.
- **Expectation.** A - B = -0.05 + 1.05p, where p is the weight on S2, so hold wins at any S2 weight above 4.8%. At Malave's 30%, hold leads +0.63 to +0.37. At 50%, it leads +0.62 to +0.14. Even at 0%, the Re-engine's +0.05 sits inside ε.
- **Execution.** The 5-year clock has no headroom against our +1 to +4-year slip prior. About $0.90B of cost growth, 18% of the $5B bill, would erase the S1 gain on its own (Malave and Pope agree).
- **Sourcing.** Only GE's GEnx upgrade is ready for a 2055 EIS. The UltraFan WB could not be ready before 2056, and Rolls-Royce says it will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. The 787 would drop from two engine sources to one, a supply risk the board does not price.
- **The Board** would veto a launch: it fails the $1B launch test in either column, and S2 sits at its -$1B limit.
- **Cash does not decide it.** The plan is fundable: stress free cash flow stays at or above $16.17B. Value decides it.
- **No option value.** 2050 is the last decision year, so I close the widebody question for this game and grow the 787 out of Charleston [BX-1317, B-2336].

**Expected column: S1 (rivals hold).**
- Airbus held the A350 Re-engine in 2045 and said so in public. It now gates any further A350 step on 'the technology, the engine and the business case' all being ready.
- Rolls-Royce says it has nothing to launch and will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody.
- My Round 3 read of S2 was wrong, and I own it [BX-1319]. Malave agrees on S1 and keeps 30% S2 as a conservative baseline.
- My own evidence on Airbus is Low. The order is the same in either column, and nothing here answers Airbus [B-2313].

**Rulings on the hard rules**
- **H1 and H3, first half:** ruled in 2030 with evidence; spent, not in force.
- **H2:** cannot bind.

   - Report in-service reliability.
   - Table the values at the Committee; don't invent numbers the brief does not give.
   - Any further step stays gated on data, not the calendar [BX-1291].

3. **Strain.** Confirm $0 on both rows: a 2050-55 Re-engine overlaps no fps development (2033-40). Does engineering capacity bind on the doctrine's one-major-development-at-a-time test [B-0341]?

   - its in-service durability and life-limited-part status [BX-1298];

   - LEAP-1B for any 737 MAX still built and its aftermarket [B-1449];

6. **Widebody and cash.** Give me your view on Charleston growth, KPI-gated, as the widebody answer that closes the question for this game [BX-1317, B-2336]. Also give me operations' claim on cash ahead of any buyback.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Five things would change my view.

1. **Re-engine.** A grid on which the 787 Re-engine clears epsilon ($1B) in the expected column with no column below -$1B. This grid has none: +0.05 / -1.00, with hold winning at any S2 weight above 4.8%. There is no later round.

2. **Risk-case ruling.** A GM or Board ruling that S2 is a risk case. That would make my test binding, but both rows still pass: A at +0.57 and B at -0.43, against a -1.43 floor.

3. **Returns on free cash flow.** If free cash flow runs below the $8B cap, which is 54% below stress, the buyback goes to zero first. The roughly $3B dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 83% below stress. A crisis on the 2019-20 scale (-$19.7B in 2020) would break it.

4. **Live problem.** If Pope reports a live quality, FAA or supply problem, including a durability finding on the Joint Venture engine, I would hold harder, fund suppliers first and set the buyback to zero until the problem is closed.

5. **Rating.** If the agencies' view comes in below solidly investment grade, or they do not confirm it, I would recommend the dividend only, or no return at all, until they do.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I read the rule as you do. The brief labels no risk case, so there is no slip leg and I hold no veto. For the Board I ran S2 as if it were one: the floor is +0.57 less $2.00B, or -1.43. Do Nothing passes by $2.00B and the Re-engine row (-0.43) by $1.00B. Advice only.

The business case decides, and it does not clear. The Re-engine adds +0.05 in S1, inside epsilon, and gives up $1.00B in S2, where the board cuts the 787 margin from 20% to 15.77%. That hits the cash engine, not one bill. A $0.9B overrun, 18% of the $5B, would erase the S1 gain. Cash is not the constraint: stress free cash flow stays above $16.1B. I see no finance reason for a second development in the last decision year. I plan on about 30% S2; hold wins above 4.8%.

Confirmed: $21.83B base, $17.23B stress, your Re-engine years to within a cent, net debt $0.0B, and the cell 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) in both rows.

On returns: a dividend of about $3B and a buyback of $0-5B, capped at $8B, 46% of stress free cash flow. Under stress, net cash builds to about $44B by end-2054, with revolvers undrawn and no new equity. The buyback goes first. Last round's rating read was inference; I withdraw it. The agencies must confirm.

We can meet this baseline and potentially beat it, barring a crisis on the 2019-20 scale.

B's worst column is S2, at -0.43, $1.00B below A. Against hold the item is worth +0.05 in S1 and -1.00 in S2, so hold wins at any S2 weight above 4.8% (0.05 / 1.05).

The fps development ran 2033-40 and a 2050 Re-engine would run 2050-55. The overlap is 0 years, so strain is $3B × 0 ÷ 5 = $0 on both rows, and H4 does not strike B.

Engineering capacity does not bind. With the fps development finished in 2040, the Re-engine would be the only major development [B-0341]. tests.name: Re-engine engine readiness and sourcing by a 2055 EIS, with concurrency (CEO ask 5). Basis: inference on the public record; doctrine [B-0940, B-1597, BX-1263]
tests.threshold: An engine ready by EIS with margin, and the 787 keeping the two engine sources it flies today (GE and Rolls-Royce [B-0940]). Sole-sourcing paced the 777X [B-1597]. No production ahead of a mature, certified design [BX-1263].
tests.numbers:
Readiness alone passes:
- GE's GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 22 years ahead of a 2055 EIS, so the engine would not pace the airframe.

Sourcing fails:
- An UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056 at the earliest (6 years), a year after EIS.
- Rolls-Royce says it will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and that it has nothing to launch.
- A Trent 1000 upgrade launched now would count from 2053 under the rules. But Rolls-Royce says its current Trent work 'is not the t1000_upgrade order', so nothing on the record puts it under way (inference).
- A 2055 Re-engine would therefore fly one source, GE, where the 787 flies two today.

Concurrency: we avoid it only if production waits for a mature design certified with the FAA [BX-1263]. On the slip prior (central 2057), that would need the date headroom the 5-year clock does not have.

This is advice, not a veto.

tests.name: Supplier readiness, engines first (CEO ask 4). Basis: doctrine [B-2308, B-1449, BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043, BX-1264, BX-1325, BX-1298], not my record
tests.threshold: No live supply-chain problem and the supplier-shortages KPI not flagged. At least two engine sources on the fps. Fragile suppliers kept funded and hot. Terms risk-share or cost-plus only.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no supply-chain problem. The fps flies CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine: two sources in 2045 and 2050, with three makers in the market.

Joint Venture engine:
- It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on NGSA since 2037 (13 years) and on the fps since 2040 (10 years).
- The brief has no durability or life-limited-part data and reports no in-service event, so there is no finding and no live problem.
- P&W says its durability record is 'still being earned', and Rolls-Royce puts life-limited parts at full declared life. These are watch items, not findings [BX-1298].
- Fleet scale: up to 8,500 fps delivered 2040-49 if every Boeing narrowbody since EIS was an fps (an upper bound, since the brief gives no mix).

CFM capacity:
- Narrowbody engine shares for 2040-49 are CFM 27%, P&W 36.5% and RR 36.5%. Of 4,000 engines a year, that is 1,080, 1,460 and 1,460.
- CFM's forward-fit load is 36% of the 3,040 a year it built in 2026-36. On the board CFM delivered about 39,600 LEAP engines in 2026-39, and that fleet is its aftermarket load (inference: share is not capacity) [BX-1264, BX-1325].
- Fragility: if the Joint Venture engine stumbles, CFM would need up to 1,880 fps engines a year (940 aircraft × 2), 62% of its pre-2037 output. That is feasible on past output, but it leaves the fps on one source.

LEAP-1B: Boeing delivered 11,080 737 MAX in 2026-39 on the board, so at least 22,160 LEAP-1B engines are in the aftermarket. LEAP-1B remains the sole source for any MAX still built [B-1449].

Keep-hot list: CFM on the fps, the Joint Venture engine, LEAP-1B, and any supplier flagged on shortages. The ladder is embed, buffer, keep above rate, requalify, fund, acquire [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043].

A third-source case outside the board would need all of the following:
- a Committee durability or life-limited-part finding on the Joint Venture engine;
- CFM as the bridge;
- a maker funding a separate engine on its own return case (P&W calls that a new capital appropriation; Rolls-Royce says anything new waits on the fleet);
- risk-share or cost-plus terms;
- that engine's own durability record before it joins the airplane;
- about 6-7 years of lead time on the rules' engine clocks (inference);
- a Board decision.
None of these is triggered today.

ops.memo:
My record is Global Services. Delivery, IP and cash conversion are my record, applied by inference. KPIs, strain and suppliers run on Boeing's operations doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. My KPI veto has nothing to bind on: the rate is hold only. Narrowbody deliveries went from 63 a month in 2040 to 78 in 2049, three steps of 5 in nine years. They stay flat at 78 through 2060; with share flat at 47%, no further step is needed. The brief gives neither the six KPIs nor in-service reliability as numbers. I table them at the Aerospace Safety Committee and invent none.

Second, engines. We sit at exactly two sources. If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, CFM would need up to 1,880 fps engines a year, 62% of what it built before 2037: feasible, but one source. Keep CFM, the Joint Venture engine and LEAP-1B funded and hot.

Third, the Re-engine. Strain is $0. Only GE is ready for 2055, so the 787 would drop from two engine sources to one. The five-year clock has no headroom against our +1 to +4-year slip prior. Each $1B at 2055 is $0.055B today, so $0.9B of cost growth, 18% of the bill, erases the +0.05.

And finally, cash. Hold keeps 2050 stress free cash flow at $17.23B. The Re-engine would take $3.95B of it over 2050-54. Supplier funding comes ahead of any buyback.

Orders: all hold, code null.

other_moves.detail:
fps production holds at about 78 a month (940 a year from 2049 on the brief). Narrowbody share is flat at 47%, so visible demand calls for no further step. Any step stays in increments of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, and is gated on the six FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. The data decides, not the calendar [BX-1259, BX-1291, B-2283].

Pope tables the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Committee meeting. The brief gives none of them as numbers, so we invent none. Any quality, FAA or supply problem goes to the Board as a live problem the day we see it. No production runs ahead of a mature design [BX-1263].

other_moves.detail:
CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, report reliability, durability and life-limited-part status to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting, where the Committee brings its propulsion expertise to bear [BX-1298].

We sit at exactly two sources, and the Joint Venture engine is the single point of fragility. If it stumbles, CFM would need up to 1,880 fps engines a year, about 62% of what it built before 2037. That is feasible, but it leaves the fps on one source. CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket stays a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325].

Third-source contingency for the fps, outside the board, held ready but not triggered
Widebody question closed for this game: 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated

We are not starting a 787 Re-engine. We grow the 787 from the capacity built in Charleston where customer orders are visible, gated on the same KPIs [BX-1317, B-2336].
