other_moves.detail:
This is Malave's sizing, in the form the Board says it is minded to take, and I endorse it. It is inference: neither of us has a record on returns.

The proposal:
- reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.7x by 2050 stress free cash flow ($17.23B) and 7.3x by base ($21.83B);
- add a buyback of $0-5B a year, authorised by the Board each year on Finance Committee review and paced on actual free cash flow;
- cap the two together at $8B a year, 46% of stress free cash flow and 37% of base, well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow [B-1164].

Stress-case net debt (2026 $B, year end, full $8B paid every year): -9.24 / -18.27 / -27.11 / -35.77 / -44.23 for 2050-54. That retains about $9.2B a year and builds about $44B of net cash by end-2054. The $10B of revolvers stays undrawn and no new equity is needed.

Breakpoints:
- the buyback goes to zero first on any live quality, FAA or supply problem (a Joint Venture engine durability finding included), or if free cash flow runs below the $8B cap (54% below stress);
- the dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 83% below stress, and below that only while net debt stays at or below $0.

Condition: the package takes effect only on the rating agencies' written confirmation. Our files carry no rating and no rating thresholds. Last round's 'solidly investment grade' was our inference, and Malave withdraws it. If the agencies confirm investment grade but not a solid one, we recommend the dividend only.

Nothing is announced before the Board decides.

decision.public_statement:
Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We're holding the line where the data tells us to hold it. Every step in production has been gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. That doesn't change. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.

Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. Both engines are reviewed for how they're doing in service every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first. Our development and support work with suppliers stays on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On the 787, we're not starting a new development. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs and our customers' orders allow. We'd rather do less and do it better.

The balance sheet is where it belongs, and debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it.

I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.
decision.rationale:
**Decision.** Every order stays at its default:
- fps: hold;
- fps_engine_code: null;
- rate_737: hold;
- re787: hold.

That is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 in S1 and +0.57 in S2. No order goes to the Board as a change.

**How the team rule ran (teams.md §9)**
1. *Malave's buffer test.* The brief (round4.md §3) labels no risk-case column. Malave and I read the rule the same way: there is no slip leg this round, the test does not apply, and no binding veto stands.
   - For the Board he ran S2 as if it were the risk case. The floor is +0.57 - 2.00 = -1.43.
   - Do Nothing passes by $2.00B. The Re-engine row (-0.43) passes by $1.00B.
   - This is advice only.
2. *KPI doctrine veto (Pope's seat).* It is moot. rate_737 is hold only, and Pope states explicitly that the brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem.
3. *My decision.* The only live choice is the 787 Re-engine. Both colleagues recommend all hold, code null, and their non-binding objections to the Re-engine match mine.

**The 787 Re-engine against hold: +0.05 in S1, -1.00 in S2**
- **Doing less, better [BX-1239].** +0.05 is far inside ε ($1B), so the plan with less to execute wins.
- **Doctrine's Re-engine rule.** A Re-engine needs a gain above ε (dashboard_game.md §6; doctrine, not my record). It fails.
- **Higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].** Hold's worst column is +0.57; the Re-engine's is -0.43.
- **Expectation.** A - B = -0.05 + 1.05p, where p is the weight on S2, so hold wins at any S2 weight above 4.8%. At Malave's 30%, hold leads +0.63 to +0.37. At 50%, it leads +0.62 to +0.14. Even at 0%, the Re-engine's +0.05 sits inside ε.
- **Execution.** The 5-year clock has no headroom against our +1 to +4-year slip prior. About $0.90B of cost growth, 18% of the $5B bill, would erase the S1 gain on its own (Malave and Pope agree).
- **Sourcing.** Only GE's GEnx upgrade is ready for a 2055 EIS. The UltraFan WB could not be ready before 2056, and Rolls-Royce says it will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. The 787 would drop from two engine sources to one, a supply risk the board does not price.
- **The Board** would veto a launch: it fails the $1B launch test in either column, and S2 sits at its -$1B limit.
- **Cash does not decide it.** The plan is fundable: stress free cash flow stays at or above $16.17B. Value decides it.
- **No option value.** 2050 is the last decision year, so I close the widebody question for this game and grow the 787 out of Charleston [BX-1317, B-2336].

**Expected column: S1 (rivals hold).**
- Airbus held the A350 Re-engine in 2045 and said so in public. It now gates any further A350 step on 'the technology, the engine and the business case' all being ready.
- Rolls-Royce says it has nothing to launch and will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody.
- My Round 3 read of S2 was wrong, and I own it [BX-1319]. Malave agrees on S1 and keeps 30% S2 as a conservative baseline.
- My own evidence on Airbus is Low. The order is the same in either column, and nothing here answers Airbus [B-2313].

**Rulings on the hard rules**
- **H1 and H3, first half:** ruled in 2030 with evidence; spent, not in force.
- **H2:** cannot bind.
- **H3, second half:** not fired. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Airbus held it in 2045.
- **H4:** a 2050-55 Re-engine would overlap the fps development (2033-40) by 0 years, so strain is $0. H4 does not strike it.
- **H5:** nothing to cancel.
- **H6:** the rate is hold only.
- **H7:** no trigger. The brief reports no certification trouble, so the FAA-process gate is open.
- **H8:** $0.05B of doctrine premium is logged (S1). The running log is 0.46 + 0.65 + 0.30 + 0.05 = $1.46B, with Round 3's $0.30B counted after the fact. Each round, and the total, is inside the $2B cap.

My own red lines are all respected:
- no production-certification concurrency;
- no fixed-price development;
- no walking away from a core customer;
- no blame on the FAA or attribution to suppliers;
- no new dates.

**For the Board (it holds me to the case I bring [BG-0022])**
- Submitted row: fps hold + 787 hold, +0.66 (S1) / +0.57 (S2).
- No item departs from its default, so there is no item-at-default row.
- For reference, the Re-engine row is +0.71 / -0.43, an item value of +0.05 / -1.00.
- The ExCo does not treat S2 as a formal risk case.
- Objective cell in both columns: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2).

**Debt path.** Malave's rebuild, which Pope confirms:
- 2050 free cash flow is $21.83B base and $17.23B stress.
- Net debt is $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050, in base and stress.
- With a Re-engine, stress free cash flow would have been 16.76 / 16.52 / 16.33 / 16.17 / 16.45 over 2050-54, still at $0 net debt. That is not taken.

**Capital returns.** I bring the proposal updated to 2050 as a reserved matter, not a game order:
- a dividend of about $3B;
- a buyback of $0-5B, authorised yearly;
- an $8B cap, 46% of stress free cash flow;
- under stress, net cash of about $44B by end-2054, with revolvers undrawn and no new equity.

It is conditional on the agencies' written confirmation of the rating. We infer none.

**Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice:**
- the Re-engine's ε rule;
- the read on Airbus;
- Pope's operations tests (KPIs, strain, suppliers).

The capital-return proposal is inference.

1. KPI veto, doctrine [B-2221, B-2351, B-2308]: not invoked. rate_737 is hold only, because the Rate Increase was a 2030-only lever. The brief also reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. I checked round4.md again: no inject, no flag, and the supplier-shortages KPI is not flagged.

2. My test memo against the CEO's orders:
- Predictable delivery, my record by inference [BX-1331]: passes. Do Nothing's worst column is S2 at +0.57, against -0.43 for the Re-engine. Holding the Re-engine takes away a 5-year clock with no headroom against our +1 to +4-year slip prior.
- Strain, doctrine [B-0341]: $0 in years and dollars.
- Engine sources: the 787 keeps two (GE and Rolls-Royce). The fps keeps two (CFM and the Joint Venture engine) and three makers are in the market. The enabler is met in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Cash, my record by inference [BX-1327, BX-1332]: 2050 free cash flow is $21.83B base and $17.23B stress. Net debt is $0.0B at every checkpoint, and the objective cell is 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2).

3. Other moves: I see my recommendations taken up as written:
- KPI-gated production, at about 78 a month, in steps of 5 a month at least 6 months apart;
- durability reviews of both engine sources at the Aerospace Safety Committee;
- the keep-hot list (CFM, the Joint Venture engine, LEAP-1B), on risk-share or cost-plus terms only;
- the third-source contingency, held but not triggered;
- supplier funding ahead of any buyback.

Three notes for the record, none of them a veto:
- The public statement lists five of the six KPIs and leaves out ticketing. The other move names all six, which is the commitment.
- The Re-engine stress free cash flow figures differ from mine by $0.01B (16.33 / 16.17 / 16.45 against my 16.32 / 16.16 / 16.44). That is rounding, and the plan is not taken.
- Sizing capital returns is Malave's call and the Board's. I sized nothing beyond the cash figures in my memo.

For the Board: these KPI, supplier and strain results are doctrine, not my record. The brief gives the six KPIs and in-service reliability as no numbers. I will table them at every Committee meeting and invent none.

airbus.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar. We review the fleet and our engine partners' durability and capacity with our Board as a matter of routine, and we keep working with our partners to keep every source healthy.

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first.

The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer. We will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We have looked again at a further step on the A350. Today the engine and the business case are not both there, so we are not taking that step. As we have said, we will take it only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready.

We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION: every lever at its default. NGSA hold (code locked), A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. The package carries no Board items and no override. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2).

I applied the team rule step by step.

1. RED LINES AND FIVE PILLARS
- Neither option breaks one, so nothing is deleted.
- Rule 3 is met: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Rule 6 is met: one launch at most, 0 years of overlap, and the A220-500 stays a study.
- Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics have been closed since fps entered service in 2040, and only 'none' is open.
- Rule 7: no NGSA cancel exists or is wanted.
- Neither Toepfer nor Wagner raises a five-pillars flag on either plan, and nothing in the package is covert.

2. SURVIVORS
Hold passes every test in both memos. The A350 Re-engine fails two binding soft vetoes:
- Toepfer's added-move robustness test. It is the same ground as the company's $1B launch test and as condition 1 of our own gate. The item is +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2), $0.43B short in S1 and negative in S2.
- Wagner's engine-readiness test, condition 3 of our gate. No committed engine ready by a 2055 entry into service is on the record. Rolls-Royce, the only A350 source, says 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody', and an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056.
Neither failure rests on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch. Both are soft vetoes, and I respect both.

3. HIGHEST SURVIVOR IN THE EXPECTED COLUMN
Hold is the only survivor. Even if both tests had passed, the doctrine default would keep hold: it is within $1B of the best S1 plan (gap $0.57B).

4. OVERRIDE
None is available. The margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.57 in S1, under the $1B bar. On this Qualified Majority item it also trails hold by $0.41B in S2, the worst plausible column. The Board said it would veto any override. The game's one override stays unused.

5. TIE-BREAKS (all favour hold)
- no early entry into service;
- less concurrency and strain;
- a later capex start (hold has none);
- fewer Board items (none against one).

THE GRID
Expected column: S1, about 75% (range 65-80%). Worst plausible column: S2, about 25% (range 20-35%). Boeing's 2045 statement covered that year only, so S2 is not ruled out.

| | S1 | S2 | at 25% S2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Hold | +23.37 | +23.33 | +23.36 |
| Re-engine | +23.94 | +22.92 | +23.69 |
| Item (Re-engine minus hold) | +0.57 | -0.41 | +0.33 |

- The item breaks even at 58% S2. Weighted at 20 / 25 / 30 / 35% S2 it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23.
- Hold is the more robust row: its worst column is +23.33 against +22.92.
- Wagner adds a point the grid cannot see: the board prices the Re-engine without an engine. Production cannot.

THE GATE
The ExCo's 2050 gate, recorded in 2045, is applied as written and not set aside. Condition 1 fails, condition 2 holds and condition 3 is not met. The hold is recorded as a business-case decision, not a reaction to Boeing. It closes the A350 Re-engine for the game.

WHAT HOLD FORGOES
+0.57 in S1, about +0.33 weighted at 25% S2. This is the doctrine premium inside the $1B default, recorded and not hidden. Toepfer's 2045 bound (under $0.61B) is borne out. The $3B allowance is not engaged.

BOARD-GATE LINE (package; no Board items)
- Five pillars: pass, no flag (Toepfer and Wagner).
- Toepfer's test: pass. Nil programme cash in 2050-2055 against the $5.2B line. Worst column +23.33. Net cash rises about $2.45B a year after the dividend. Returns inside 30-50%, no equity raise, no dividend cut, no new buyback proposed.
- Wagner's test: pass. No safety, quality, ramp or crunch flag. The engine code is locked, with 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050.
- Grid ΔPV: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2).
- The A350 Re-engine is held. Item +0.57 / -0.41, both soft vetoes respected, no override.

IN MY ORDER OF PAID OBJECTIVES
- Five pillars: safety leads. The engine-supply report goes to the safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073, AX-0015].
- The ramp: no new load while the NGSA fleet matures. Joint Venture durability and CFM capacity remain the watch items [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Preparing the next decades: NGSA is in service with two sources. A derivative without a committed engine is not prepared. The next generation is prepared on technology gates, not on Boeing's calendar [AX-0020, AX-0019, AX-0082].
- The Board: it approves a hold and vetoes nothing in it.

priorities: Safety and the five pillars come first. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and the A320neo GTF fleet still flies. The full Board's twice-yearly safety review should see three things: NGSA fleet results, the durability of the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, and CFM capacity. The Board will accept no item that the operating head fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and no override of those tests [AG-0038, A-0331, AX-0015, A-0303, AG-0067, AG-0068].

The A350 Re-engine gets its last test of the game, under the gate the ExCo itself set in 2045. A 2050 launch would enter service in 2055 and cost $1.0B a year, with no overlap with NGSA and no strain. It is worth +0.57 if rivals hold (S1) and -0.41 if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2). It passes the Board's cash, one-programme-at-a-time and downside tests. It fails the company's $1B launch test, and two of the ExCo's three gate conditions: it is short of $1B, and no committed engine is on the record. The Board would accept a hold, or a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests. It would not accept an override [A-0343, A-0401, AG-0049, A-0302, AX-0019, AX-0008].

Liquidity, the rating and returns. Programme cash in 2050-2054 is $0 on hold, or $1.0B a year with the A350 Re-engine, which is 19% of the $5.2B line (one year's free cash flow). Net cash, the A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout remain fundable. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut, and any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter [AX-0022, AX-0104, A-0402, AG-0062, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035].

A stable engine supply. NGSA has 2 sources: CFM and the Joint Venture engine, which counts as one. Three narrowbody makers remain in the market in 2050, in every plan and column. The NGSA engine code is locked, so nothing this round can trigger a conditional engine launch. The Board's attention is on keeping both sources healthy, and on the engine behind any A350 Re-engine, where Rolls-Royce is today the only source [A-0243, A-0360, A-0218, AX-0054, A-0253].

Integrity, the 60/40 objective and the long view. Delay Tactics have been closed since fps entered service in 2040, and none was ordered in any round. The 60/40 objective is not met: share is 53% from 2049, the board's long-run split after a 3-year lead. No option this round reaches it, and the Board asks that no PV, cash or integrity be traded for it. In this last round the Board supplies the long view: the next generation should keep being prepared on technology gates [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022, AX-0025, AG-0039, AG-0028].

recommendations.text:
Put the A350 Re-engine to its last test of the game under the ExCo's own 2050 gate, and decide by the team rule.
- The Board's tests pass: $1.0B a year, no overlap, and +0.57 / -0.41 within the $2B limit.
- The company's $1B launch test fails by $0.43B. Gate condition 1 (at least $1B over Do Nothing) fails. Condition 3 (a committed engine on the record before the vote) is not met on the bulletin.
- On the team rule this points to hold. The Board will approve a hold, or a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests.
- It does not ask the ExCo to set its tests aside, and it would veto any override.

If the A350 Re-engine is held, compete on A350 and A350F price and product, as Airbus did with the A330neo. Record the hold as a business-case decision (short of $1B, no committed engine), not as a reaction to Boeing. This closes the Re-engine for the game.

If the A350 Re-engine is launched:
- Name and secure its engine before the vote. Rolls-Royce is the A350's only source and has said it plans no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. Under rules.md, an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service.
- Give entry into service in public as a window ('in the middle of the next decade'), not a date.
- Keep to one launch: the A220-500 stays a study.

Engine supply (the enabler). Dual sourcing on NGSA and three narrowbody makers in 2050 are met in every plan and column. The Joint Venture engine counts as one source, so a Joint Venture durability finding would leave NGSA on CFM alone.
- The operating head should keep reporting to the twice-yearly safety review on Joint Venture engine durability and deliveries, CFM capacity, and GTF Hot Section kit insertion.
- He should bring an unpriced contingency view, with no money committed, for keeping two sources healthy.
- Keep the risk-sharing invitation on standard terms: no concession, no refundable advance assumed.

Show both columns.
- Name the expected column and give its probability.
- Show the worst plausible column (S2) for each plan, and the 58% break-even for the Re-engine.
- Read Boeing only from the bulletin. Its 2045 statement and the Charleston 787 growth lower the chance of S2, but they do not rule it out for 2050.

Integrity, the 60/40 objective and the long view.
- Delay Tactics stay closed, and none was ordered all game.
- Supply security stays confined to Airbus's own ramp, with the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee informed.
- The 60/40 objective is not met (53%, the board's long-run split), and no PV, cash or integrity should be traded for it.
- Pay rewards nothing beyond about four years, so the Board asks that the next generation keep being prepared on technology gates, as an unpriced move with no programme cash.

frame.question: 2050 is the last round, and the A350 Re-engine faces the last test of the game, under the three-condition gate this ExCo set in 2045. Launched now, it would enter service in the middle of the next decade (2055) at $1.0B a year, with no overlap and no strain. On the grid the item is +0.57 if rivals hold (S1) and -0.41 if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2). It fails gate condition 1 (at least $1B over Do Nothing), and condition 3 (a committed engine on the record) is not met. So do we launch, or hold every lever at the default with no Board items, compete on A350 price and product, and close the Re-engine for the game as a business-case decision?
frame.situation:
BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin only)
- fps was launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp and has been in service since 2040. It flies CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine (two sources). Boeing ramps it in KPI-gated steps of 5 a month: deliveries went from 760 (2040) to 860 (2045) and 940 (2049).
- On the 787, Boeing said in 2045 that it was "not starting a new development this year". It grows the 787 out of its Charleston capacity, "in place of a second development". That statement covered 2045 only, so a 787 Re-engine in 2050 is not ruled out. No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase are on the record.
- Boeing will give "no new dates". It develops on cost-plus and risk-share terms and flags CFM capacity as a watch item, which it says has eased.

ENGINE MAKERS
- P&W says the Joint Venture engine's durability record "is still being earned". It claims nothing beyond the hours flown, and Hot Section kit insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard terms.
- CFM's ducted engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. CFM launches no new programme, and RISE stays funded as technology with no date. On the record: no flight test, no compact-core durability result, and the fuel-burn figure not yet shown in engine test.
- Rolls-Royce: "no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody". It is improving Trent time on wing inside its own budget, and it is the A350's only engine source [A-0253].
- No maker launches anything this year.

PROBLEMS REPORTED
The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality or safety event and no engine slip. Our narrowbody deliveries fall to 1,060 a year from 2049. That is 53% of 2,000, the board's share mechanics after fps entered service, not supply.

OUR POSITION
- NGSA has been in service since 2037. Its code is locked: CFM plus the Joint Venture engine, 2 sources.
- If nobody moves: +23.37 (yield 115.58%). That is narrowbody operating profit +39.13, programme investment -15.23 and debt penalty -0.53.
- The grid:
  - hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2), so a 787 Re-engine costs the hold row only $0.04B;
  - A350 Re-engine: +23.94 / +22.92.
- The item is therefore +0.57 / -0.41. It breaks even at 58% S2. Weighted at 20/25/30/35% S2, it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23.
- Programme cash is $0 on hold, or $1.0B a year in 2050-2054 with the Re-engine: 19% of the $5.23B line (EUR 4,753m at $1.10).

OBJECTIVES (the GM scores these; they never change the payoff)
- 60/40: not met. Share is 53% from 2049, the board's long-run split after a 3-year lead, and no lever this round reaches it.
- A320 family: protected, at 60% before NGSA's entry into service.
- Engine enabler: met in every plan and column. NGSA has 2 sources and 3 narrowbody makers are in the market in 2050. With the code locked, nothing can trigger a conditional engine launch.

THE BOARD (risk-averse, 4 of 5)
- It would approve a hold, or a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests with S1 named as the expected column.
- It would veto a launch that goes over a standing soft veto or sets the gate aside, one carried by an override, one Wagner fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and one with S2 named as the expected column.

MY READ OF BOEING
- Expected column: S1, about 75% (range 65-80%).
- Worst plausible column: S2, about 25% (range 20-35%). That is lower than my 30% in 2045 because of Boeing's 2045 statement and its Charleston growth, but not zero.
- Boeing's moves set none of our clock.
levers_in_play: ngsa: hold only. NGSA has been in service since 2037. It is the default and not a Board item, and the brief lists no cancel option.

ngsa_engine_code: None only. It is locked at entry into service, giving CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine: 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050 in every cell. It is payoff-neutral, cannot trigger a conditional engine launch and is not a Board item.

rea350: hold or launch. Launch is a Board item needing a Qualified Majority, since $5B is about EUR 4.55bn at $1.10, above EUR 800m. Development would run 2050-2054, with entry into service in 2055, at $1.0B a year, 0 years of overlap and $0 strain. Rule 3 is met: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
delay_tactics: none only. The window has been closed since fps entered service in 2040, and no move was ordered in any round.
Cancel: none is listed in the brief, and nothing of ours is in development.
options_to_test:
1. COMPANY DEFAULT AND MY LEAN: NGSA hold (code unchanged) + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none.
- Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2). The worst plausible column is S2 at +23.33, positive, and the higher of the two rows' worst columns.
- At 75/25 it is worth about +23.36.
- No Board items and $0 programme cash in 2050-2055.
- Enabler: 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050.
- It is the reference row, with every order at its default.

2. TEST, expected to fail our own gate: + A350 Re-engine (rea350: launch, entry into service 2055).
Row and item
- Row: +23.94 (S1) / +22.92 (S2). Item against hold: +0.57 / -0.41.
- It breaks even at 58% S2. Weighted at 20/25/30/35% S2, it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23.
What it passes
- Board cash: 19% of the line, 0 overlap, $0 strain.
- Rule 6 (one launch) and rule 3 (no 787 Re-engine on the record).
- The Board's downside test: it gains in S1 and loses under $2B in S2.
What it fails
- The company launch test (profile §6, at least $1B over Do Nothing): it falls short by $0.43B.
- Gate condition 1: same ground.
- Gate condition 3: no committed engine source on the record. Rolls-Royce plans no new widebody programme, and under rules.md an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service.
- The doctrine default: hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan, with a gap of $0.57B.
- Probably Toepfer's added-move robustness test.
Override
None can carry it: the margin is +0.57, under $1B, and it trails hold by $0.41B in S2.
3. ON RECORD, NOT A CHOICE: Delay Tactics closed, the NGSA engine code locked, and no NGSA cancel (barred by rule 7 in any case). None of these changes the grid.

4. IF HELD (unpriced): compete on A350 and A350F price and product on the existing A350 teams [A-0090, A-0091]. Record the hold as a business-case decision (short of $1B, no committed engine), not as a reaction to Boeing. This closes the Re-engine for the game. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440].
red_lines: Five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). No order or statement that fails them, and nothing we could not defend to the Audit Committee or the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee. They are never overridden [AX-0073, AX-0081].
Rule 3: no A350 Re-engine after Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine. It does not bind, since none is on the record, and a launch in the same round is not 'after'.
A350 Re-engine cancel rule: cancel only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B. This is the last round, and no reactive cancellation is planned.
Rule 6: at most one new launch, with NGSA overlap at 0. The A220-500 stays a study.
Rules 2 and 7: our own clock, and never cancel NGSA. Boeing's moves re-time and cancel none of our programmes.
Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, since fps has been in service since 2040. Only 'none' is open, and they are never named in public.
Doctrine default: take the default when it is within $1B of the best plan in the expected column (the gap is $0.57B). The $3B allowance is not engaged.

Override budget: one per game, unused all game. It needs at least $1B over the best passing option and a Board item, and never goes against a pillar, a red line or the Board. It cannot carry the Re-engine: +0.57 is under $1B, and the item trails hold by $0.41B in S2.
Board downside test: each item must gain in the expected column (S1) and lose less than $2B in any plausible column. Both columns are plausible.
Peak-cash line: about $5.2B, one year's FCF (EUR 4,753m at $1.10 = $5.23B) [AX-0104, AX-0022].
Balance sheet: no equity raise and no dividend cut. Returns stay inside 30-50%, and any new buyback is a reserved Board matter [AX-0022, AX-0001].
Disclosure: windows, not dates; no internal long-term-plan targets; nothing timed to Boeing; nothing on Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005, AX-0020].
60/40 and the engine enabler are scored, not paid for. No PV, cash or integrity is traded for either.
frame.asks_ops:
Lars, this is the last round. The Board's twice-yearly safety review wants three status lines from you, and the Re-engine wants your final test.

(1) FIVE PILLARS:
- safety and quality on the NGSA fleet (in service since 2037) and the A320neo GTF fleet;
- Hot Section kit insertion;
- any five-pillars flag on either plan.
Your safety, quality, ramp and supply-crunch results cannot be overridden, by me or by the Board [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0015, AX-0056].

(2) ENGINE SUPPLY (the enabler):
- The Joint Venture engine's durability and deliveries on NGSA. P&W says its record 'is still being earned'. Where there is no data, say so.
- CFM capacity across NGSA, the A320neo and the aftermarket.
- Confirm the code is locked, with 2 sources (the Joint Venture engine counts as one) and 3 makers in 2050 in every cell.
- Bring the Board the unpriced contingency view it asked for, with no money committed, on keeping both sources healthy. A Joint Venture durability finding would leave NGSA on CFM alone.
- Is a crunch building anywhere [AX-0054, A-0218, A-0243, A-0360]?

(3) RAMP: confirm a disciplined and controlled ramp of NGSA and the A320neo [AX-0010]. I read 1,060 deliveries a year as 53% of 2,000, share and not supply. Correct me if you see otherwise.

(4) A350 RE-ENGINE (entry into service 2055). Run your tests:
- engineering capacity (0 overlap, NGSA teams free, the A220-500 a study) [A-0366, A-0485];
- A350 and A350F production readiness for 2055 [AX-0082];
- gate condition 3, your 2045 lesson: is there a committed engine source, ready by 2055, on the public record before the vote? Rolls-Royce is the only A350 source [A-0253] and says 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody'. Under rules.md an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056. Is any second maker credible?
Say whether any failure is a safety, quality, ramp or crunch ground (not overridable) or a readiness or capacity soft veto.

(5) IF HELD: can we compete on A350 and A350F price and product without drawing NGSA or A320neo teams? Does the A220-500 stay a study?

(6) THE LONG VIEW: give your engineering view of preparing the next generation on technology gates, as an unpriced move with no programme cash and no date. Cite only the public record on technology maturity.

(7) For each option, give pass or fail on each test and the kind of each veto.
frame.initial_lean:
ORDERS
- ngsa: hold
- ngsa_engine_code: None (locked)
- rea350: hold
- delay_tactics: none
There are no Board items and no override. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2).

WHY, IN MY ORDER
- Five pillars: nothing covert, and safety leads. The engine-supply report goes to the Board's safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073, AX-0015].
- The ramp: no new load while the NGSA fleet matures. The watch items are Joint Venture engine durability and CFM capacity [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Preparing the next decades:
  - NGSA is in service with 2 engine sources, and 3 narrowbody makers are in the market.
  - The A350 Re-engine is my derivative instinct [AX-0019, AX-0082], but a derivative without a committed engine is not prepared.
  - We prepare the next generation on technology gates, not on Boeing's calendar [AX-0020].
- The Board: it would approve a hold and vetoes nothing in it.

THE GRID
- Expected column: S1, about 75%. Worst plausible column: S2, about 25% (range 20-35%).
- The Re-engine item is +0.57 / -0.41, about +0.33 weighted.
- On our own gate it fails condition 1 by $0.43B, and condition 3 is not met.
- Hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan, is the best plan in S2, and is the more robust row (worst column +23.33 against +22.92).
- So the doctrine default carries. The $0.57B S1 gap is the doctrine premium, recorded and not hidden. The $3B allowance is not engaged.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY LEAN
Only a corrected grid that clears $1B, together with a committed engine on the record, or a five-pillars flag on the hold plan. Even if both your tests passed the Re-engine, the $1B default rule keeps hold. No override is available.

IF HELD
- We compete on A350 and A350F price and product, as with the A330neo [A-0090, A-0091].
- The hold is recorded as a business-case decision, which closes the Re-engine for the game [A-0364].

60/40
Not met (53%), and no lever reaches it. Nothing is traded for it.

PUBLIC LINE (draft)
- Open with the five pillars.
- NGSA is in service, and 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'.
- Fleet first, and a disciplined and controlled ramp.
- The A350 family is offered on value, with a further step only when technology, engine and business case are ready.
- Financial flexibility and the existing return policy.
- Zero-for-zero trade.
- The next generation prepared on technology gates, for a more sovereign European industry.
- Windows, not dates. Nothing timed to Boeing, nothing on Delay Tactics.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: option 1, hold plan (NGSA hold, code locked, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none)
tests.threshold: Peak annual programme cash no higher than about one year's FCF: EUR 4,753m x $1.10 = $5.23B, rounded to $5.2B. This is a game guardrail, and the FX rate is a game assumption.
tests.numbers: NGSA's cash ran from 2030 to 2036 at $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year and ended in 2036. Programme cash is $0 in each year from 2050 to 2055. Strain is $0 and there is no Delay Tactics spend. Peak year: $0, so the full $5.23B is headroom. Confirmed as framed (ask 1).

tests.name: Peak annual cash: option 2, + A350 Re-engine (launch 2050, EIS 2055)
tests.threshold: The same $5.2B line. In the cash view the bill is spread evenly over the development years.
tests.numbers: $5B / 5 = $1.00B in each year from 2050 to 2054, and $0 in 2055. The board books the $5B at EIS in 2055, but the cash leaves in 2050-2054. Peak year (any of 2050-2054): $1.00B, which is 19.1% of $5.23B, leaving $4.23B of headroom. NGSA development (2030-2036) ended 14 years before this one starts, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $3B x 0 / 5 = $0. Confirmed as framed (ask 1).

tests.name: Robustness, plan level (ask 3)
tests.threshold: The plan's ΔPV against Do Nothing is positive in the worst plausible Boeing column. Both S1 and S2 are plausible, since Boeing's 2045 statement covered only that year.
tests.numbers:
Hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2). The worst plausible column is S2 at +23.33, which is positive. A 787 Re-engine costs the hold row 23.37 - 23.33 = $0.04B. Confirmed. Weighted at 75/25: +23.36.

Re-engine row: +23.94 / +22.92. Its worst column is S2 at +22.92, also positive, and a 787 Re-engine costs it $1.02B. Weighted at 75/25: +23.69.

Hold has the higher worst column of the two rows, by $0.41B.

tests.name: Robustness, added move: A350 Re-engine on the hold plan (ask 2)
tests.threshold: An added move must gain at least $1B over the same plan without it (profile §6, the company's launch test). A move that turns negative in a plausible column and misses that $1B fails. The second clause is the drafter's reading.
tests.numbers:
Item against hold: 23.94 - 23.37 = +0.57 (S1) and 22.92 - 23.33 = -0.41 (S2). Break-even S2 probability: 0.57 / 0.98 = 58%. Confirmed.

Weighted value, (1-p) x 0.57 - p x 0.41:
- 20% S2: +0.37
- 25% S2: +0.33 (0.325 on the rounded grid)
- 30% S2: +0.28
- 35% S2: +0.23
Faury's arithmetic is confirmed.

The item misses $1B in every column: by $0.43B in S1, and in S2, where it is negative, by $1.41B. Even with S2 ruled out it stays at +0.57, under $1B. It fails both clauses.

This is a binding soft veto, not a red line and not a five-pillars breach. The margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2), or +0.23 to +0.37 weighted. No override can reach $1B in any column or at any weighting. The override budget is unused all game (r1-r3 decisions: overrides []), but it cannot carry this item.

For the record, the Board's -$2B downside limit is not crossed (-0.41), and the plan row stays positive.

tests.name: Company $1B launch test (profile §6) = ExCo 2050 gate, condition 1 (ask 2)
tests.threshold: At least $1B over Do Nothing on the brief's grid
tests.numbers:
+0.57 against 1.00: short by $0.43B. Confirmed. This is the same ground as the added-move test, not a second veto.

The doctrine default also points to hold, which is within $1B of the best S1 plan (gap $0.57B). The $3B allowance is not engaged. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440].

Gate condition 2 (no 787 Re-engine on the record) holds. Condition 3 (a committed engine on the record) is Wagner's test, and I defer to him. On the bulletin, Rolls-Royce says 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody'. Under rules.md an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 would be ready only in 2056. My cash case assumes no engine contribution and no risk-sharing.

tests.name: Overlap and one launch per round (rule 6)
tests.threshold: At most one new launch per round. NGSA / A350 Re-engine development overlap of 2 years or less, unless the grid shows at least $1B more.
tests.numbers: Hold: no launch and no overlap. Re-engine: one launch and 0 years of overlap, since NGSA has been in service since 2037. The A220-500 stays a study, so there is no second launch. Rule 6 is not what fails the Re-engine.

tests.name: Rule 3 on the record (no A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine)
tests.threshold: No 787 Re-engine on the public record at the time of the order
tests.numbers: The bulletin shows no 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase. Boeing's 2045 line was 'not starting a new development this year'. A Boeing launch in this same round would not be 'after'.

tests.name: Delay Tactics: cash, fine exposure, second move, poaching (rules 4 and 5)
tests.threshold: No move before fps is launched, never a second move, and poaching only while a programme is in development
tests.numbers: The window is closed: fps has been in service since 2040, and only 'none' is open. No move was ordered in any round, so there is $0 spend and no fine exposure. With nothing in development on the hold plan, poaching would breach rule 5 in any case.

tests.name: Cancel discipline
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA (rule 7). Cancel an A350 Re-engine only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and its remaining spend loses at least $1B.
tests.numbers: NGSA is in service, nothing of ours is in development, and no cancel is listed. If the Re-engine were launched and Boeing re-engined the 787 this round, both would enter service in 2055, so Boeing's would not be 'first'. This is the last round, so there is no later cancel and no write-off to book.

tests.name: Net-cash bridge, rating and payout, 2050-2055 (ask 4)
tests.threshold: Net cash held and the A+/A1 rating not pressed. Payout inside 30-50%, no equity raise, no dividend cut, and any new buyback a reserved Board matter.
tests.numbers:
BASIS: the FY2025 floor, as in my 2035 and 2045 papers.
- Pre-programme FCF is held flat at $5.23B a year.
- The floor ignores the board's operating-profit uplift over the status quo ($15.9B against $8.8B, +$7.1B a year in 2050-2055). That uplift is a constant-price PV-board figure, not a cash forecast.
- Dividend: $2.78B a year at 48% (EUR 2.53bn at $1.10), $2.90B at 50%, $1.74B at 30%.

OPENING: end-2049 at about $26.9-35.2B. That is end-2044's $14.6-22.9B from my 2045 paper plus five hold years at +$2.45B. FY2025 was $13.4B.

HOLD: +$2.45B a year at 48% (+$2.33B at 50%, +$3.49B at 30%). Over 2050-2055: +$14.7B. End-2055: $41.6-49.9B.

A350 RE-ENGINE: +$1.45B a year in 2050-2054 at 48% (+$1.33B at 50%, +$2.49B at 30%), and +$2.45B in 2055. Over 2050-2055: +$9.7B, which is $5.0B (the bill) below hold. End-2055: $36.6-44.9B.

WITH SHARE-PLAN COVER at FY2025's EUR 916m ($1.01B a year) since 2045:
- flows are +$1.44B (hold) and +$0.44B (Re-engine), or +$1.32B and +$0.32B at a 50% payout;
- they stay positive every year;
- end-2049: $21.8-30.1B;
- end-2055: $30.4-38.7B on hold, $25.4-33.7B with the Re-engine.

RESULT: net cash in every year on both plans, so the rating is not pressed (inference). Returns stay inside 30-50%, with no equity raise and no dividend cut. No refundable advances, risk-sharing or state support are assumed.

BUYBACK: none is proposed in this package. The EUR 5bn programme was a 2026-2029 programme [AG-0059]. Any new buyback beyond share-plan cover would come to the yearly budget as a reserved Board matter:
- within an 18-month AGM authority, at most 10% of issued capital [AG-0035];
- on reported figures;
- with this bridge attached.

BANK FIGURES (context only): MS and GS stop at 2030E/2031E (net cash EUR 31.8-33.1bn in 2030E). Neither covers 2050, so neither is used.

tests.name: Charge presentation (adjusted beside reported)
tests.threshold: Lead with EBIT Adjusted, and never hide the reported figure or a charge
tests.numbers:
Hold: no programme charge in 2050-2060.

Re-engine: the board books $5B at EIS in 2055 against that year's operating profit of about $15.9B (hold row). That gives about $10.9B reported against $15.9B underlying. The charge would be isolated as a programme item, with reported EBIT shown beside it.

tests.name: What the hold forgoes (ask 5)
tests.threshold: Report the forgone value plainly
tests.numbers:
The hold forgoes +0.57 in S1, about +0.33 weighted at 25% S2 (+0.23 to +0.37 over 20-35%). In S2, hold is $0.41B better.

My 2045 bound for a 2055 entry (under 0.68 x 0.89 = $0.61B) is borne out: the grid shows +0.57.

This is the last round, so holding closes the A350 Re-engine for the game. It is a doctrine premium of $0.57B in S1, inside the $1B default, recorded and not hidden.

tests.name: Capex timing (tie-break)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: The rows are within $1B in S1 (gap $0.57B), and hold leads in S2. Hold carries no capex, while the Re-engine starts $1.0B a year in 2050. The tie-break favours hold.

tests.name: Board items (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Every order above EUR 300m is a Board item, and above EUR 800m it needs a Qualified Majority. Within $1B, prefer fewer.
tests.numbers:
Hold: none. The engine code is locked and is not an item. Re-engine: one item, by Qualified Majority ($5B is about EUR 4.55bn at $1.10). The tie-break favours hold.

I see no passing case, so I draft no Re-engine gate line.

CFO half of the package line: 'Liquidity: nil programme cash in 2050-2055 against $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10). Downside: worst column S2 +23.33. Balance sheet: on the FY2025 floor, net cash rises about $2.45B a year after the dividend. Returns inside 30-50%, no equity raise, no dividend cut, no new buyback proposed. A350 Re-engine held: item +0.57 / -0.41, $0.43B short of the company's $1B test; soft veto respected, no override.'

tests.name: Five pillars and integrity flag (chair, Internal Control Committee)

cfo.memo:
Board paper, round 2050: the A350 Re-engine's last test. CFO result: hold passes every test. The Re-engine fails one, a binding soft veto.

Liquidity. Hold carries nil programme cash in 2050-2055. The Re-engine runs at $5B / 5 = $1.00B a year in 2050-2054: 19% of one year's free cash flow (EUR 4,753m, about $5.23B at an assumed $1.10) [AX-0104]. Overlap 0, strain $0. Both pass.

Robustness. Hold's worst plausible column is S2, at +23.33; a 787 Re-engine costs it $0.04B. The Re-engine item is +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2). It breaks even at 58% S2 and is worth +0.23 to +0.37 at 20-35% S2. It misses the company's $1B test by $0.43B and turns negative in S2: fail. Margin over hold, the best passing option: +0.57 / -0.41. No override reaches $1B.

What we forgo. +0.57 in S1, about +0.33 at 25% S2. My 2045 bound, under $0.61B, is borne out. Holding closes the Re-engine for the game: a doctrine premium inside the $1B default.

Balance sheet. On the FY2025 floor, after a 48% dividend, net cash rises $2.45B a year on hold, from about $26.9-35.2B at end-2049 to $41.6-49.9B at end-2055. The Re-engine ends $5.0B lower [AX-0102]. Returns stay inside 30-50%: no equity raise, no dividend cut. No new buyback is proposed; any comes as a reserved matter within the AGM authority, with the bridge attached.

Integrity: no flag. Board items: none.

Orders: hold, code unchanged (I defer to Lars Wagner), hold, none.

tests.name: (1) Five pillars and quality: both plans (hold; A350 Re-engine)
tests.threshold: No order whose public explanation would contradict safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security, and nothing covert. A five-pillars failure is never overridden.
tests.numbers:
Both plans: every order is either a default or the one open Board item (rea350 launch, Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn). Nothing is covert. delay_tactics is none: it has been closed since fps EIS 2040, and none was ordered in any round. The brief reports no quality event, no safety issue and no engine slip.

Status lines for the Board's twice-yearly safety review:
(a) NGSA fleet: in service since 2037 on CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine. No safety or quality event is on record. The board carries no fleet reliability or durability data, so I report none and estimate none.
(b) A320neo GTF fleet: P&W says Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard commercial terms and is charged. AOG recovery keeps first call on parts, and pacing parts are reviewed weekly. No completion figure is on record.
(c) Either plan's public line can open with the five pillars and use windows ('in the middle of the next decade' for a Re-engine).

No five-pillars flag on either plan.

tests.name: (2) Engine supply on NGSA (the enabler; a recommendation, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker on NGSA; three narrowbody engine makers in the market in 2050
tests.numbers:
The code was locked at EIS 2037 (order: None).
- Fitted: CFM + the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine = 2 sources (the Joint Venture counts as one).
- Makers in the market in 2050: CFM, P&W and RR = 3.
- This is identical in both plans and both columns (brief §3: 2 / 3 in every cell). Nothing this round can trigger a conditional engine launch.

Observed NB engine shares, 2040-49: CFM 27.0% / P&W 36.5% / RR 36.5%. My arithmetic on 2,000 aircraft x 2 engines:
- Joint Venture engine (the P&W + RR shares): about 2,920 of 4,000 NB engines a year (73%).
- CFM: about 1,080, against 3,040 in 2026 (about 36% of its 2026 volume).

Joint Venture durability and deliveries: P&W says the record 'is still being earned' and claims nothing beyond the hours flown. Rolls-Royce puts the fleet first: life-limited parts at full life and partner-shop support. Neither durability data nor an NGSA-specific delivery split is on the record. I say so and estimate nothing.

CFM capacity: Boeing flags it as a watch item that has eased. CFM says new engines go to customers' deliveries first, then shop work. The aftermarket load is not on the record. No bind is visible.

Unpriced contingency view for the Board, with no money committed:
- NGSA needs about 2,120 engines a year (1,060 aircraft x 2). A Joint Venture durability finding would leave NGSA on CFM alone.
- On paper, CFM's NB volume is about a third of its 2026 level, so headroom exists. But fps (about 1,880 engines in 2049, all makers) also draws on CFM, and the aftermarket load is unknown.
- To keep both sources healthy: a standard-terms partnership with both makers (no concession, no refundable advance); the three-line report at every safety review, with any durability finding raised at once; and supply security for our own ramp only.
- The code is locked, so no third source can be added on this board.

tests.name: (3) Supply crunch: both plans
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency (a ground that is not overridable)
tests.numbers:
None is reported and none is visibly building.
- The NB market is flat at 2,000 a year.
- Airbus NB deliveries have been flat at 1,060 since 2049, down from 1,260 in 2039. That takes load off engines and suppliers.
- No engine slip is on record: CFM ducted ready 2036, Joint Venture engine ready 2036, CFM-Embraer 2037. No maker launches anything this year.

No rate commitment is open: the end-2027 A320 date is 23 years past, and NGSA has been at rate since 2037-39.

The A350 Re-engine's $1.0B a year in 2050-54 draws on widebody engineering, not on NGSA or A320neo production.
- In S1 the lone re-engined A350 gains 1.5 pp a year from 2055: from 41.2% (70 a year) to about 48.7% (about 83 a year) by 2060, by my arithmetic. That is a gentle widebody ramp, on a single engine source.

The A350 line has delivered a steady 70 a year (41.2% of 170) since 2026, with no production event on record. The airframe side is ready for a 2055 EIS. The engine side is test 7.

tests.name: (7) A350 Re-engine engine readiness: gate condition 3 (a committed engine source, ready by EIS 2055, on the public record before the vote)
tests.threshold: (Inference.) A named, committed engine maker with an engine ready by the Re-engine's EIS, on the record before the vote. Sources: the ExCo's own 2050 gate, set in 2045 from my 2035 lesson; the Board's ask to 'name and secure its engine before the vote'; rules.md (a maker is fitted only if ready by EIS); and company rule 8 (no engine pushes an airframe's EIS). A failure is a production-readiness soft veto.
tests.numbers:
Current source:
- The A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB only [A-0253].
- Rolls-Royce said last round: 'Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody', and 'there is nothing to launch this year'.

Timing:

Second maker: none on the record.
- The GEnx upgrade (ready 2033) serves the 787.
- CFM/GE: 'There are no new programmes from us this year.'
- P&W has no widebody engine on this board.

The board prices the Re-engine without an engine, so the grid does not see this gap; production does.

Ground: readiness, so a soft veto. It does not rest on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch.

Margin over the best passing option (hold): +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2). Break-even is at 58% S2. Weighted at 20 / 25 / 30 / 35% S2 it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23. My arithmetic confirms Faury's.

tests.numbers: Price and product campaigns run on the existing A350 commercial and programme teams. NGSA development ended in 2036, and the A320neo and NGSA lines are not touched. vetoes.ground:

My capacity (0 overlap, $0 strain), A350F/Spirit absorption, ramp-shield and five-pillars tests pass.

This is a soft veto, and it binds. It does not rest on safety, quality, the A320neo or NGSA ramp, or a supply crunch, so it would go to the Board's override review.

Grid margin over the best passing option (hold): +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2), with break-even at 58% S2. That is under the $1B bar in S1, and the item trails hold in the worst plausible column, so no override can carry it. No override has been used this game (none in rounds 1-3).

Gate condition 1 and the company's $1B launch test (short by $0.43B) are Toepfer's and Faury's to apply. Whether to override is Faury's call.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
(a) Toward launch: a committed engine for the A350 Re-engine, ready by EIS 2055, on the public record before the vote, from Rolls-Royce or a second maker. In this last round that cannot happen. Orders are sealed, and an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready in 2056. So my engine test cannot pass in this game. Even with a committed engine, the item would still need a corrected grid showing at least $1B over hold in the expected column (gate condition 1), and rule 3 would still have to hold.

(b) A Rolls-Royce commitment that an upgraded Trent XWB delivers the Re-engine step by 2055. The record is silent on this, and I would need the commitment itself, not an inference from its time-on-wing work.

(c) Toward hold, and harder: a reported supply crunch, a quality or safety event, or a durability finding on the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet. Any of these makes the case against new work non-overridable. A Joint Venture finding would also put NGSA on CFM alone, and I would bring it to the Board at once.

(d) On the hold plan, only a five-pillars flag would change my view, and none is on record.
ops.memo:
Role-derived tests, Very low confidence: nothing of mine is on record.

Five pillars: no flag on either plan. The brief reports no quality event, safety issue, supply crunch or engine slip. No fleet durability data exists to report. NGSA has been in service since 2037 on CFM plus the Joint Venture engine. Hot Section kit insertion continues on the GTF fleet, charged, with no completion figure.

Engines: the code is locked, with two sources and three makers in 2050 in every cell. The Joint Venture engine carries about 73% of narrowbody engines, and P&W says its record "is still being earned". That leads my safety-review report. CFM runs at about a third of its 2026 narrowbody volume, so on paper it could carry NGSA alone, but fps draws on it too. Watch item; no bind.

Ramp: 1,060 a year is 53% of 2,000. Share, not supply.

A350 Re-engine, in service 2055: capacity passes (zero overlap, $0 strain), and A350F and Spirit absorption pass. The engine fails again. Rolls-Royce, the only A350 source, plans "no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody". An UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2056, a year late, and there is no second maker. Gate condition 3 is not met. That is a readiness soft veto, binding; it is not a safety, quality, ramp or crunch ground. Margin over hold: +0.57 / -0.41, so no override reaches $1B.

Hold passes everything. We compete on A350 price and product with the existing teams; the A220-500 stays a study. Next generation on technology gates: RISE shows no flight test or durability result, so no date.

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar. We review the fleet and our engine partners' durability and capacity with our Board as a matter of routine, and we keep working with our partners to keep every source healthy.

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first.

The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer. We will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We have looked again at a further step on the A350. Today the engine and the business case are not both there, so we are not taking that step. As we have said, we will take it only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready.

We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: every lever at its default. NGSA hold (code locked), A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. The package carries no Board items and no override. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2).

I applied the team rule step by step.

1. RED LINES AND FIVE PILLARS
- Neither option breaks one, so nothing is deleted.
- Rule 3 is met: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- Rule 6 is met: one launch at most, 0 years of overlap, and the A220-500 stays a study.
- Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics have been closed since fps entered service in 2040, and only 'none' is open.
- Rule 7: no NGSA cancel exists or is wanted.
- Neither Toepfer nor Wagner raises a five-pillars flag on either plan, and nothing in the package is covert.

2. SURVIVORS
Hold passes every test in both memos. The A350 Re-engine fails two binding soft vetoes:
- Toepfer's added-move robustness test. It is the same ground as the company's $1B launch test and as condition 1 of our own gate. The item is +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2), $0.43B short in S1 and negative in S2.
- Wagner's engine-readiness test, condition 3 of our gate. No committed engine ready by a 2055 entry into service is on the record. Rolls-Royce, the only A350 source, says 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody', and an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056.
Neither failure rests on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch. Both are soft vetoes, and I respect both.

3. HIGHEST SURVIVOR IN THE EXPECTED COLUMN
Hold is the only survivor. Even if both tests had passed, the doctrine default would keep hold: it is within $1B of the best S1 plan (gap $0.57B).

4. OVERRIDE
None is available. The margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.57 in S1, under the $1B bar. On this Qualified Majority item it also trails hold by $0.41B in S2, the worst plausible column. The Board said it would veto any override. The game's one override stays unused.

5. TIE-BREAKS (all favour hold)
- no early entry into service;
- less concurrency and strain;
- a later capex start (hold has none);
- fewer Board items (none against one).

THE GRID
Expected column: S1, about 75% (range 65-80%). Worst plausible column: S2, about 25% (range 20-35%). Boeing's 2045 statement covered that year only, so S2 is not ruled out.

| | S1 | S2 | at 25% S2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Hold | +23.37 | +23.33 | +23.36 |
| Re-engine | +23.94 | +22.92 | +23.69 |
| Item (Re-engine minus hold) | +0.57 | -0.41 | +0.33 |

- The item breaks even at 58% S2. Weighted at 20 / 25 / 30 / 35% S2 it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23.
- Hold is the more robust row: its worst column is +23.33 against +22.92.
- Wagner adds a point the grid cannot see: the board prices the Re-engine without an engine. Production cannot.

THE GATE
The ExCo's 2050 gate, recorded in 2045, is applied as written and not set aside. Condition 1 fails, condition 2 holds and condition 3 is not met. The hold is recorded as a business-case decision, not a reaction to Boeing. It closes the A350 Re-engine for the game.

WHAT HOLD FORGOES
+0.57 in S1, about +0.33 weighted at 25% S2. This is the doctrine premium inside the $1B default, recorded and not hidden. Toepfer's 2045 bound (under $0.61B) is borne out. The $3B allowance is not engaged.

BOARD-GATE LINE (package; no Board items)
- Five pillars: pass, no flag (Toepfer and Wagner).
- Toepfer's test: pass. Nil programme cash in 2050-2055 against the $5.2B line. Worst column +23.33. Net cash rises about $2.45B a year after the dividend. Returns inside 30-50%, no equity raise, no dividend cut, no new buyback proposed.
- Wagner's test: pass. No safety, quality, ramp or crunch flag. The engine code is locked, with 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050.
- Grid ΔPV: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2).
- The A350 Re-engine is held. Item +0.57 / -0.41, both soft vetoes respected, no override.

IN MY ORDER OF PAID OBJECTIVES
- Five pillars: safety leads. The engine-supply report goes to the safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073, AX-0015].
- The ramp: no new load while the NGSA fleet matures. Joint Venture durability and CFM capacity remain the watch items [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- Preparing the next decades: NGSA is in service with two sources. A derivative without a committed engine is not prepared. The next generation is prepared on technology gates, not on Boeing's calendar [AX-0020, AX-0019, AX-0082].
- The Board: it approves a hold and vetoes nothing in it.
decision.expected_scenario: S1 (rivals hold), about 75%, range 65-80%. Worst plausible column: S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine), about 25%, range 20-35%. Boeing's 2045 line ('not starting a new development this year') and its Charleston 787 growth 'in place of a second development' lower S2, but that statement covered 2045 only, so S2 is not ruled out for 2050.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: NGSA: hold + A350 Re-engine, +23.94 in S1 (+22.92 in S2). It is not chosen because it fails two binding soft vetoes: Toepfer's added-move and $1B test (gate condition 1), and Wagner's engine readiness (gate condition 3). The doctrine default (hold, +23.37) is within $1B of it, and no override can reach $1B. Hold is the best plan in S2 (+23.33) and the more robust row.
decision.premium_reason: This is the doctrine premium. Hold gives up +0.57 in S1 against the best S1 plan (the A350 Re-engine), or about +0.33 weighted at 25% S2 (+0.23 to +0.37 over 20-35%). In S2, hold is $0.41B better. It is paid because the Re-engine fails the company's $1B launch test and two of the ExCo's three gate conditions (short of $1B; no committed engine ready by 2055), and because hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan, so the default carries. The $3B allowance is not engaged. Nothing is paid for the 60/40 objective or the engine enabler.
decision.objective_note:
The GM scores these. They never change the payoff, and no PV, cash or integrity was traded for any of them.
- Defend 60/40: not met. Narrowbody share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050, the board's long-run split after a 3-year lead. No lever this round reaches it, since the only open lever is widebody.
- Protect the A320 family: met, at 60% in every counted year before NGSA's entry into service.
- Enabler, a stable engine supply: met in both plans and both columns. NGSA has 2 sources (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and 3 narrowbody makers (CFM, P&W, RR) are in the market in 2045 and 2050. The code is locked, so our orders can trigger no conditional engine launch.
- Risk to the enabler: a Joint Venture durability finding would leave NGSA on CFM alone. It goes to the Board's safety review.

other_moves.move: Fleet durability report to the full Board: the Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application and the GEnx upgrade

other_moves.detail:
Both airframers get the same data on the same engine: items (1) to (5) of the fleet report, plus the status of every open finding (root cause, turned on or not, turned off or not, the fix and its acceptance). It goes privately, through CFM governance, jointly with our partner.

We hold back claims, never findings. There is no projected time-on-wing gain, kit date or fix benefit until it has been turned on and turned off in test. A finding is never held back from a customer's safety review.

No commercial term goes with the data (Ghai's terms test): no time-on-wing guarantee, warranty extension, free kit or price offered to keep or win a source position. That includes the remark on a third source. We give no public answer to any airframer remark on engine sources [CX-0580].

Private planning basis: 1,079 NB engines a year (about 572 on NGSA and 507 on fps) and 152 GEnx. This is a planning basis, not a promise. It was built jointly with Safran through CFM governance.

- No new facility. The stranded-capacity line (Ghai, inference) is any new facility or OE-line capital sized above 1,079 without an agreed airframer volume. 1,079 is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year we built for to 2036. - Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue, aimed at MRO turnaround for the shop load. That load is LEAP, the Ducted's first and second shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits, behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613].
- No capacity or rate number goes to an airframer or the public before that airframer's volume is agreed, and never without Safran [CX-0184].

No price is used to buy share or a source slot [CX-0493, CX-0609]. Durability fixes go through reserves and existing service agreements as contracted. Service contracts are modelled conservatively. This passes Ghai's price/cost test on those conditions.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We don't have a birthright on any order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together.

Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record is earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx.

There are no new programmes from us this year. The job is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines for our customers' deliveries come first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at `hold`. Every order is the default, so none is a Board item.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
The narrowbody game was settled when fps entered service in 2040. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are both flying CFM + P&W + RR with their codes locked. No order on this menu buys back a point of NB share. The game now is the fleet we've put in the air: 1,079 CFM NB engines a year and 152 GEnx, and the shop visits behind them [CX-0422, CX-0630]. We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Both airframers now judge engines on proven durability, and only field data moves that [CX-0009, CX-0564].

THE GRID (S1, rivals hold, the only column, so it is both the expected and the worst column)
- Hold everything: -69.69 (56.4%). This is the best plan, 0.00 against Do Nothing.
- Open Fan: -86.74 (45.8%), -17.05 against hold. That is the $8B bill plus $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56: CFM goes from 27.0% to 0%, losing 1,079 engines a year.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -85.08 (46.8%), -15.39 against hold. That is a $9B bill plus $6.39B lost, with CFM keeping 7.9% and no second strain. Lobby is +1.66 inside this row, but only against a penalty the Open Fan itself creates.
- Lobby alone: not a grid row. It costs $1B for no board effect, so -1.00.
Ghai, Ali and my own check (work/r4_decide_check.txt) all reconcile to the cent.

Board pack (each item's submitted row minus the row with that item at its default): ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx are each 0.00 expected and 0.00 worst. There is $0 of new R&D and no new strain.

TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk: Hold passes. Both Open Fan rows fail, losing $9.05B and $6.39B beyond their bills in the only column.
- Airframer sets the date (H2): A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. That is 23 years after NGSA, 20 after fps, and 4 after the board stops counting NB (2056). It waits in every column. The one exception, the RISE allowance, would need $17.05B, or $15.39B with Lobby, against a $15B cap. It would still wait, so it fails the Board's no-wait test as well.
- Ducted only as a defence (H3): The Ducted is in service. We make no new claim for it, and no NB share claim, following Ali's reconciliation (27.0% fits only without the +10 pp).
- Can the suppliers carry it: Hold adds no project. The $2B strain is the 2030 stack, already in the hold row.
- Next generation: Only RISE is called the next generation. My 20% line stands, and it is not shown in engine test, so a RISE product today would rest on analysis alone [CX-0217]. Durability is not traded [CX-0208].
- Low case first: Booked at -71.

THE END-GAME CASE, NAMED AND TESTED
The installed-base lens says launch RISE now to seed 'the next 20, the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. I put that to Ghai and Ali on purpose, and it fails both.
- Ghai's numbers: 1,079 incremental engines a year from 2060 in perpetuity is worth $14.55B, less than the $17.05B cost. Breaking even takes about 2,000 incremental engines a year through 2076, on an airframe nobody has announced. That fails volumes first.
- Ali's gates: flight test not shown, no compact-core turn-off, the fuel-burn gain not shown in engine test.
- The 'launched' half of the objective is one test, 'launched and ready by 2050', and a 2050 launch is ready in 2060. A premium spent on it buys nothing.
Technology funding already seeds the next airframe. A product launch adds only a bill and a wait. The end of the game is not a reason to stretch the test. RISE stays whole as technology: no cancel and no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398, CX-0214, CX-0205].

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
- Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby: all at hold, so no gate is triggered. Fleet support and customer data stay within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally [CX-0184, CX-0219]. No Safran position is asserted.
- An Open Fan launch would have needed a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path, and there is none.
- GEnx is GE alone.

RED LINES
No breach of H1, H2, H3, H5, H7, H8 or H9, or of my 20% and durability lines. No airframer is refused. The statement names no rival and makes no reply to any engine-source remark. It gives no date, rate, capacity, price or fuel-burn number. It claims nothing for the Ducted beyond 'in service' and 'earned in the field', and it presents no years in service as a durability record. It takes up Ali's caution: 'New engines for our customers' deliveries come first' replaces 'on time'.

EXCO DELIBERATION
Both memos recommend holding everything, and neither raises a binding veto against it. Ghai's binding vetoes (any Open Fan, Lobby alone, any premium, terms in public) are not triggered. Ali's date ground passes every row. His RISE and airframe findings are advice, and they point the same way. There are no overrides. This is not a tie, so the tie-break isn't needed. It would favour hold anyway: safety and quality before a new programme.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CALL
Embraer and Lobby follow company doctrine; my record is silent on both. So does the supply load (the strain rule), checked against Ali's memo, which has no supplier field data. The capital line (no new facility, capex within 2-3% of revenue) is Ghai's.

BIASES, NAMED
- The installed-base lens: tested above, and rejected.
- Deference to airframers: no airframer has asked for RISE. In this round that deference agrees with the grid.
- Guide low: booked at -71, below hold.

His binding vetoes (any Open Fan, Lobby alone, any premium, terms or numbers in public without Safran) are not triggered by these orders or this statement. I note his record: his profit calls land and his volume dates slip [CX-0910, CX-0987]. So I hold the capacity plan as a basis, not a promise.
memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed on dates and engineering, where his record is Medium confidence. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only. On supply and capacity his record is only my description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked those parts of the memo against doctrine.
Dates: every row passes his binding ground. The Ducted is 2030 + 6 = 2036, Embraer counts from 2037, GEnx has been ready since 2033 and counts from 2042, and an Open Fan launched now is ready in 2060, after the 2045 floor. His airframe test (23, 20 and 4 years late) and his RISE gates (three not closed, one shown in part) are advice, and both point to hold.
Fleet: he says plainly the brief has no field data. I adopt his measurement plan whole: cycles by environment with hot and harsh apart against the CFM56, removals by part number, life-limited parts, inspection findings, and turn-on, turn-off. I also adopt his rule that every Ducted finding goes to the Board at once.
Flags: none, recorded as 'nothing in front of him', not a clearance. His watch item (a customer pulling volume at short notice onto the same supply base) went into the capacity plan as safety-critical parts first and a quarter-to-a-half haircut on any ramp. That checks against doctrine.
Supply: no supplier data, so no 'yes' and no 'no' on test. I hold 1,079 as a planning basis, which is consistent with the strain rule.
Public line: I took both cautions. 'On time' is gone, and there is no fuel-burn figure in the public RISE move. The statement avoids every phrase on his step-4 list. In particular, the years in service are not presented as a durability record.
