ops.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view on any of the following.
- Fleet data showing a durability shortfall on the Joint Venture engine: removals or short time on wing in hot-and-harsh operation, a fix campaign, or a finding at Boeing's safety committee. Then: fleet first, a dated recovery, and a Committee report at once. If parts are short, I invoke ground 2 against the rate.
- A finding from the 2040 capacity look-back, or an escape: contain first, before anything else.
- UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative proposed for the in-service engine without its own durability programme, or a public 'proven' or time-on-wing claim before the data: I invoke ground 1.
- Joint Venture terms that move the gear or the core: I flag the red line.
- A revised brief offering a Board item: I re-run readiness against each live airframe's EIS before proposing anything but hold.
ops.memo:
Bad number first: I still don't have one. NGSA is in year thirteen of service, fps in year ten. The board shows no fleet hours, removals, fix campaigns, AOG count, pacing-parts count or kit-insertion figure. The look-back on the 2040 capacity has no result on the record. I asked for a date on it in 2045, and the order went out without one. I can't tell you what the quarterly Committee report showed. That's on us.

What is on the record: the engine was ready in 2036, a year ahead of NGSA and four ahead of fps. Both airframers fitted it on their own durability test. My parts passes in 2030, 2035, 2045 and today rest on the board, not on data.

Boeing's line is fair. All of our new single-aisle share rides on one engine, one configuration, one set of life-limited parts and one casting and disk supply. One finding hits both fleets at once. The answer is the data Boeing's safety committee already reviews: reliability, durability and LLP status split by environment, removals against plan, and every fix campaign with a date to finish it. Not price.

Publishing that we share the data passes ground 1, if we write it as our rule and attach no claim. Restating 'learned our lesson' as a commitment measured by fleet data clears my flag.

Orders: hold and hold, the only legal values; neither ground triggered.

My record is one investor day, June 2023, before the recall. The rest is seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet, charged
other_moves.detail: Insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard commercial terms. The kit is charged, not given away, and there are no discounted spares and no concessions [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. The fleet comes first [PX-0080], and AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. This respects Mitchill's conditional ground-3 veto. We publish no insertion percentage, because Eddy has no 2050 figure. No effect on the game board.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture governance: one engine, P&W modules, P&W design authority
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and shares risk and investment, not technology [P-1233]. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules under P&W design authority [P-1744], and design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240]. It is one engine and one support chain [P-1875]. Any configuration change to the in-service engine is not on this board, whether UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative. It would be a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and its own durability programme under Eddy's ground 1. We do not speak for Rolls-Royce. Change from 2045, on Eddy's advice: the geared-IP clause [P-2004] is taken out of public text and kept in the private governance move below.

other_moves.move: Fleet-data rule toward Airbus and Boeing (the fact of the rule only)
other_moves.detail: This is our answer to the 'one source' line, given with product and data and not with price [PX-0055][P-0768]. We publish the rule, not the data and not what the data shows. Time-on-wing, removal and fix-campaign data on the Joint Venture engine go to both airframers as the fleet flies, with no claim beyond the hours flown. It is written as a rule because the board cannot evidence that the 2045 cadence ran (Eddy; Mitchill's advice). It carries no figures and no characterisation such as 'on plan' or 'mature'. Standard commercial terms, with no concession, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee (Mitchill ground 3). It passes Eddy's ground 1 and Mitchill's ground 4. Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062].

other_moves.move: Data pack to both airframers' in-service reviews
Fleet ring-fence, weekly pacing-parts review and a DATED records look-back on the 2040 capacity step
other_moves.detail:
The weekly pacing-parts review [PX-0131] ring-fences the 1,460-a-year rate. Neither the Joint Venture rate nor any Joint Venture engineering may take castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from GTF fleet AOG recovery or from kit insertion. New capacity is qualified before it ships.

The records look-back covers every part made on the capacity added for the 2040 step (990 to 1,460 a year, +47.5% in one year). It now carries a date: its result goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee's next quarterly meeting, and at once on any finding. If it cannot close by then, we say so plainly and give a new date. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062], and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039].

Contain first. If the review or the look-back shows the fleet short, Eddy's ground 2 binds and the rate waits.

other_moves.move: Standing durability and parts report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
other_moves.detail:
Weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, and at once on any escape [PG-0050][P-1360]. The first 2050 report must state in writing what earlier reports showed. Where nothing can be evidenced, it says 'not available' instead of filling the gap.

Contents:
- Joint Venture engine fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122], against the ~1M-hour benchmark [P-0847]. The benchmark surfaces problems; it does not prove durability.
- Removals and time on wing against plan, LLP status, and fix campaigns.
- AOG on both fleets and the GTF fleet.
- The pacing-parts count at the 1,460 rate (the last count was about 30, in 2023 [PX-0123]).
- Kit insertion as a % of the GTF fleet [PX-0116].
- Capacity qualification status and the look-back result.

other_moves.move: Top enterprise risks to the Audit Committee and the full Board
other_moves.detail:
Three entries go into the annual top enterprise risks [PG-0034]:
(1) The Joint Venture engine's in-service durability, with hot-and-harsh operation named.
(2) The capacity added for the 2040 step to 1,460 engines a year.
(3) The concentration of all P&W new NB share (36.5%) on one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply. This is common-mode risk across both airframes.

On Eddy's advice, the lack of fleet data on the record is logged as a control gap.

Value at stake, on Mitchill's numbers:
- +2.39 $B in 2026 PV from deliveries in 2051-56 is still to be earned on the board.
- The board does not count deliveries after 2056 (about $1.1B in 2026 PV), share loss from a durability finding (codes are locked at EIS), an in-service charge (the last one was a $5.4B sales charge), negative engine margin or partner shares.
We book nothing either way.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture technical governance, private clauses
other_moves.detail: P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data, which keeps Rolls-Royce's geared-IP claim closed [P-2004]. This is kept out of public text on Eddy's advice, because in public it reads as a point scored off our partner. Any pressure for UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative is reported to ExCo at once and treated as a new appropriation with its own durability programme. Eddy sees none on the 2050 record.

other_moves.move: Capital-order note to the Finance Committee
other_moves.detail:
Written as an order of priority, not as a 2050 status: the dividend first [PX-0081], then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669]. The dividend never funds an engine.

The analyst baseline runs to 2030E only:
- dividend $5.0-5.6B, covered 2.3-2.4x by FCF;
- net debt 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, back below Mitchill's pre-ASR approximation by about 2028E (inference);
- buybacks $4.0-5.0B.
From 2031 to 2050 the line rests on the board alone, and the note says so.

Lifecycle value is not cash. The 2050 figure is $14.7B against $9.7B nominal, +$5.0B. Of that, about $3.1B is engine price (sales value, not margin) and about $1.9B is aftermarket collected later. Free cash flow from it this year: $0. The extra 500 engines a year likely cost cash first, at a negative engine margin (inference). The 5.4x is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return.

Mitchill's advice is recorded: the Board's ease toward 3 should wait until debt is shown to be held at pre-ASR levels, not just reached. Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B needs a new appropriation through his gate and Finance, with a return case against hold and a buyback.

other_moves.move: Whole-programme close-out against plan, reported to the Board

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. All of our new single-aisle business now rides on one engine, and that engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We have said we learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, not a finding, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement.

Our customers have said plainly where the bar is. An engine joins an aircraft, and stays on it, on proven durability, and any durability finding is a live problem. That is fair, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Our rule is that time on wing, removals and fix campaigns go to both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft, and how many sources it carries, is our customers' decision and theirs to announce.

What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first.

The fleet still comes first. Insertion of the Hot Section durability kit continues across the GTF fleet, charged, on standard commercial terms. Our rules: we review the pacing parts every week, new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us, with containment and a dated recovery. We control what we can control.

On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case.

We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce.
decision.rationale:
CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: gtf2_solo: hold, jv_with_rr: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00. predictions S1 = 1.00, expected_pv_b +8.88, premium_b 0, and the cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap.

NO BOARD ITEM IS LEGAL, AND WHY
- The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready.
- A withdraw is not legal: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is legal only before formation.
- launch and launch_if_selected cannot be ordered: no airframe is waiting to enter service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040).
- So the Board's standing tests (Premature exit, Committed airframe) have nothing to bite on, and Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles were taken.

DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE
- I start from Eddy's proposal, hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same.
- Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds: no new cash; the engine is fitted on both airframes, so it is not unselected; there is no terms order; the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: the engine was ready in 2036, against EIS dates of 2037 and 2040, and the brief shows no live fleet problem.
- Conditional vetoes, all respected in the moves and the statement:
  - Mitchill ground 4: no 'proven', no time-on-wing claim, no published fleet figure, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative value.
  - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged and the answer to Boeing carries no concession.
  - Eddy ground 1: no configuration change without its own durability programme.
  - Eddy ground 2: the ring-fence; the rate waits if the fleet is short.
- Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through the other moves, not the orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- Overrides: none.

ANSWER TO BOEING'S 'ONE SOURCE' LINE
- It is fair, and it is the right test. Eddy calls it common-mode risk: one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply serve both airframes. One finding touches both fleets at once.
- We answer with product and data, not price [PX-0055][P-0768][PX-0100]:
  - a public rule that fleet data goes to both airframers as flown;
  - a private data pack that matches what Boeing's safety committee reviews, split by environment with hot-and-harsh shown separately.
- No concession, discount, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee. Mitchill confirms that ground 3 passes.
- Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062].

WHOLE-PROGRAMME CLOSE-OUT AGAINST PLAN [P-1191] (Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own)
- 2030: launch_if_selected fired on code 7. Expected +0.23 (mine) and -1.72 (his); booked 0.00. Against Do Nothing it was worth +16.20 (mine) and +13.69 (his). The +22.00 S5 column assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine and was never the plan.
- 2035 grid:
  - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37;
  - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88.
  - Expected: +0.39 (mine) and +0.07 (his). Booked: +3.37, with the commit at $0. The outcome was S4, +8.88, so the commit realised +5.51 over hold. The cancel he advised against would have written off $1.67B to save $0.33B, against rows of -32.79 to -11.47.
- 2045 and 2050: expected = booked = +8.88. That is +8.81 over his 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected.
- Return: $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.44x on the board's basis. It beats a buyback at about $0 NPV at the 10% grid rate.
  - It is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return.
  - Against the PV of the phased R&D it is about 10x; we do not book that figure.
- Payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal (cumulative +4.4 against 2.00) and 2041 discounted (+2.15). Cash payback is later and not on the board.
- Cost: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35 (5.6% of the envelope, on his phasing). The fold write-off was $0. There has been no R&D or write-off since 2035, no Joint Venture cash beyond $2B, and no use of the stretch.
- Value split, on my arithmetic confirmed by Mitchill: about +8.43 from deliveries through 2050 and +2.39 from 2051-56 (total +10.82 against the brief's +10.88; the gap is rounding).

WHAT I OWN
(1) The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (his). In a sealed round, Rolls-Royce's conditional commit was as free for it as ours was for us. The order was right because it was weakly dominant (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), not because we read Rolls-Royce well.
(2) The 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan.
(3) The Board's 2035 statement tightening was not taken up. The 2036 date held on the board, which is counter-evidence to my date optimism, not a licence; I state no date this year.
(4) The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot be evidenced.
(5) The 2045 look-back went out undated, against Eddy's advice. It is dated now: the Committee's next quarterly meeting, and at once on any finding.
(6) We still have no fleet data on the board. Eddy says plainly "I don't have it" on hours, removals, campaigns, AOG, pacing parts and kit insertion. His parts passes in every round rested on the board. So we disclose rules and commitments, not claims, and log the gap as a control gap for the Audit Committee.

CAPITAL: dividend, then debt, then buybacks.
- The analyst context runs to 2030E only: the dividend is covered 2.3-2.4x and net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA. Past 2030 the line rests on the board alone, so it is written as an order of priority, not as a 2050 status.
- The $14.7B against $9.7B (2050, nominal) is lifecycle value at engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow.

BIAS CHECK
- Optimism on dates: none stated. The look-back date is a reporting date.
- Architecture loyalty: the test now is time on wing, not the gear.
- Value capture: the kit stays charged, and Boeing gets no concession.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record has no Joint Venture evidence (Low). The following are company doctrine and Eddy's seat inference:
- the Joint Venture governance [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004];
- the Committee cadence;
- the Audit Committee entries.
Applying 'miss a cycle' [PX-0071] and demand visibility [PX-0109] to engines was inference throughout.

READ BACKWARDS, MY QUESTIONS
- Was the demand visible? Yes: two airframers put us on the record.
- Was durability mature at EIS? The board says ready. The data has not shown it yet, and I won't claim it.
- Was it a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010]? On the board, yes: 5.4x, and payback in 2040-41 on lifecycle value.
- Is the dividend safe [PX-0081]? Nothing on this board touches it; past 2030 that rests on the board alone.

memo_weighing.ops:
Weighted on doctrine, with care, and valued most for its candour. Eddy's own record is one event, the June 2023 investor day before the recall, so his Joint Venture, capacity, Committee and data-sharing views are seat doctrine and inference. He says so.

Adopted:
- His proposal, hold/hold. His readiness check passes: ready 2036, a 1-year margin on NGSA and 4 years on fps. He invokes neither ground.
- His plain 'I don't have it' on every fleet figure. It sets the statement: rules and commitments, no numbers.
- His caveat that the board's 'ready' is a schedule rule. Severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs at each EIS are not evidenced, and I say so to the Board.
- His common-mode read of Boeing's line, and his six-item data pack (a)-(f), split by environment.
- Dating the look-back to the Committee's next quarterly meeting. He asked for this in 2045 and we did not do it; that is owned.
- Taking the geared-IP clause out of public text.
- Writing the data cadence as a rule.
- 'with containment and a dated recovery' in place of 'first'.
- Naming the missing fleet data as a control gap, and hot-and-harsh operation, in the Audit Committee entry.

His restatement test passes: 'learned our lesson' now reads as a commitment measured by fleet data, which clears his 2045 flag. His standing conditional vetoes (ground 1 on configuration change and claims; ground 2 on the rate drawing from the fleet) are written into the other moves.

decision.objective_note:
Both parts of the objective are met on the board (brief §2), and $0 of PV is given up this round.
- Restore credibility: a new P&W engine is in service on a new airframe by 2050. The Joint Venture engine, GTF2 by the 2035 fold, has been on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040, under code 7.
- Capitalise on the GTF: ΔPV +8.88 $B, which is ≥ 0, a 5.4x value return on $2.00B of R&D.
Off the board, credibility lasts only as long as the time-on-wing record does, and we have no fleet data on the record. We do not claim the objective in public; the fleet data has to carry it.

cfo.note:
I concur. I re-ran the four grounds on the exact orders, the public statement and the public moves, and none of them is breached.

The orders are gtf2_solo: hold and jv_with_rr: hold, the only legal values in brief §3. Neither is a capital order, and neither goes to the Board.
- **Grid.** There is one row and one column: 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 (108.1%) in S1. That is engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00. Expected, worst and booked are all +8.88, and every part of it is on the public record: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, the engine was ready in 2036, it is fitted on NGSA (2037) and fps (2040), and our NB share has been 36.5% since 2040.
- **Ground 1 (dividend or debt path): not applicable.** There is no new R&D, no write-off and no Joint Venture cash call. The R&D column is '—' for 2036-60, so there is nothing for the envelope test to catch. The capital note sets out the order of priority (dividend, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks) and does not claim a 2050 status.
- **Ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine): pass.** The engine is selected and fitted on both airframes under code 7. No launch can be ordered, and the cancel window closed in 2035.
- **Ground 3 (aggressive terms): pass.** My conditional binding veto is met. The kit is charged on standard commercial terms. The answer to Boeing's 'one source' line is product and data. No answer carries a discount, concession, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee.
- **Ground 4 (booking upside before it is proven): pass.** My conditional binding veto is met:
  - The statement says nothing is proven and makes no time-on-wing claim beyond the hours flown.
  - 'Learned our lesson' now reads as 'a commitment, not a finding'.
  - The statement does not claim the objective and carries no figures.
  - Data sharing is written as our rule, not as a claim that it is already running.
  - 'first' is dropped.
  - Lifecycle value ($14.7B against $9.7B) and the 5.4x appear only in private moves, and both are labelled as not cash.
  - Nothing is booked for a derivative, UltraFan NB content or a Joint Venture cash call.

**Numbers rechecked from the brief's year table**, discounted at 10% to 2026:
- Deliveries through 2050 are worth +8.43 and deliveries in 2051-56 +2.39. The total is +10.82, against the brief's +10.88; the gap is rounding.
- The 2050 delta is +5.0 nominal, or +0.51 in 2026 PV.
- Payback on lifecycle value comes in 2040 nominal (cumulative +4.4 against 2.00) and 2041 discounted (+2.15).
- The return is 10.88 / 2.00 = 5.44x.

The CEO's close-out, Audit Committee entries and capital note all carry these figures correctly.

**Advice, not binding:**

OPERATING SIDE (Watson):
(1) Design authority, stated plainly. On the record P&W holds the gear, the core and GTF2 as its modules under its design authority. It is one engine and one support chain. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network. We hold no module design authority.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] belongs to a later engine under our own design authority, not this one.
(3) Data. Hot-section, life-limited-part and severe-environment fleet data through the joint support agreement, in proportion to our equal 36.5% share of the risk. Without it Watson cannot report durability to the Committee beyond the public record.
(4) Support network. Our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service shops. Induction slots, spares and a spare-engine pool planned jointly ahead of the 2037-40 wave. Any kit goes in at shop visit through these shops.
MONEY SIDE (McCabe):
(5) Work share and revenue share at 36.5% each, matching the equal engine shares. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points of content below half takes about $7.7B off the narrowbody value: at 40% content engine value is about +30.3 and hold about +24.6; at 30%, about +22.6 and +16.9. Service revenue counts as much as build work share.
(6) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Planning figure: half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; worst case about £2.2bn. That anchor comes from a smaller widebody fleet, so it is a planning figure, not a ceiling. Any finding comes to the Board with a fresh number before anything is public.
(7) Cash. Our money stays within the $4B share. No Rolls-Royce money beyond it without the Board.
(8) Configuration. Any UltraFan NB content or merged derivative is a new programme: it comes to the Board on its own return case and its own durability record, as P&W's public terms also require.
(9) Alignment. Who books the service contracts on our 36.5% is to be settled in the note, so the narrowbody float is proven, not assumed. We left IAE for want of alignment; we will not drift there again.

recommendations.text:
Defend the widebody core inside the existing budget, and hold both widebody orders in this last round. Continue Trent time on wing as an unpriced other move: HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life-limited-part life extension, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down.

Airbus says it will take a further A350 step only when 'the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready'. Our part is to keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically, on standard terms, without a programme order. We power the A350 alone, so watch that exposure.

If a Re-engine goes on the record this round, record in `rationale` how we would answer it after the game: an airframe on the record first, the strain shown, and the case made on its own return. We are a long-term business with very long investment cycles. Long-term widebody presence is earned through the fleet we have.

Funding discipline. McCabe should keep reporting each quarter on our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with Pratt & Whitney, against her base of about $1.9-4.3B and her reasonable worst case of about $7.5B ($9B if we carry a retrofit alone). The report should also cover the net LTSA balance, time on wing and any onerous-contract provision.

Our order holds: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, as in 2015, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes to the board before it arises. Gross R&D stays broadly flat.

frame.question:
So, 2050. This is the last round. There is nothing left to launch on the narrowbody, and the question is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054].

Where we stand:
- The Joint Venture formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036, on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040.
- We hold 36.5% of narrowbody engines, 1,460 a year: about 17,533 in our share by end-2049 and 18,993 by end-2050 (brief year table).
- Widebody share is 55.2% in 2050 (58.0% in S3).
- Hold is worth +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.70 in S1-S3.

The question has three parts.
(1) Does the installed fleet turn into durable, profitable aftermarket cash?
- Boeing now says in public that the Joint Venture engine is one of exactly two fps sources, and that any durability finding would make it want a third.
- P&W says the engine's durability record is 'still being earned'.
- So our narrowbody position rests on durability in service, not on a next programme.
- The Trent 1000 is the movie I have seen before [RX-0087, RX-0114].
(2) Does any widebody spend earn its keep beside the narrowbody in the last round? Frankly, no.
- The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62 against hold, and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32.
- Each loses more than its own bill in every column, with a permanent $5B of strain stacked on it.
(3) Is the partnership aligned on terms that protect our cash? The governance note is due now. It covers:
- design authority;
- data on the hot section and life-limited parts;
- retrofit liability;
- work and revenue share against equal 36.5% shares;
- our cash staying within the $4B share.

'I worry about tomorrow's financials' [RX-0125]. We close the game on cash, not on a launch.

Any of five things would change my view.
(1) The grid moves a widebody row inside the caps. For the upgrade, that means no more than $2.00B below hold in every plausible column, which needs about +$5B more engine value. For UltraFan WB, it means within $1.00B of hold, with an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, on the record. Neither can happen on this brief.
(2) RR widebody share heads toward the 50% line, which triggers the franchise test.
(3) Delivered numbers put Joint Venture early-unit or durability costs above the top of my shared base ($4.3B), or a retrofit bill lands. That goes to the Board with a fresh number, and buybacks give way first.
(4) Evidence that our work or revenue share per Joint Venture engine is below half, or that the venture needs RR cash beyond $4B. I would re-price the engine value at about $7.7B per 10 points of content and take it to the Board.
(5) A flying-hour shock that threatens cash breakeven at twice 2019's fall.

Safety first, then the balance sheet. Nothing this round touches either.

I confirm Tufan's weights, 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08, and his numbers. Hold is +32.38, worst column +32.35, premium $0. The upgrade is -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62 against hold, -6.71 weighted, on a $2B bill. UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32, -8.91 weighted, on a $4B bill. Both lose more than their own bill in every column, under any weights. I withhold my co-signature on each.

Capex: £0 of new development at hold. Either widebody item would add about £0.49bn a year, over half of 2030E company-funded R&D.

The number that matters most is not on the grid. Narrowbody is about +38.6 of our +38.07 engine value; widebody is about -0.5. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which holds only if our content and revenue per Joint Venture engine is half. Each 10 points below half takes off about $7.7B, a fifth of the narrowbody value. Work and revenue share at 36.5% each heads the governance note.

Retrofit: plan on £1.1bn, worst case £2.2bn, with cost following design authority. That anchor comes from a smaller widebody fleet: a planning figure, not a ceiling.

Our cash stays within the $4B share. No balance-sheet trigger stands. Buybacks give way first.

Control: own narrowbody money is $5.71B, not met and final. Strain is held at $0.

My record is thin on Joint Venture terms; this is inference. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: In-service durability of the Joint Venture engine (report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee) and the retrofit rule
tests.threshold: Mature in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support able to respond quickly and intervene early (attr.). If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. The board does not model durability.
tests.numbers:
WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS:
- In service on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040.
- Ready in 2036 with no slip.
- No in-service durability event appears on the public record.
- Boeing reviews both fps sources at each Aerospace Safety Committee meeting: 'If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone', and it would want a third source.
- P&W: the durability record is 'still being earned', and it is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet.
- CFM's ducted engine is also earning its record in the field.

OUR EXPOSURE:
- 17,533 engines in our share by end-2049, at an equal share of risk and investment.
- On the board: none. The NGSA code is locked and the fps is in service.
- Off the board: aftermarket cash, a retrofit bill, and our place as one of two fps sources.

WHAT WE CAN AND CANNOT SEE:
- We can see the public record, fleet delivery numbers and our own partner shops.
- We cannot see hot-section or life-limited-part data. The gear, the core and GTF2 are P&W modules under P&W design authority.
- Whether GTF2 carries the GTF Hot Section exposure is not on the record. Severe-environment fleet data is P&W's.
- I claim nothing beyond this.

RETROFIT RULE, on the Trent 1000 model (confirmed):
(1) the Committee hears first, before anything is public;
(2) protect the fleet with inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool;
(3) the design authority issues the kit, inserted at shop visit through the joint partner shops. The Board's precedent is a fleet retrofit within two years;
(4) anything new waits;
(5) McCabe and the governance note set the cost split.
No retrofit or kit date in public.

Civil veto. The team rule makes it binding if triggered. It rests on attributed turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283). Grounds:
(a) An early date. That means any public date for a new programme earlier than launch plus development years: UltraFan WB before 2056 if launched in 2050, or the upgrade counting before 2053. (b) Counting on an engine before its ready year. Examples: UltraFan WB counted against a 2050 Re-engine's 2055 EIS, or an UltraFan-content Joint Venture engine claimed in service.

ops.memo:
The fleet comes first. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036: on NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040, 1,460 engines a year in our share, 17,533 by end-2049. No readiness test applies to this round's orders, and no Civil ground arises at hold.

Durability: the record shows no in-service event, and I claim nothing beyond it. What we can't see is the hot section and the life-limited parts. P&W holds design authority there and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. Boeing has told us the stakes: our engine is one of two fps sources. The governance note must give us that data in proportion to the risk we carry, and the Trent 1000 rule: Committee first, inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool, the design authority's kit through the joint partner shops, anything new waits.

Support: the 2037-40 cohorts are 4,393 engines in our share. The board shows no shortfall. My watch items are shop induction slots, life-limited-part and hot-section spares, and spare engines for severe-environment operators, ahead of the first wave.

Widebody: 55.2% in 2050, 58.0% in S3, above the line. I'd normally back the upgrade, but it's -6.72, and -1.72 even without the strain. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2050 Re-engine's EIS. Hold both; time on wing inside the budget does the job.

Statement clean. Every field at hold.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service
other_moves.detail: The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. We report what the fleet data shows and claim nothing beyond it. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.

other_moves.move: Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson)
Joint Venture governance note to the Board, delivered now (Watson and McCabe)
other_moves.detail:
The note the Board asked for before 2050. Company doctrine (the IAE lesson) and inference: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms.
OPERATING SIDE (Watson):
(1) Design authority, stated plainly. On the record P&W holds the gear, the core and GTF2 as its modules under its design authority. It is one engine and one support chain. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network. We hold no module design authority.
(2) Our technology role. UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] belongs to a later engine under our own design authority, not this one.
(3) Data. Hot-section, life-limited-part and severe-environment fleet data through the joint support agreement, in proportion to our equal 36.5% share of the risk. Without it Watson cannot report durability to the Committee beyond the public record.
(4) Support network. Our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service shops. Induction slots, spares and a spare-engine pool planned jointly ahead of the 2037-40 wave. Any kit goes in at shop visit through these shops.
MONEY SIDE (McCabe):
(5) Work share and revenue share at 36.5% each, matching the equal engine shares. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points of content below half takes about $7.7B off the narrowbody value: at 40% content engine value is about +30.3 and hold about +24.6; at 30%, about +22.6 and +16.9. Service revenue counts as much as build work share.
(6) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Planning figure: half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; worst case about £2.2bn. That anchor comes from a smaller widebody fleet, so it is a planning figure, not a ceiling. Any finding comes to the Board with a fresh number before anything is public.
(7) Cash. Our money stays within the $4B share. No Rolls-Royce money beyond it without the Board.
(8) Configuration. Any UltraFan NB content or merged derivative is a new programme: it comes to the Board on its own return case and its own durability record, as P&W's public terms also require.
(9) Alignment. Who books the service contracts on our 36.5% is to be settled in the note, so the narrowbody float is proven, not assumed. We left IAE for want of alignment; we will not drift there again.

other_moves.move: Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe)
other_moves.detail:
Our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with P&W, held at the top of the base range until actuals exist: about $4.3B (£3.1bn) against a base of about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn). Reasonable worst case about $7.5B (£5.5bn) with a retrofit shared 50/50, or about $9B (£6.7bn) if we carry a retrofit alone. The window rolls forward to the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts.
Also each quarter: the net LTSA balance (no narrowbody float booked until the governance note settles who holds the service contracts), time on wing (no upside booked before it is delivered), and any onerous-contract provision, booked plainly if a Joint Venture contract turns loss-making.
Order: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No balance-sheet trigger stands.

other_moves.move: Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson)
other_moves.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the `t1000_upgrade` order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. We keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically for the A350 family on standard terms, and watch our sole-source exposure there. No dates disclosed.

other_moves.move: Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing
other_moves.detail: Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. Now it has to earn its keep in the fleet. The fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
Every field is at hold. This is my framing proposal, unchanged, and both memos recommend it:
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`
- `jv_with_pw: hold`
- `ultrafan_wb: hold`
- `t1000_upgrade: hold`
None of these is a Board item. Do Nothing on widebody (Trent only) is right because no airframe can use a new widebody engine in time, and neither widebody order earns its bill [RX-0058].

GRID (brief rows, S1 / S2 / S3), weights 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08
- "UltraFan NB: hold": +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.70. Expected +32.38 (+32.385 at the Board's 0.80 / 0.10 / 0.10, +32.42 at McCabe's stress 0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20). Worst column +32.35. Best row in every column.
- "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade": +25.63 / +25.63 / +26.08. Against hold: -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62, so -6.71 weighted. Worst -6.72, 3.4x its $2B bill. Without the $5B strain it is still -1.72 / -1.72 / -1.62. It counts only from 2053, so 2050 widebody share does not move.
- "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB": +23.35 / +23.68 / +24.38. Against hold: -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32, so -8.91 weighted (-8.90 at the Board's weights). Worst -9.00, 2.25x its $4B bill. Without the strain it is -4.00 / -3.67 / -3.32. It would be ready in 2056, a year after a 2050 Re-engine's 2055 EIS.
- Upgrade plus UltraFan WB together: not allowed (exclusive).
The verdict does not depend on the weights: hold is best in every column.

VETO CHECKS
- McCabe: she withholds her co-signature on both `t1000_upgrade: launch` and `ultrafan_wb: launch`, on hurdle and downside. These are binding, and I give neither order. No balance-sheet veto arises: no new money, debt unchanged, no equity, leverage well below about 1.5x.
- Watson: no Civil veto at hold. Nothing is compressed, no early date is disclosed, and no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit needs a support plan. He cleared the draft statement. The one line I added ('We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more') has no date, no terms and no claim of RR module content, so it stays inside his test. He keeps his re-check of the final text.
- No revision is needed. `overrides` is empty.

RED LINES (checked before return)
- McCabe's note that an UltraFan WB launch would also breach 'no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it'. Confirmed and struck: no UltraFan WB launch is ordered.
- Overlap: no UltraFan is in development, so the upgrade rule is not engaged. No Solo stands, so the UltraFan WB-beside-Solo rule is not engaged.
- Strain: none ordered. Control's strain line stays at $0.
- Disclosure: no new programme, retrofit, kit or growth-engine date. Nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates. No Joint Venture terms beyond the record. No claim of RR module technology in the in-service engine.
- Cancel: none is open, and none is needed. No orphan programme stands.
No red-line flag is left unresolved.

PREMIUM: $0, item by item. No doctrine-favoured order is kept against the grid.

WHAT THE GRID DOES NOT SHOW
1. Content per engine. McCabe's rebuild puts about +38.6 of our +38.07 engine value in narrowbody and about -0.5 in widebody. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points below half costs about $7.7B. So work share and revenue share at 36.5% each heads the governance note.
2. Durability. P&W says the record is 'still being earned' and is still inserting its Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet. Boeing says that if the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone. The share risk and the retrofit bill sit off the board. We cannot see the hot-section or life-limited-part data, so getting it is the note's first operating ask. Actually, I've seen this movie before [RX-0087]: the Trent 1000 is the precedent we will not repeat.

IF A RE-ENGINE GOES ON THE RECORD THIS ROUND (orders are sealed, so this is the answer after the game)
- The airframe goes on the record first. For UltraFan WB, that means an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine on which Boeing has named UltraFan.
- The strain is shown: $5B, permanent, beside the Joint Venture.
- The case is made on its own return against hold, inside the caps ($1B for UltraFan WB).
- Readiness is Watson's: UltraFan WB at launch + 6 against the Re-engine's EIS. On this brief, 2056 misses a 2050 Re-engine's 2055 EIS by a year.
- Until then, we defend the widebody through the fleet we have: Trent XWB time on wing and shop-visit cost, on standard terms.

RECORD AND DOCTRINE
- From my record: the cash framing, 'won't do anything not profitable', choices not options.
- Company doctrine and my colleagues' inference, because my record is Low there: the Joint Venture governance asks (the IAE lesson). The cash figures are McCabe's; the readiness and support views are Watson's.

NONE INVOKED. At step 2 I reserved three grounds. I checked each against the final statement, the three public other moves (fleet first, Trent time on wing, commercial terms), the three private moves (Committee report, governance note, McCabe's funding report) and the rationale. All three are clear.

(a) Early date: none.
- The statement's only date is 'formed in 2035', which is on the public record (bulletin: formed 2035, ready 2036).
- 'Its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies' matches the record: NGSA in service since 2037 and fps since 2040, with RR fitted on both.
- The line the CEO added ('We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more') and 'Now it has to earn its keep in the fleet' carry no date and no terms.
- No public text dates a new programme, retrofit, kit or growth engine, or gives a Joint Venture date other than the record's. It says nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates. The public moves say 'No dates', 'No dates disclosed' and 'We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates'.
- 'Keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically for the A350 family' refers to the engine already in service. It names no new engine and no date.

(b) Counting on an engine before its ready year: none.
- The rationale counts the Joint Venture engine from 2036, its ready year on the record.
- Its arithmetic for the held options is correct: the upgrade would count from 2053 (2050 + 3), and UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056 (2050 + 6), a year after a 2050 Re-engine's 2055 EIS. Neither is ordered or counted.
- 'UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet' is about the Trent fleet. It is not a claim of RR module content in the Joint Venture engine. The governance note says plainly that P&W holds design authority over the gear, the core and GTF2.

(c) Support before EIS: does not arise. No narrowbody launch, trigger or commit is ordered, and both EIS dates are past (NGSA 2037, fps 2040).

Good.
